proofCandidates.title: Why AI Compute Comes in Rectangles — Erik Bernhardsson, Modal CEO — Latent Space
proofCandidates.summary: Modal CEO Erik Bernhardsson discussed the company's growth, including a $750 million Series D at a $16B valuation and nearly three billion sandboxes. He explained that GPU demand is irregular, not rectangular, and that sandboxes now account for about a third of revenue. He also noted the risk of GPU prices falling if capacity is locked in.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Warm welcome to Basil Chatha, our newest cohost from the Forward Deployed side of the AI Engineering world! We’ll be ramping up a new show with him and couldn’t pass up an interview with Modal’s CEO Eric on the occasion of their monster Series D! Two years ago, we spoke with Erik Bernhardsson about his vision for truly serverless AI infrastructure: developers should be able to run code without provisioning clusters, predicting load, or paying for idle resources. CTO Akshat then joined us to talk about Modal’s infra primitives and stack to offer those primitives and agent experience. A lot has changed in the past 5 months. Since their $5B series C, Modal now reports it crossed $1 billion in annualized run rate, raised a $750 million Series D at a $16B valuation, and has spun up nearly three billion sandboxes. In this conversation, Erik joins Vibhu to explain the infrastructure and economics behind that growth—and why demand for compute rarely looks like the contracts used to buy it. Watch the full conversation on YouTube → GPU demand isn’t rectangular A typical capacity contract gives a customer a fixed number of GPUs for a fixed period. Plot capacity against time and you get a rectangle. Real workloads behave differently: they grow, spike, and fall throughout the day. Buy enough for the peak and you pay for idle hardware; buy less and you risk missing demand. Erik describes Modal’s bet as a kind of duration transformation: pool demand across thousands of customers, secure capacity underneath, and let each customer use what they need when they need it. The smoother the aggregate demand, the more useful that pool can be. It’s a useful companion to our conversation with SF Compute’s Evan Conrad: Evan focuses on making capacity tradeable; Erik focuses on making it usable in smaller, elastic slices. There is a financial risk on the other side. If a provider locks in capacity at today’s prices and GPU prices later fall, it can be left holding expensive supply. Erik says he doesn’t expect an imminent collapse, but thinks the possibility matters when building the business. Jump to the GPU price discussion → The sandbox that almost didn’t make it Modal launched sandboxes after Erik and cofounder Akshat Bubna noticed that language models could generate code—and that someone would need a place to run it. Early adoption was modest enough that the team discussed shutting the product down. Then coding agents, background agents, and reinforcement learning created new demand. Erik says sandboxes have grown to roughly a third of Modal’s revenue, a result he didn’t predict at launch. That growth also changes what infrastructure has to do. An agent may create an environment, run code, inspect the result, and try again many times. The latency of starting and restoring those environments becomes part of the experience. In our recent interview with Akshat, we explored this shift from developer experience to agent experience; here Erik adds the product and business story. Jump to the sandbox discussion → Fast startup is an infrastructure feature Elasticity only works if capacity can arrive quickly enough to matter. Modal’s serverless GPU write-up describes the machinery: a buffer of available GPUs, a custom filesystem, process checkpointing, and GPU memory snapshots. Those pieces reduce the work needed to bring another model replica online. It is a concrete example of how infrastructure decisions show up in an application’s responsiveness and cost. We also discuss Erik’s path from Spotify’s recommendation system to Modal, how the company buys compute, alternatives to NVIDIA, forward-deployed engineers, and why code review is optional at Modal. Nvidia wins fast-growing AI startup Modal for new central processors
Modal, a cloud-computing startup dedicated to AI development, has partnered with Nvidia to adopt their new Vera chip, transitioning away from Intel and AMD processors. This strategic shift comes after raising $750 million in funding, boosting Modal's valuation to $15.75 billion. The company has also reported substantial revenue growth over the past year and will continue to explore additional hardware options as they arise.
Nvidia has won central processor chip business with another fast-growing AI startup that until now relied entirely on chips from Intel and AMD, an early sign that its push into a market long controlled by those two rivals has traction.
Modal, a cloud-computing startup that rents out computing power to AI developers, said it plans to start using Nvidia's new Vera central processor for the first time for hosting agents, the AI systems that can carry out long-running tasks for human users. Modal until now has run such work only on Intel and AMD chips.

proofCandidates.title: Modal taps Nvidia Vera CPUs after firm's internal tests show 2x throughput over Intel and AMD chips — AI agentic workflows said to favor Arm chips, but firm will keep x86 chips deployed in heterogeneo
proofCandidates.summary: Nvidia's Vera CPUs delivered twice the throughput of AMD and Intel processors in Modal's tests, but Modal will keep x86 chips in a heterogeneous fleet. Modal expects $1 billion in annual revenue within a year, and Nvidia expects Vera sales to generate at least $20 billion this fiscal year.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Nvidia has earned billions selling AI accelerators, but with the emergence of agentic AI, CPUs are going to play a considerably more significant role than before, which creates new opportunities for the company. Reuters reports that Nvidia has secured a major design win with its Vera CPUs with AI cloud provider Modal. According to Modal, preliminary evaluations showed that Vera could deliver twice the throughput of its existing AMD and Intel processors, although the company does not intend to cease using CPUs from its current suppliers.

Modal provides cloud infrastructure that enables AI developers to deploy AI agents that can perform complex operations autonomously over extended periods. Such workloads require substantial CPU resources for software execution, data processing, and other tasks that cannot be efficiently handled by GPUs. Modal currently relies exclusively on AMD and Intel processors for these operations, but its tests indicate that Nvidia's new Vera CPUs could significantly improve performance in its specific workloads. Of course, since Vera is based on an Arm instruction set architecture, Modal's decision to adopt Vera will require substantial modifications to its software. Nevertheless, Modal believes that the potential performance improvements justify the additional engineering effort.

The reported 2x throughput advantage is particularly interesting because agentic AI workloads can involve numerous independent tasks that compete for CPU cores, cache capacity, and memory bandwidth. However, Modal has not disclosed detailed benchmark configurations it used, specific AMD and Intel processor models, or performance-per-watt figures. Consequently, it remains unclear whether Vera's advantage is enabled by advantages of its Arm v9.2-based Olympus CPU cores that can decode and execute up to 10 instructions per cycle, its memory subsystem with 1.2 TB/s of bandwidth, or other architectural characteristics. Also note that tests compared Vera against currently available AMD and Intel processors rather than their upcoming generations that will compete against Vera in the coming years.

Latest Videos From Tom's Hardware Watch full video here:

Since Modal cannot port all of its software to Arm ISA overnight, the company will continue using x86 CPUs from AMD and Intel, according to Modal chief executive Erik Bernhardsson. Rather than sticking to one ISA for everything, Modal intends to operate a heterogeneous server fleet and select the most suitable processors for each workload. Naturally, the company intends to evaluate upcoming AMD and Intel processors once they become available to make its choices in the future.

For Nvidia, the agreement represents a major step toward making Vera a standalone server processor that commands a major share of the server market. The company expects Vera sales to generate at least $20 billion during its current fiscal year and estimates the potential total available market for these CPUs is approximately $200 billion. The company is on track to sell at least four million Vera CPUs in fiscal 2026.

The announcement comes shortly after Modal secured $750 million in financing led by Accel, which valued the company at $15.75 billion. Modal expects its annual revenue to reach $1 billion within the next year. The company's service consumption has increased 3X in the last 12 months, while revenue has surged more than 15 times compared with the previous year, Reuters reports.

proofCandidates.title: Modal Sees A 2x Performance Jump After Moving To NVIDIA’s Vera CPU From Intel & AMD, Says “Vera Gets Better Under Heavy Load”
proofCandidates.summary: Modal moved to NVIDIA's Vera CPUs for its Agentic AI sandboxes, requiring infrastructure changes. Benchmarks show up to 2x task throughput per core over Intel Xeon and over 6x over AMD EPYC at 150 concurrent containers. Vera's high memory bandwidth prevents throttling under load, enabling denser packing.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Modal Sees A 2x Performance Jump After Moving To NVIDIA’s Vera CPU From Intel & AMD, Says “Vera Gets Better Under Heavy Load”

NVIDIA's Vera CPUs give Modal a 2x performance uplift in Agentic AI sandboxes over Intel and AMD CPUs. Modal Had To Make Massive Changes To Move To NVIDIA's Vera CPUs As They Previously Relied on x86 Chips, But The Shift Granted Them A 2x Boost The NVIDIA Vera CPU continues to be changing the market perception of Arm-based CPUs for Agentic AI use cases. Arm itself has highlighted the advantages of its AGI CPUs over x86 options, but NVIDIA's option seems to be quickly becoming the choice for many firms that were previously running an x86 chip. Related Story Intel’s Jeff McVeigh Says Developers Shouldn’t Need Separate Software Paths For x86 CPUs, As AMD Folds Its ZenDNN Optimizations Into oneDNN Modal is one such firm that recently received its first Vera CPU servers at their San Francisco offices. The company has so far relied solely on x86 systems featuring AMD & Intel chips, so the move to an Arm-based ecosystem required changes to the infrastructure & image-built systems. Despite the painstaking changes, Modal terms the move to NVIDIA Vera as very impressive, delivering a 2x increase in AI throughput across Agentic AI sandboxes, and calling it an "incredibly compelling option". In most systems, throughput and latency are a tradeoff. Latency can be defined as the time that elapses from the start to the end of a task.

Throughput is the quantity of completed tasks per unit time. This tests the host system’s ability to concurrently interleave processes and make progress on them all simultaneously. The more densely you pack tasks, the higher the throughput. But once the CPU becomes fully utilized, individual task latency suffers due to contention. In terms of the Modal scheduler, it’s always tempting for us to run at a higher packing density, to squeeze more juice out of the host machines we have, and to offer a higher absolute scale that users can reach. But just as workloads are spiky within their containers, the absolute scale of the containers in our cluster is also spiky, which leaves us at the risk of overpacking host machines. To test NVIDIA Vera, Modal built a set of representative workloads and benchmarks for agentic sandboxes. This involves the development of "Agentless Agent Bench," which hosts a collection of 50 Terminal-Bench oracle solutions and verifiers. The benchmark shows both linear completion and concurrent throughput figures. The first tests showcased a nice improvement over x86 chips, but these were run without any load, essentially making them a pure straight-line latency test. Under load, NVIDIA's Vera CPU becomes a completely different beast. In throughput, Vera offered a 2x increase over an equivalent Intel Xeon "Granite Rapids" chip. This lead comes from the fact that unlike x86 CPUs, Vera doesn't slow down as jobs accumulate but rather rips through each one of them at its original pace. The results speak for themselves: Versus Intel Xeon: Up to 2x the task throughput per core.

Versus AMD EPYC: Over 6x the task throughput at 150 concurrent containers, with 124 logical CPUs enabled on each system. Vera’s killer feature is the ability to hold up under contention. Its high memory bandwidth allows for significantly more container workloads to pack per core, without CPU throttling - which explains why Vera pulls so far ahead of the alternatives in our benchmarks. At added CPU counts, the alternatives hit early throughput plateaus, while Vera continues to improve, suggesting we could push it even further than the node we had access to for benchmarking. Modal’s shift to NVIDIA’s Vera CPUs, despite the significant infrastructure and image-building changes needed to move from x86, delivered a clear 2× throughput boost in Agentic AI sandboxes. Under load, Vera maintains strong performance without the throttling typical of Intel and AMD CPUs, thanks to its high memory bandwidth and ability to pack more concurrent workloads per core. The result is a compelling Arm-based option that scales more effectively for dense, contention-heavy agentic workloads. proofCandidates.title: Modal Plans NVIDIA Vera Rollout for Sandboxes in First Arm Move
proofCandidates.summary: Modal announced plans to roll out NVIDIA's Vera Arm-based CPUs for its Sandboxes, its first departure from an all-x86 fleet. Benchmarks showed up to double the task throughput of an equivalent x86 machine under load. The company will work with NVIDIA and cloud providers to scale the Vera fleet.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Modal said in a company blog post on October 19, 2026 that it plans to roll out support for NVIDIA’s Arm-based Vera CPU to power Modal Sandboxes, the company’s first departure from an all-x86 fleet, after benchmark results it published showed up to double the task throughput of an equivalent x86 machine under load. NVIDIA hand-delivered Modal’s first Vera CPU server to the company’s San Francisco office in the week before the announcement, Modal said. Vera is NVIDIA’s Arm-compatible processor, built for the Vera Rubin GPU platform but also available as a standalone CPU server. Bringing Arm into the fleet would require changes across Modal’s infrastructure and image build system, which the company described as a huge change after a long history of running exclusively x86 machines. Multi-Tenant Noise and Burst Capacity Orchestrating a Sandbox product means running hundreds of concurrent containers and virtual machines on each cloud host, and Modal said the resulting multi-tenant clusters are noisy. Resource usage can be extremely spiky: a sandbox may sit mostly idle while waiting on a language model and then see CPU usage surge 10x above baseline because of an npm install or an expensive grep command. The shape of each workload is only known at runtime, so resource sizing is often a guess, and heterogeneous tenants packed into a single pool of compute create noisy-neighbor problems, where one customer’s behavior degrades another’s performance. Rather than require fixed reservations sized to maximum usage, Modal Sandboxes support bursting, which lets users reserve guaranteed capacity for their P50 usage and trust that padding inside the host node will absorb transient spikes. Modal said the approach has saved users millions of dollars, but acknowledged that it raises exposure to the noisy-neighbor effects that strict limits would otherwise avoid. Modal identified two prevalent Sandbox use cases: background agents, citing Ramp Inspect and agents running on Niteshift, and reinforcement-learning rollouts. Most training setups are still synchronous, the company said, so an entire fanout of CPU-bound rollouts must complete before idle GPUs can move to the next step, which means time saved on CPU is time saved on GPU. For background agents, the company said, faster execution means faster answers and lower CPU time, driving down the cost of goods sold. The Agentless Agent Bench To measure Vera, Modal built and released Agentless Agent Bench, a collection of 50 Terminal-Bench oracle solutions and verifiers with all network calls stripped out, prewarmed in concurrent Docker containers. Modal said building an agentic benchmark is difficult because most of the work done on its sandbox servers is not CPU-bound, so it assembled a concurrent and heterogeneous mix of the tasks agents and reinforcement-learning processes actually perform on the CPU, including compilation, file grepping, git operations and device emulation. According to the public repository, the benchmark is built on the terminal-bench-2.1 task dataset with Dockerfiles ported for Arm compatibility, and a run counts as completed only if the task verifier passes. In serial testing on an unloaded machine, which measures straight-line per-task latency, Modal found Vera was often faster than the other processors tested — Intel GNR, AMD Zen 5, and AWS Graviton 4 and 5 — but not always, and not by a particularly large margin, and the post’s author described being initially skeptical of the results. Under load, Modal reported, the results diverged. The throughput test increases the number of concurrent containers on the machine and loops as many verified task completions as possible in a fixed time. Modal said its early benchmarking runs showed up to double the task throughput on Vera compared with an equivalent x86 GNR machine, while individual task latency measured equal to or lower than on x86. In most systems, throughput and latency trade off as packing density rises until the CPU saturates, but Modal said Vera did not slow down as jobs accumulated and kept completing tasks at its original pace. Modal reported that Vera kept improving as logical CPU counts rose, while the other tested processors hit early throughput plateaus. The physical core boundaries of the tested machines were 128 for Intel GNR, 96 for Graviton and the GNR virtual machine, and 88 for Vera. Because the alternatives plateaued early, Modal said its results suggest it could push Vera even further than the single benchmark node it had access to. The company attributes Vera’s advantage under contention to its high memory bandwidth, which it said allows significantly more container workloads to pack onto each core without CPU throttling. For Modal’s scheduler, that means greater packing density and more forgiving burst protection; for Sandbox users, the company said, it means higher absolute scale and throughput without sacrificing latency. Vera’s Design and Production Status NVIDIA launched Vera on March 16, 2026 at its GTC conference, describing it as a processor purpose-built for agentic AI and reinforcement learning. The chip has 88 custom NVIDIA-designed Olympus cores, each able to run two tasks through a feature NVIDIA calls Spatial Multithreading, and a second-generation low-power memory subsystem built on LPDDR5X that delivers up to 1.2 TB/s of bandwidth. NVIDIA claims Vera delivers results with twice the efficiency and 50% faster than traditional CPUs. At the launch, NVIDIA also introduced a Vera CPU rack integrating 256 liquid-cooled CPUs, which it said can sustain more than 22,500 concurrent CPU environments, each running independently at full performance. NVIDIA said Vera is in full production, with partner availability in the second half of 2026, and named Alibaba Cloud, ByteDance, CoreWeave, Lambda, Nebius, Nscale and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure among the cloud providers planning to deploy the CPU. Modal said it intends to work closely with NVIDIA and cloud providers to scale up its Vera fleet as the rollout proceeds.

Sandboxes are isolated computers where AI agents run code they write. The product makes $300M a year, Modal said last week when it raised $750M at a $15.75B valuation.
Sandbox workloads are hard to plan for, Modal said. An agent may sit idle while it waits for an AI model, then use ten times more computing power during a software install. Hundreds of these run side by side on each server, so one customer’s spike can slow down another’s work.
To test the chip, Modal built a benchmark of 50 coding tasks, such as compiling software and searching files. Run one at a time, Vera was often faster than chips from Intel, AMD and Amazon, but not always, and not by much.
The gap grew when Modal packed the server with containers. Vera kept finishing tasks at the same speed, while rival chips hit a ceiling, Modal said. The company credits Vera’s high memory bandwidth.
That matters for two uses, Modal said: background coding agents and reinforcement learning. In reinforcement learning, expensive GPUs often sit idle until the CPU work finishes.
Nvidia unveiled Vera in March as a CPU built for AI agents, with 88 cores, and has named Anthropic and OpenAI among its first users. Perplexity has said it will run agent work on the chip, after reporting 1.5 times faster coding tasks. Rivals are building up their own sandbox offerings too, with Baseten buying Blaxel in September.
Modal did not say when the Vera-powered sandboxes would reach customers.

News NVIDIA's Vera CPUs Attract Modal as Chip Rivalry Heats Up NVIDIA has won AI cloud startup Modal as a customer for its Vera CPUs. The deal could strengthen NVIDIA's position in the processor market, where Intel and AMD remain major competitors.

Written By: Soham Halder Reviewed By: Pranchal Srivastava









Copied NVIDIA has secured a new customer for its central processing units (CPUs), with AI cloud startup Modal planning to use the company's Vera processors to run AI agents. The deal marks a step forward for NVIDIA as it looks to expand beyond graphics processing units (GPUs) and compete in a market long dominated by Intel and AMD. Modal provides cloud computing power to developers building artificial intelligence applications. Until now, the company has relied on Intel and AMD processors for running AI-agent workloads. Its decision to add NVIDIA's Vera chips suggests the company is gaining ground in the CPU market as demand for AI computing continues to grow. Early Tests Show Higher AI-Agent Performance Modal said initial tests showed NVIDIA's Vera processor could handle twice as much AI-agent work as the Intel and AMD chips it currently uses. The results encouraged the startup to support NVIDIA's design, although integrating the new processors will require significant software changes. AI agents are systems designed to carry out tasks over extended periods, rather than simply responding to individual prompts. They can help users with multi-step tasks, making performance and efficiency important for companies providing AI services. Modal Will Continue Using Intel and AMD Chips Despite the positive test results, Modal is not planning to abandon its existing chip suppliers. Chief Executive Erik Bernhardsson said the company intends to operate a mix of NVIDIA, Intel and AMD processors. This approach will allow Modal to select hardware based on how well it performs each task. Early comparisons included NVIDIA's Vera processor and Intel and AMD chips already on the market. Both rivals are developing newer processors, which could narrow the performance gap when they become available. Modal plans to evaluate those future chips before making further decisions about its hardware mix. Also Read: Volvo Expands NVIDIA Partnership to Bring Hands-Free Driving to Future Cars NVIDIA Targets a USD 200 Billion CPU Market The Modal deal comes as NVIDIA seeks to expand its presence in a processor market it estimates is worth around USD 200 billion. The company told investors it expects to generate at least USD 20 billion in revenue from Vera processor sales this fiscal year. NVIDIA has also identified OpenAI, Anthropic and Oracle as planned users of its new chips, alongside AI startup Perplexity. Winning customers that previously relied on competing processors could help NVIDIA strengthen its market position. Modal's own growth adds weight to the partnership. The startup recently raised USD 750 million in a funding round led by Accel, reaching a valuation of USD 15.75 billion. It expects sales to reach USD 1 billion over the coming year, while reporting that service usage has tripled and revenue has grown more than 15 times year over year. For NVIDIA, the challenge now is turning early performance results into wider adoption. For Modal, using several chip suppliers offers flexibility as AI workloads evolve and newer processors enter the market. AI cloud company Modal has secured $750 million in a Series D funding round. In the company's announcement, it stated that the round gave Modal a $15.75bn post-money valuation.

– Modal Labs

The funding round was led by Accel, with participation from Kleiner Perkins and existing investors including Menlo Ventures, General Catalyst, Redpoint, Lux Capital, Amplify Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures. Every shift in software changes both what people can build and the infrastructure they need to build it. At Modal, we’re designing a new set of building blocks for the next generation of software." Modal offers access to compute through a serverless infrastructure platform. The company has a self-developed storage and compute layer, which it says has enabled it to "achieve outcomes that seem impossible," for example, reportedly enabling users to scale from zero to 1,000 GPUs in minutes without reservations by pooling capacity across "hundreds of data centers around the world." The company does not own/operate data centers, but works with other cloud providers. Currently, it has 13 cloud partners and is a known customer of WhiteFiber, which was founded in 2024 by Bitcoin mining company Bit Digital. proofCandidates.title: Modal Labs Sandboxes Hits $300M Run Rate: Isolated Code Execution Becomes Its Own Market
proofCandidates.summary: Modal Labs crossed $1 billion in annualized run rate and closed a $750 million Series D at a $15.75 billion valuation. Its Sandboxes product, an isolated code execution environment, now generates $300 million in annualized revenue, accounting for 30% of total ARR. The company plans to expand reinforcement learning and post-training infrastructure.
proofCandidates.fullText: AI infrastructure startup Modal has crossed $1 billion in annualized run rate and closed Modal's $750M Series D announcement at a $15.75 billion post-money valuation, cementing its status as New York City's highest-valued private AI infrastructure company — more than tripling a number it had set just five months earlier. The round's headline figure is striking, but the detail that signals a structural shift in the AI stack is buried a few paragraphs into CEO Erik Bernhardsson's October 14 announcement blog post: a product Modal launched in 2023 that almost nobody predicted would become a standalone business — Sandboxes, the company's isolated virtual machine execution environment — has grown into a $300 million annualized revenue line on its own, accounting for roughly 30 percent of Modal's total ARR and powering close to 3 billion sandboxes spun up since launch. That number is not a rounding error or a promotional figure. It is the first public evidence that isolated code execution — the infrastructure layer that lets AI agents run untrusted, dynamically generated code safely — has crossed the threshold from niche feature to billion-dollar market category. Bernhardsson wrote in the announcement: "Just five months ago, when we announced our Series C, I wrote that demand was accelerating. Since then, usage has tripled and we've grown more than 15x year-over-year. We recently crossed $1B in annualized run rate with no sign of slowing down." From $300M to $1B in Five Months When Modal announced its Series C at $4.65 billion in May 2026, it had just crossed $300 million in annualized revenue. In the five months since, usage tripled and revenue grew more than 15 times year over year. The leap from $4.65 billion to $15.75 billion — a 3.4x step-up in under half a year — reflects a market now pricing AI infrastructure companies at premiums that would have looked implausible in any prior software cycle. The $750 million raise brings Modal's cumulative funding past $1.2 billion. Kleiner Perkins joined as a new investor alongside Accel's lead, with returning backers Menlo Ventures, General Catalyst, Redpoint, Lux Capital, Amplify Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures all participating. The near-consensus participation from that group of investors is itself a data point: each of those firms had already evaluated Modal's growth trajectory and chose to increase its exposure. What Modal Actually Does Founded in 2021 and headquartered in New York, Modal lets developers run compute-intensive workloads — AI model training, large language model inference, batch processing, agent pipelines — without managing their own servers. To do it, the company discarded most of the standard cloud software stack and built a custom Rust container runtime from scratch alongside its own file system, image builder, scheduler, and networking layer. That infrastructure draws on spare capacity from a pool now spanning more than 20 clouds, including AWS, Google Cloud, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The result is a platform that can spin up a container in milliseconds and scale GPU workloads elastically from zero to thousands of GPUs in seconds — without the provisioning overhead of traditional cloud infrastructure or the Kubernetes complexity of managing it manually. Modal's core primitive, called Functions, lets a developer write ordinary Python code with a decorator — @app.function() — and have it execute on GPUs anywhere in the capacity pool with a .remote() call. Real-world deployments include image generation with diffusion models, music generation (Suno's AI music platform runs on Modal), LLM inference via open-source serving frameworks including vLLM and SGLang, and large-scale model training runs. Sandboxes: Isolated Code Execution Becomes Its Own Market Perhaps the most editorially significant detail in Bernhardsson's announcement is what the Sandboxes numbers reveal about the AI stack's evolving structure. The product launched in 2023 after Modal's team noticed a pattern: developers were using large language models to generate code that also needed to run, and they needed a safe place to execute it. Sandboxes provide ephemeral, isolated virtual machine environments for running untrusted or dynamically generated code. Infrastructure now supports up to 1 million running concurrently, and the virtual machine layer became generally available with the Series D announcement. Customers including Ramp and Cognition have deployed Sandboxes in production for background agent pipelines; additional customers span AI coding platforms, reinforcement learning researchers, and teams building autonomous agent systems. Sandboxes have grown this fast because AI systems are changing. As agentic AI — models that autonomously plan and execute multi-step tasks using tools, loops, and code — moves from prototype to production deployment, the need for isolated execution environments scales proportionally. Every agentic system that generates and runs code needs a clean, parallel container that cannot interfere with its host or adjacent runs. Reinforcement learning post-training pipelines, which require thousands of simultaneous rollout executions, are the same story at training scale. Modal's ability to spin up and tear down a million concurrent containers positions it as potential default infrastructure for both workload classes. The Founders Behind the Platform Modal was co-founded by CEO Erik Bernhardsson and CTO Akshat Bubna. Bernhardsson, a Swedish engineer who trained in physics at KTH in Stockholm, joined Spotify in 2008 and spent roughly six years there building Spotify's music recommendation engine — including the groundwork for Discover Weekly, Related Artists, and Radio. Along the way he open-sourced two widely adopted infrastructure tools: Luigi and Annoy open-source tools — Luigi being a workflow engine with more than 10,000 GitHub stars, and Annoy an approximate nearest-neighbor library. He later served as CTO of online mortgage lender Better.com, where he ran an engineering organization of roughly 300 people, before founding Modal in 2021. Bubna, Modal's CTO, previously worked as an early engineer at Scale AI, the data infrastructure company. The team has grown past 200 people and operates from offices in New York, San Francisco, and Stockholm. Modal opened a London office in Marble Arch earlier this year with capacity for up to 40 staff. What's Next: Reinforcement Learning and Post-Training Infrastructure Modal has been explicit about where the fresh capital is headed. The company is building dedicated reinforcement learning and post-training products — the techniques used to refine and align AI models after initial pre-training — and plans to expand its multi-node training clusters for customers running large-scale GPU jobs. On the inference side, Modal is expanding Modal Servers, its product for persistent HTTP model serving, and shipping new features for LLM serving efficiency, including Endpoint Candidates. The push into RL and post-training reflects a structural shift in competitive AI development. As frontier model weights from Meta, Mistral, and others become widely available, differentiation for AI product companies is shifting to the post-training layer—custom fine-tuning, reward modeling, and continual learning loops. All of those workflows require elastic, parallel GPU infrastructure at scale, and Modal's architecture is built for exactly that kind of bursty, massively parallel compute demand. A Market Pricing Infrastructure Aggressively Modal's decacorn milestone arrives as its immediate competitive tier is moving equally fast. Inference-serving platform Baseten closed a $1.5 billion Series F at a $13 billion valuation in June 2026. Fireworks AI Series D round — $1.5 billion at a $17.5 billion valuation — closed in July 2026. Modal, however, is positioning itself as a broader platform than pure inference-serving competitors: a single roof covering serverless compute, code execution environments, and training infrastructure — with a developer experience centered on Python rather than infrastructure configuration. Demand for cloud GPU capacity tied to AI workloads continues to outpace what hyperscalers alone can deliver, and infrastructure startups like Modal are filling that gap by aggregating capacity across dozens of providers and removing the operational overhead from engineering teams building on top of them. At $15.75 billion, Modal is currently the highest-valued private company in the AI infrastructure serving space — a distinction that would have been implausible when a 200-person New York startup with a Python-native serverless platform was competing against cloud-native hyperscalers for the same workloads. By the Numbers Metric Figure Series D round size $750M Post-money valuation $15.75B Total funding raised ~$1.2B Annualized run rate (ARR) >$1B ARR growth (YoY) >15x Sandboxes ARR ~$300M Sandboxes spun up (total) ~3 billion Max concurrent sandboxes 1 million Cloud providers in capacity pool 20+ Employees 200+ Series C valuation (May 2026) $4.65B Valuation step-up in 5 months ~3.4x Frequently Asked Questions What is Modal Labs, and how is it different from AWS or Google Cloud? Modal is a serverless compute platform purpose-built for AI workloads. Unlike AWS or Google Cloud, which require teams to provision and manage GPU instances, containers, and schedulers, Modal abstracts all of that behind a Python interface. A developer adds a single decorator to a Python function, and Modal handles everything — spinning up GPUs from a pool of 20+ cloud providers, scaling from zero to thousands of instances in seconds, and tearing down when the job is done. The key architectural difference is that Modal built its own Rust container runtime, file system, image builder, and networking from scratch, enabling sub-second cold starts that traditional cloud orchestration cannot match. What does it mean that Sandboxes is a $300M business, and why does it matter beyond Modal? Sandboxes is Modal's product for running untrusted or dynamically generated code in isolated virtual machine environments. Its growth to $300 million in annualized revenue — accounting for 30 percent of Modal's total ARR — is the first public evidence that isolated code execution has moved from a niche feature to a standalone infrastructure category. The demand driver is agentic AI: systems that autonomously write and execute code at runtime need clean, parallel containers to run that code safely. The same need exists in reinforcement learning post-training, where thousands of simultaneous execution environments are required. Sandboxes' scale suggests this demand is not experimental — it is already a multi-hundred-million-dollar production workload, and growing. Who are Modal's investors and how did the Series D valuation compare to the Series C? Accel led the Accel-led $750M Series D, with Kleiner Perkins joining as a new investor and returning backers Menlo Ventures, General Catalyst, Redpoint, Lux Capital, Amplify Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures all participating. The post-money valuation of $15.75 billion represents a 3.4x step-up from the $4.65 billion valuation set at Modal's Series C in May 2026 — a five-month gap. That pace of valuation appreciation reflects the AI infrastructure market's current pricing dynamics, in which GPU compute platforms with documented revenue trajectories are being valued at multiples that would have been unusual in any prior software cycle. Is Modal planning to go public, and what does the RL and post-training roadmap mean for enterprise customers? Modal has not publicly commented on IPO plans. On the product roadmap, the company's stated priorities — dedicated reinforcement learning infrastructure, expanded multi-node GPU clusters, and new Modal Servers capabilities for persistent LLM serving — indicate that it is targeting the post-training layer of the AI development stack, not just inference. For enterprise customers currently running RL fine-tuning or reward modeling jobs on traditional cloud infrastructure, that roadmap is relevant: it signals that Modal is building for the compute-intensive, massively parallel workloads that define the next wave of AI model development, not just the deployment and serving workflows that define the current one.

This is a weekly feature that runs down the week’s Top 10 announced funding rounds in the U.S. Check out last week’s biggest funding deal roundup here.

Startup investors aren’t exactly hitting pause, but they did scale back on giant rounds this past week, with just two startup financings in the multiple hundreds of millions. The biggest round went to AI infrastructure provider Modal Labs, which picked up $750 million, followed by construction automation unicorn Icon, which secured $200 million. Other sectors that attracted larger rounds this past week included biotech, insurance and AI.

1. Modal Labs, $750M, AI infrastructure: Modal Labs, a provider of cloud infrastructure for AI inference and other applications, secured $750 million in a Series D funding round led by Accel at a $15.75 billion valuation. The New York-headquartered company said it recently exceeded an annual revenue run rate of $1 billion.

2. Icon, $200M, construction tech: Austin-based Icon, a developer of robotic construction systems known for its 3D-printed homes, closed on $200 million in Series D funding led by Baillie Gifford and BlackRock. The company says it is on pace for 4x revenue growth in 2026.

3. Soufflé Therapeutics, $135M, RNA therapies: Boston-based Soufflé Therapeutics, a developer of RNA therapies, raised $135 million in Series B funding led by Juvia Group as part of a large syndicate of investors.

4. Estuary Biotherapeutics, $103M, gene therapies: Menlo Park, California-based Estuary Biotherapeutics, a developer of genetic medicines for patients with serious kidney diseases, launched with $103 million in financing. The funding includes $93 million in a Series A round led by RA Capital Management as well as $10 million in previously undisclosed seed capital.

5. Labelbox, $100M, AI tools: Labelbox, a developer of technology to train and evaluate AI models and to help deploy agents that improve with experience, picked up $100 million in Series E funding. Infinitum Partners led the financing for the 8-year-old, San Francisco-based company.

6. Suki, $90M, health AI: Redwood City, California-based Suki, a provider of AI tools that turn clinical conversations into intelligence for documentation, coding and other healthcare workflows, announced a $90 million Series E financing from backers including Healthier Capital and Crosslink Capital.

7. Abby Care, $82M, caregiver platform: Abby Care, a platform for family members to become certified, paid caregivers and deliver care at home, closed on $82 million in Series C funding, per a Fortune report. Transformation Capital led the financing for the 5-year-old, San Francisco-based startup.

8. Stand, $70M, insurance: Stand, a provider of insurance for homes in areas at higher risk of natural disasters, secured $70 million in Series C funding at a $1 billion valuation. Saga Ventures led the financing for the 3-year-old, San Francisco-based company.

9. Mueon, $65M, semiconductor systems: Mueon Corp., a semiconductor systems company building a modular platform for AI and hyperscale computing, completed a $65 million Series A funding round. Maverick Silicon led the financing for the Portland, Oregon-based company.

10. North.cloud, $60M, AI spend management: New York-based North.cloud, provider of an infrastructure spend intelligence and automation platform, raised $60 million in a Series B round led by PeakSpan Capital.

Methodology

We tracked the largest announced rounds in the Crunchbase database that were raised by U.S.-based companies for the period of Oct. 10-16, 2026. Although most announced rounds are in the database, there may be a small time lag, as some rounds are reported late in the week.

proofCandidates.fullText:
- Modal raised $750M at a $15.75B valuation, led by Accel, with Kleiner Perkins joining.
- The valuation is more than three times the $4.65B set in its May 21 Series C.
- Its run rate passed $1B, and its Sandboxes product alone reached $300M.
Erik Bernhardsson helped build Spotify’s music recommendations, then spent six years as CTO of Better.com, and came away convinced the cloud held developers back. On October 14, the company he founded in 2021, Modal, said it had raised $750M at a $15.75B valuation, led by Accel, less than five months after it was valued at $4.65B.
Kleiner Perkins joined the round, and all of Modal’s existing investors took part, including Menlo Ventures, General Catalyst, Redpoint, Lux Capital, and Bain Capital Ventures.
Modal said usage has tripled since its Series C, has grown more than 15x year on year, and its annualised run rate has crossed $1B.
Bernhardsson’s pitch starts with scarce graphics processing units (GPUs) and large AI models that are slow to load. Developers can work around both on older tools, he wrote, “but you end up in YAML hell and GPU procurement purgatory.”
The sandbox business behind the run rate
Modal, founded in 2021, pools computing capacity from more than 20 cloud providers into one network and lets developers run code on it without managing servers. It built its own file system, container runtime, scheduler, and networking to do that, and it does not run its own data centres.
The sharpest growth is in Sandboxes. Modal launched the product in 2023, when developers began using large language models to write code that needed somewhere isolated to run.
For example, a coding assistant can test a script it just wrote inside a sandbox, away from the customer’s own systems. Sandboxes have since reached a $300M run rate, just under a third of the total, with close to 3 billion sandboxes launched and capacity for 1 million running at once.
Customers include DoorDash, whose AI platform team uses Modal to move apps from experiment to production, Cognition, Ramp, Linear, and Hebbia, which build background agents on it. Runway generates video there, while Physical Intelligence, Generalist AI, and 1X train robots.
Modal says TypeSafe AI’s Jev, which it calls one of the fastest-growing products ever, served 1 trillion tokens, the chunks of text a model reads and writes, on the platform in its first three days.
Bernhardsson, who created the open-source Annoy library for search and recommendations, is chief executive. Co-founder Akshat Bubna, an early engineer at Scale AI, is chief technology officer. Modal has more than 200 staff across New York, San Francisco, and Stockholm, up from more than 120 at the time of the Series C.
How fast the price moved
Modal was valued at $1.1B in September 2025, when it raised an $87M Series B led by Lux Capital. Its $355M Series C followed on May 21 at $4.65B, led by General Catalyst and Redpoint. The Series D at $15.75B is more than 14 times the Series B figure in just over a year.
The Series C came in two tranches, Reuters reported: the first at a $2.5B valuation, the second at $4.65B once more investors came calling. Accel and Menlo Ventures were in the second tranche, so Accel went from first-time investor at $4.65B to leading this round at $15.75B. Modal has raised roughly $1.2B across its disclosed rounds, including a seed round led by Amplify Partners and a $16M Series A in October 2023.
Two investors weighed in on X. Mamoon Hamid, a partner at Kleiner Perkins, wrote that every serious AI team his firm talks to eventually says the same thing: “We run it on Modal.” Lux Capital partner Grace Isford, whose firm led the Series B, wrote that Modal “radically reimagined a seamless developer experience” from the start.
A crowded race for inference
The money is chasing a market that has changed shape. Gartner forecasts worldwide spending on AI-optimised infrastructure-as-a-service of $42B in 2026, up 96%, and expects inference, the running of trained models, to account for $23.3B of it, ahead of $19B for training.
Rivals are raising just as fast. Baseten took $300M at a $5B valuation in January, then a $1.5B Series F at $13B on June 22. Bloomberg reported on September 23 that Baseten and Modal were both in talks to at least double their valuations, with Baseten’s talks at $26B. Together AI raised $800M at $8.3B on July 1, led by Aramco Ventures, and said its annual bookings passed $1.15B in the prior quarter. Fireworks AI raised $1.505B at $17.5B on July 16 and reports a run rate above $1B.
Modal’s valuation is no more than about 16 times its run rate. Fireworks sits at no more than about 17.5 times, and Together AI at roughly seven times its bookings, though the two measures are not the same. While Together AI and Fireworks centre on running and customising open models, Modal describes itself as a set of building blocks, from functions to Sandboxes to training, that developers combine themselves.
The number to watch is Sandboxes. If AI agents keep writing code that needs a safe place to run, a product launched in 2023 could carry more of Modal’s valuation than GPU rental ever did. If the biggest clouds or the model makers build their own sandboxes, a multiple near 16 will be hard to defend.

Modal has crossed $1B in annualized run rate and raised a $750M Series D at a $15.75B post-money valuation [1][1], with usage tripling in just five months since its Series C and 15x year-over-year growth [1][1]. The round, led by Accel with participation from Kleiner Perkins and all existing investors [1], positions Modal to expand its purpose-built AI infrastructure stack into reinforcement learning, post-training, and LLM serving as the AI platforms market approaches $181.3B in 2026 [2]. The company, which built its own file system, container runtime, scheduler, and networking across 20+ clouds [1], serves customers including DoorDash, Cognition, Ramp, Runway, and Physical Intelligence [1]. Modal Hits $1B Run Rate: AI-Native Infrastructure's Breakout Moment Analyst Take: Modal's milestone is not simply a fundraising story. It reflects a structural shift in how enterprises procure and consume AI compute. The company's 15x year-over-year growth [1] arrives as the AI platforms market is forecast to reach $181.3B in 2026 under the base scenario, growing at a 28.7% CAGR through 2030 [2], and Modal is positioning itself to capture a disproportionate share of that expansion. Infrastructure Built for AI, Not Adapted to It Modal's core thesis is that legacy cloud tooling was never designed for AI workloads. The company discarded most of the existing stack and built its own file system, container runtime, scheduler, and networking from scratch, spanning a capacity pool across 20+ clouds [1]. This matters because nearly half of organizations flag high GPU and compute costs as a top adoption barrier [4]. Modal's serverless, on-demand GPU model with no capacity commitment directly addresses that friction. The recent launch of multi-node training with RDMA-connected clusters [1] extends this philosophy into the most demanding workloads, where enterprises previously faced GPU procurement delays and rigid reservation contracts. The AI infrastructure segment is currently led by AWS at 19.1% share, Google Cloud at 14.5%, Microsoft at 13.7%, and CoreWeave at 11.6% [2], illustrating both the scale of the market Modal is entering and the competitive intensity it faces. Sandboxes: The Agentic AI Infrastructure Layer Modal's Sandboxes product has become a bellwether for the agentic AI era. Launched in 2023 to address LLM-generated code execution, it has grown to a $300M annualized run rate on its own [1], with close to 3 billion sandboxes spun up and the ability to scale to a million concurrent executions [1]. The use cases span background agents, reinforcement learning, vibecoding platforms, and code-executing LLM workflows. This growth is structurally supported by a persistent enterprise pain point: 55.4% of AI decision-makers cite AI agent reliability and hallucination management in production as a top adoption challenge [3]. Isolated, scalable sandbox execution directly mitigates that risk by containing agent-generated code in controlled environments. As agentic workflows move from prototype to production, Sandboxes positions Modal as the default execution layer for a broad class of AI applications. Valuation, Syndicate, and Competitive Positioning The $15.75B post-money valuation on $750M raised [1] implies investors are pricing Modal as a platform company, not a GPU reseller. The syndicate, anchored by Accel and joined by Kleiner Perkins alongside existing backers Menlo Ventures, General Catalyst, Redpoint, Lux Capital, Amplify Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures [1], reflects broad institutional conviction in the AI-native infrastructure category. The competitive context is instructive: 63.9% of enterprises currently deploy AI on provider-managed cloud platforms such as AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, and Azure AI Studio [3]. Modal's multi-cloud, developer-first model offers an alternative that trades hyperscaler lock-in for composability and speed. The customer roster, which includes DoorDash, Cognition, Ramp, Runway, and Physical Intelligence [1], spans enterprise software, robotics, drug discovery, and consumer AI, demonstrating that Modal's building-block approach generalizes across verticals rather than serving a single niche. proofCandidates.title: Startup Funding News Today, October 15, 2026: Modal, Labelbox, OMass Therapeutics, Skeleton Technologies & More
proofCandidates.summary: Over $1.51 billion in funding flowed into 10 startups over 24 hours, led by Modal's $750 million Series D at a $15.75 billion valuation. OMass Therapeutics raised $310 million for hormonal and autoimmune treatments, while Skeleton Technologies secured over $100 million in Siemens-led financing. The activity reflects investor focus on AI infrastructure and specialized technologies.
proofCandidates.fullText:
0 Shares

More than $1.51 billion in newly announced funding transactions flowed into 10 major startups over the past 24 hours, alongside a separate €50 million investment in France. The biggest deals reveal a venture market financing two very different priorities: the infrastructure needed to run artificial intelligence at scale and specialized technologies that can solve expensive problems in healthcare, manufacturing, energy, and enterprise operations. San Francisco-based Modal led the day’s funding activity with a $750 million Series D at a $15.75 billion valuation, after reporting that its annualized revenue run rate surpassed $1 billion. Oxford biotech startup OMass Therapeutics secured $310 million to advance experimental treatments for hormonal and autoimmune diseases. Meanwhile, European energy-storage company Skeleton Technologies raised more than $100 million in Siemens-led financing, becoming a unicorn as it expands into the U.S. AI data center market. The activity extends across several layers of the AI economy. Salience Labs raised $125 million to commercialize optical networking chips that connect increasingly large GPU clusters. Labelbox announced more than $100 million in financing for reinforcement learning and enterprise AI agents. Harmonic Security secured $50 million to address the security risks created by employee AI use, while Duvo raised $32 million to automate operational processes across retailers and consumer-goods companies. Beyond AI software, India’s Scimplify raised $25 million to expand specialty-chemical and critical-materials production, with Hitachi Ventures leading the investment. France’s Dougs secured €50 million to accelerate AI-based accounting services. Boston-based Tamr raised $21 million to improve the fragmented enterprise data that increasingly autonomous AI systems depend on. The broader signal is that investors are financing the systems that make AI commercially useful, not just the models themselves. That includes computing capacity, optical networking, energy management, reliable data, security controls, and industry-specific execution. The 10 selected transactions represent more than $1.513 billion in disclosed dollar-denominated financing, plus €50 million. This is a headline transaction total, not a pure equity total: Labelbox’s financing includes a credit facility, while Skeleton’s transaction has not been fully broken down between primary investment and possible secondary share purchases. Those distinctions matter when measuring how much new capital actually enters startup balance sheets. The Macro Environment: AI Infrastructure Spending Meets a Growing Demand for Financial Discipline The latest funding activity arrives as venture investors confront an increasingly complicated AI economy. Demand for AI computing continues to grow, but the financial requirements of building and operating that infrastructure are becoming harder to ignore. GPU clusters require enormous capital commitments, substantial electricity supplies, specialized networking, and increasingly sophisticated workload-management systems. That creates opportunities for companies such as Modal, Salience Labs, and Skeleton Technologies. Each addresses a different constraint in the same market: Modal provides computing infrastructure developers can access without managing their own GPU clusters; Salience is developing optical switches to improve communication between processors; and Skeleton is building energy-storage systems designed to manage sudden fluctuations in data-center electricity demand. The distinction matters because AI infrastructure economics extend far beyond GPU prices. A data center can own expensive accelerators and still operate inefficiently because of networking bottlenecks, power fluctuations, poor utilization, or software overhead. Growing evidence also suggests public-market investors are becoming more sensitive to those costs. Shares of AI cloud provider CoreWeave fell sharply on October 14 amid concerns about borrowing costs and the sustainability of debt-financed infrastructure expansion. Financial Times reporting has also highlighted a slowdown in AI-related debt issuance as lenders become more selective. That does not mean private investors are abandoning AI infrastructure. Modal’s $750 million financing shows strong, ongoing demand for businesses that can turn compute into commercial revenue. But it suggests investors may increasingly distinguish between companies with demonstrated customer demand and infrastructure projects whose financial returns depend on uncertain future utilization. Outside computing infrastructure, OMass Therapeutics and Scimplify show that substantial capital remains available for difficult scientific and industrial problems. OMass is financing clinical development, where success ultimately depends on generating convincing evidence that experimental medicines work safely in patients. Scimplify is building a distributed manufacturing network for chemicals and critical materials, where customer qualification and production consistency determine commercial value. Those risks differ significantly from software economics. Yet both investments reflect a willingness to fund businesses whose capabilities require years of research, specialized facilities, regulatory expertise, and operating experience. The day’s enterprise software rounds introduce another important theme: AI is moving from experimentation into operational responsibility. Labelbox, Harmonic Security, Duvo, Tamr, and Dougs address different consequences of that transition, from reinforcement learning and agent execution to data accuracy, security, and regulated professional services. Together, the announcements suggest investors are looking beyond whether AI can perform a task. They increasingly want to know whether companies can deploy it reliably, measure its performance, control its risks, and generate durable revenue. Modal raises $750M in funding to expand AI infrastructure as annualized revenue run rate tops $1B San Francisco-based Modal raised $750 million in Series D financing at a $15.75 billion post-money valuation, led by Accel. Kleiner Perkins joined the investor base, while existing investors Menlo Ventures, General Catalyst, Redpoint, Lux Capital, Amplify Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures participated. The financing follows a $355 million Series C announced five months earlier. Modal disclosed the latest round on October 14 alongside a major operating milestone: the company says its annualized revenue run rate has surpassed $1 billion, with usage tripling since May and year-over-year growth exceeding 15x. Founded by Erik Bernhardsson, Modal provides cloud infrastructure designed around workloads that increasingly define AI development and deployment. Its platform supports model inference, training, reinforcement learning, and isolated computing environments in which AI agents can execute code. Instead of requiring developers to manage GPU servers, container infrastructure, scheduling systems, and networking, Modal provides software interfaces that let developers allocate computing resources as needed. The company says its infrastructure spans more than 20 cloud providers. Customers include DoorDash, Cognition, Ramp, Linear, Hebbia, Runway, and companies developing robotics and drug-discovery applications. A billion-dollar run rate changes the investment case Modal’s financial milestone is important, but the terminology deserves attention. Annualized revenue run rate is not the same as annual recurring revenue. A run rate extrapolates current revenue activity into an annual figure. It does not necessarily represent contractual commitments that customers will maintain for the next 12 months. That distinction matters most for usage-based infrastructure businesses, where customer spending can fluctuate with workloads and demand. Modal also reports that its Sandboxes product, which provides isolated environments for executing code, has reached a $300 million annualized run rate. The product has become especially relevant as coding agents generate and execute more software. For investors, Modal represents a bet that the next major software infrastructure category will be built around AI workloads rather than traditional application hosting. Its competitive position depends on developer experience, workload efficiency, reliability, pricing, and the ability to manage computing capacity across different providers. However, the company faces substantial competition from established cloud platforms and specialized AI infrastructure providers. The biggest question is whether its software architecture can maintain attractive margins as customers demand lower inference costs and greater computing capacity. Funding Details Startup: Modal

Investors: Accel, Kleiner Perkins, Menlo Ventures, General Catalyst, Redpoint, Lux Capital, Amplify Partners, Bain Capital Ventures

Valuation: $15.75 billion post-money OMass Therapeutics raises $310M in funding to advance treatments for hormonal and autoimmune diseases Oxford-based OMass Therapeutics raised $310 million (£230 million) in an oversubscribed Series C financing, co-led by Bain Capital Life Sciences, Forbion, and Novo Holdings. Additional investors include Janus Henderson Investors, SV Health Investors, and Jefferson Life Sciences. Existing shareholders Syncona, Oxford Science Enterprises, GV, Northpond Ventures, Sanofi Ventures, British Business Bank, and the University of Oxford also participated. OMass is a biotechnology company developing small-molecule medicines for diseases involving difficult biological targets. The company originated from research conducted in Professor Dame Carol Robinson’s laboratory at the University of Oxford. Its drug-discovery platform combines native mass spectrometry, specialized biochemistry, and chemistry techniques to study proteins and their interactions in biologically relevant environments. The goal is to identify medicines that can act on targets that have historically been difficult to address. Investors are financing clinical evidence, not simply scientific discovery The largest portion of OMass’s new financing will support development of OMS1620, an experimental medicine targeting the melanocortin-2 receptor. The company is developing the drug for congenital adrenal hyperplasia and ACTH-dependent Cushing’s syndrome, conditions involving abnormal hormone regulation. OMass plans to advance the medicine through Phase 2 clinical development. It will also use the financing to support an experimental SLC15A4 inhibitor intended for lupus and other diseases associated with abnormal immune signaling. The investment is significant because OMass is moving toward clinical milestones that could establish whether its scientific approach produces meaningful therapeutic benefits. That creates a different risk profile from AI software. A promising discovery platform can identify potential medicines, but clinical trials must establish safety and efficacy in patients. Even substantial financing cannot eliminate that uncertainty. The participation of Bain Capital Life Sciences, Forbion, Novo Holdings, and established biotechnology investors indicates confidence in the company’s pipeline and research approach. Still, the next material valuation events will likely depend on clinical data rather than funding announcements. For founders, OMass illustrates the importance of financing long-duration scientific programs around specific technical milestones. For investors, it represents a bet that differentiated biology can support valuable medicines even in a market where clinical development remains expensive and uncertain. Valuation: Not disclosed Salience Labs raises $125M in funding to scale optical networking chips for AI data centers Oxford-based Salience Labs raised $125 million in Series B financing led by Bullhound Capital. AMD Ventures, Intel Capital, SBI Group, Hudson River Trading, and British Business Bank joined the round. Existing shareholders Applied Ventures, Oxford Science Enterprises, Cambridge Innovation Capital, and Silicon Catalyst Ventures also participated. Salience develops photonic chips designed to improve communication inside AI data centers. The technology addresses a problem that becomes more significant as computing clusters grow. Thousands of GPUs may need to communicate across multiple racks while training or running increasingly complex AI models. Traditional electrical networking systems can introduce limitations involving bandwidth, latency, energy consumption, and the cost of moving data. Salience is developing optical circuit switches that use light to connect computing resources. Its architecture is designed to improve connectivity while reducing overhead associated with conventional switching infrastructure. AI computing is becoming a networking problem Salience recently demonstrated a 64-port optical circuit switch at ECOC 2026. The company plans to develop larger 128-port and 256-port products while expanding manufacturing capabilities. Its technology draws on more than a decade of research associated with the University of Oxford and the University of Münster. The investment’s strategic significance is reinforced by AMD Ventures and Intel Capital’s participation. Both investors operate in industries directly affected by the growing complexity of AI computing infrastructure. For investors, Salience offers exposure to AI growth without requiring the company to compete in the GPU market itself. As computing clusters grow, the network connecting processors can influence overall system performance and cost. However, optical networking technologies must meet demanding commercial requirements. Salience will need to demonstrate manufacturing yields, reliability, integration with existing infrastructure, and measurable economic advantages. The company also faces competition from established networking vendors and other photonics startups. Its ability to move from a successful demonstration into high-volume production will determine whether the technology becomes a commercially significant part of AI infrastructure. Valuation: Not disclosed Skeleton Technologies secures over $100M in Siemens-led investment to expand AI data center energy systems Estonian energy-storage company Skeleton Technologies secured more than $100 million in Siemens-led financing, valuing it at over $1 billion. The company disclosed the investment on October 14, alongside a strategic partnership with Siemens focused on AI data center infrastructure. The exact financing amount was not disclosed. Skeleton described the transaction as a nine-digit investment, while Bloomberg reported it exceeded $100 million. The transaction includes a broader strategic relationship involving Siemens’s investment and rights to commercialize Skeleton technology. A separate shareholder disclosure also identified a partial secondary stake sale to Siemens, meaning the precise amount of fresh primary capital cannot be determined from the public announcements. Skeleton develops energy-storage systems based on supercapacitors and its proprietary Curved Graphene material. Unlike conventional batteries, which are designed primarily to store large amounts of energy for extended periods, supercapacitors can respond extremely quickly to changing power demands. That capability is becoming relevant to AI data centers. GPU clusters can shift between operating states in milliseconds, creating abrupt changes in electricity consumption. Those fluctuations can stress electrical infrastructure and complicate efficient operation of large computing systems. Skeleton’s products are designed to manage rapid power changes close to computing workloads. Siemens is buying access to a data center infrastructure category Skeleton says its technology can deliver energy savings of up to 40% in certain applications and improve GPU performance by double-digit percentages. Those are company-reported performance claims, not independently established results across all AI data centers. The Siemens partnership matters because it offers a potential route into major industrial and hyperscale infrastructure projects. Siemens plans to integrate Skeleton’s products into its broader electrical infrastructure offering, and the companies are collaborating on AI data center technologies. Skeleton intends to invest more than $200 million in manufacturing expansion and research activities in Silicon Valley. That figure represents planned expenditure, not the amount Siemens is newly investing. The company is also planning U.S. manufacturing capacity that would support production from energy-storage cells through complete systems. For investors, Skeleton represents a way to participate in AI infrastructure growth through electricity management. Its competitive advantage may depend more on material science, manufacturing capability, system integration, and customer relationships than on software alone. Remaining questions include commercial margins, manufacturing expansion costs, customer concentration, and whether performance improvements translate into attractive economics for data center operators. Valuation: More than $1 billion Labelbox raises over $100M in funding to expand reinforcement learning and enterprise AI agents San Francisco-based Labelbox announced more than $100 million in Series E financing, led by Infinitum Partners. Wipro Ventures, Andreessen Horowitz, B Capital, Tau Ventures, Snowpoint Ventures, and other investors participated. The financing combines equity with a credit facility. Labelbox did not disclose the size of each component. That distinction matters because the full announced amount should not be treated as new equity investment. Labelbox originally built its business around data-labeling tools used in machine learning. Its current strategy extends into two related markets: improving frontier AI models through reinforcement learning and helping enterprises deploy AI agents. The company’s Horizon platform provides training environments, feedback, and evaluation systems that allow AI models to practice complex tasks. Its Recursion Managed Agents product helps businesses deploy agents that operate within existing applications. Reinforcement learning is becoming commercial infrastructure As AI models improve, developers increasingly need ways to evaluate whether those models can complete complicated tasks across multiple steps. A model that performs well on a benchmark may still fail when it needs to operate business software, follow procedural constraints, or respond to unexpected situations. Reinforcement learning environments can help developers test and improve those capabilities. Labelbox says it works with more than 400 customers, including major U.S. AI laboratories. The company also reports reaching profitability in 2026 while growing more than fivefold year over year. Those are company-reported figures. The financing suggests investors see continued demand for the tools and environments required to improve AI systems after their initial training. However, Labelbox operates in a market where frontier AI developers are also investing heavily in internal training and evaluation infrastructure. Its commercial position will depend on the quality of its evaluation environments, customer relationships, proprietary data, and ability to deliver measurable improvements. The company must also demonstrate that its enterprise agent business can scale without excessive implementation and support costs. Funding Details Startup: Labelbox

Valuation: Not disclosed Dougs raises €50M to bring AI automation into regulated accounting services French accounting technology company Dougs raised €50 million from Expedition Growth Capital, an existing investor. Based in Lyon, Dougs provides accounting, legal, and financial management services directly to small businesses. The startup says it serves more than 50,000 businesses and generates more than €50 million in annual recurring revenue. Unlike software vendors that sell accounting tools to professional firms, Dougs operates as the accounting service provider itself. Founded in 2015, Dougs has developed proprietary software to automate bookkeeping and financial administration. The company employs more than 100 engineers and has accumulated extensive operating information from preparing financial statements and tax filings. Its next objective is to use AI agents to complete more of the accounting process, with qualified accountants reviewing and approving the results. The company’s regulatory status and professional responsibilities are central to its business model. Automation is changing the economics of professional services Dougs says its technology-enabled operations generate gross margins above 80%. That is an unusually high figure for a company delivering accounting services, although the reported margin should be evaluated in the context of the company’s accounting policies and cost classifications. Dougs also says it has been profitable since inception. Its growth strategy is particularly interesting because it combines software automation with professional accountability. A customer does not necessarily want an AI accounting tool. Customers want accurate financial statements, compliant filings, and reliable advice. Dougs aims to deliver that outcome directly, using automation to reduce the labor required for routine work. The investment case is therefore different from traditional accounting software. The company controls the customer relationship and the underlying service, while its technology may allow each accountant to support more businesses. That creates potential operating advantages, but it also introduces regulatory and quality-control responsibilities. For investors, the opportunity is to build a professional services business with more attractive software-like economics. The remaining challenge is proving that automation can improve productivity without weakening accuracy or the professional oversight customers require. Funding Details Startup: Dougs

Valuation: Not disclosed Harmonic Security raises $50M in funding to address the security risks of workplace AI adoption Harmonic Security raised $50 million in Series B financing led by Crosspoint Capital Partners, bringing total funding to $76 million. Existing investors also participated. The company announced the financing on October 14 and plans to expand its engineering and commercial teams in the United States and United Kingdom. Founded in 2023 by Alastair Paterson and Bryan Woolgar-O’Neil, Harmonic develops software that helps enterprises monitor and control how employees use AI applications. The problem is growing as workers adopt chatbots, coding assistants, desktop AI tools, and autonomous agents. Employees may share confidential documents with external systems, use personal accounts for business tasks, or allow agents to access information outside approved workflows. Traditional security tools were not necessarily designed to interpret the context of AI interactions. Harmonic uses specialized smaller language models to analyze AI activity and identify potentially sensitive behavior. Security is becoming a requirement for enterprise AI expansion The company’s approach differs from simply blocking AI applications. Businesses increasingly want employees to use AI because of potential productivity benefits. The challenge is allowing useful applications while reducing the risk of sensitive information exposure. Harmonic aims to provide visibility into which tools employees use, what tasks they perform, and where additional controls are needed. That creates an investment opportunity because enterprises must address AI security alongside broader adoption. However, Harmonic faces competition from established cybersecurity vendors and newer companies developing AI-specific security products. Its differentiation will depend on detection accuracy, policy enforcement, compatibility with different AI systems, and whether customers can deploy the software without disrupting legitimate work. The financing brings total funding to $48 million. Duvo announced the round on October 14 and plans to expand its enterprise AI business, initially focusing on retailers and consumer packaged goods companies. Duvo develops AI agents designed to execute operational processes across business software. Many companies use separate systems for inventory, purchasing, supplier communications, financial management, and customer operations. Employees often spend considerable time moving information between those systems. Duvo attempts to automate that work by connecting to enterprise resource planning systems, supplier portals, spreadsheets, email, and other applications. Its technology can capture existing business processes and then execute approved steps while referring exceptions to human employees. Enterprise AI must work across existing systems The investment reflects growing interest in AI systems that do more than provide answers. Retailers and manufacturers operate complicated businesses where information is distributed across software platforms and external partners. An AI agent that can reliably execute an approved process may provide measurable value by reducing errors, delays, or administrative work. Duvo’s founder has experience building technology businesses, including online grocer Rohlik. That background matters because the startup targets operational problems that software vendors often underestimate. The company’s challenge is making automation reliable across environments where business rules and exceptions vary significantly between customers. Investors will need to evaluate implementation time, customer retention, recurring revenue, and the level of technical support each deployment requires. Duvo must also compete with established enterprise software vendors developing their own agent capabilities. Its opportunity lies in managing processes that span multiple systems rather than staying within a single application. Funding Details Startup: Duvo
