proofCandidates.fullText:
Canadian-founded go-to-market startup wants to become “the AI growth engine for every company.”

Canadian-founded, New York City-based go-to-market (GTM) startup Clay has closed another major financing, securing a $115-million USD ($159 million CAD) Series D round.

The news: Clay develops and sells AI software and agents designed to help other firms automate marketing, sales, and other GTM tasks. The company announced its Series D on Wednesday. It was led by Wellington, with support from Andreessen Horowitz, CapitalG, Meritech, Sequoia, and others. The round values Clay at $7.1 billion USD, more than double the $3.1-billion USD valuation it was given with its $100-million Series C in August 2025. It comes as Clay surpasses 17,000 clients, up from 10,000 a year ago, including Anthropic, ElevenLabs, Google, OpenAI, Siemens, and Stripe.

From the source: “AI is unleashing the biggest wave of company creation in history, and Clay’s goal is to be the engine those companies use to grow to their full potential,” Clay co-founder and CEO Kareem Amin said in a release. “We started by aggregating the best data for [business-to-business] companies. Then, we built the infrastructure to run any personalized campaign on top of it. Now, we’re building agents that can help grow your company for you.”

The context: Clay was launched in 2017 by McGill University graduates and repeat entrepreneurs Amin and Nicolae Rusan. Rusan (who is Canadian) has since left Clay. Amin, who is originally from Egypt, attended McGill before moving to the United States over a decade ago. There, he built a New York startup with Rusan called Frame, an e-commerce tech firm they sold to Sailthru in 2012. Clay, which also counts Canadian-founded Maple VC among its early investors, was recently featured on VC Antoine Nivard’s Dominion List, which tracks influential Canadian founders building in the US.

Final thought: Clay has invested heavily in developing “a self-learning revenue engine” featuring agents capable of autonomously finding prospective clients, monitoring their intent, drafting personalized outreach, and updating customer relationship management systems. “Just as [large language models] predict the next best word in a sentence, Clay will predict the next best action to grow your business,” Maple VC general partner Andre Charoo told BetaKit. Charoo added that he thinks Clay has the potential to become the agentic successor to Salesforce.

Feature image courtesy Clay.

proofCandidates.title: Venture Capital & Startup Funding Roundup, September 9, 2026: Coatue, Andreessen Horowitz, Greylock, Kleiner Perkins, Sequoia & More
proofCandidates.summary: Ten venture rounds totaling roughly $1.47 billion were reported on September 9, 2026, with about 91% concentrated in six deals. The largest was Harvey's $550 million at a $15.5 billion valuation, while others included Cylake, Solstice Oncology, and Clay. Capital is shifting toward companies that control high-value workflows like legal, sales, and weather operations.
proofCandidates.fullText:
0 Shares

Venture capital’s center of gravity today isn’t in one neat category called AI. It is moving toward companies that control high-value workflows: legal work, sales, wealth management, cybersecurity, industrial production and even weather-risk operations. The ten most consequential rounds verified inside the past twelve hours total roughly $1.47 billion, with about 91% of that capital concentrated in the six largest financings. That distribution is telling: investors are still willing to write very large checks, but mostly where they see a path to owning an operational system rather than selling a thin feature on top of somebody else’s model. The biggest signal came late in the research window. Legal AI company Harvey announced a fresh $550 million round at a $15.5 billion valuation, while Lightfield surfaced with a $47 million Andreessen Horowitz-led Series A aimed directly at rebuilding customer relationship management for an agent-driven software era. Between those two poles sit a $245 million cybersecurity financing for Cylake, an unusually large $225 million Series A for Solstice Oncology, and triple-digit rounds for Clay, Perry Weather and Savvy Wealth. The Macro Environment: Capital Is Moving From Models to Operational Control The venture market is drawing an increasingly sharp distinction between companies that merely use artificial intelligence and those that can turn it into a durable system of record, execution or infrastructure. Harvey is becoming an operating layer for legal work; Clay and Lightfield are competing to control customer data and revenue workflows; Euno wants to supply the organizational context that autonomous agents need; CloudNC brings AI into CNC machining. These are not ten variations of a chatbot. They are attempts to insert software into processes where errors are expensive, data accumulates over time, and switching costs can become substantial. That helps explain the check sizes. Investors appear increasingly comfortable funding AI applications at infrastructure-like valuations when those applications sit directly in the flow of work. Harvey has gone from an $8 billion valuation in December 2025 to $11 billion in March and now $15.5 billion in September. Clay, meanwhile, has more than doubled its valuation from $3.1 billion in August 2025 to $7.1 billion today. The market is effectively saying that a small number of application companies may become very large platforms if they own proprietary workflow data, distribution, and execution rather than relying solely on model differentiation. The public-market backdrop is supportive but not indiscriminate. Barclays raised its 2026 S&P 500 target on strong corporate earnings and continued AI spending, while simultaneously warning about demanding valuations, persistent inflation, geopolitical risk and a more hawkish rate environment. That combination helps explain why private capital is concentrating rather than spreading evenly: when the cost of being wrong remains high, investors gravitate toward category leaders, clear enterprise budgets, technically differentiated security products and software connected to measurable operating outcomes. Secondly, a less visible thread running through today’s deals: the digitization of physical and regulated operations. Perry Weather sells safety and weather-operations software; WINT addresses water management; CloudNC automates precision machining; Solstice is applying venture-scale capital to immunotherapy development. Capital is not abandoning software. It is expanding software’s addressable territory into sectors where operational data, regulation, physical assets, or scientific risk create stronger barriers to entry than a generic AI interface can provide. Top Funding Rounds Harvey raises $550 million to turn legal AI into an enterprise operating layer Harvey is the day’s largest qualifying round and arguably its clearest valuation signal. The San Francisco legal AI startup raised $550 million at a $15.5 billion valuation, with new investors Diffusion and Lightspeed Venture Partners co-leading. Existing investors, including Sequoia, Kleiner Perkins, Andreessen Horowitz, Coatue, Conviction, GIC, and Goldman Sachs Alternatives, also participated. Harvey builds AI software for law firms and corporate legal departments, covering contract analysis, due diligence, compliance, and litigation workflows. Why does a vertical-software company need this much capital? Harvey increasingly behaves less like conventional SaaS and more like an applied AI platform. The company says it will put the financing into model training, product expansion and international hiring, and it also announced the acquisition of agent-security startup Guardrails AI — Harvey’s fourth acquisition this year. Its valuation has risen from $11 billion in March to $15.5 billion now, a roughly 41% step-up in less than six months. Reuters reported in March that Harvey had already raised more than $1 billion; adding today’s round takes disclosed cumulative funding above $1.55 billion. The competitive implication extends well beyond legal tech. Harvey demonstrates that application-layer companies can command model-company-style financing when investors believe the application owns valuable data, domain-specific evaluation, customer relationships and the workflow itself. The risk is equally clear: at $15.5 billion, Harvey must grow into a much larger revenue base while competing with specialist rivals such as Legora and Clio, as well as broader AI platforms entering professional services. Reuters noted that Harvey is already used by 80% of the 100 highest-grossing U.S. law firms, giving investors evidence that distribution is becoming a genuine barrier rather than a theoretical one. Funding Details

Startup: Harvey

Investors: Diffusion, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Sequoia, Kleiner Perkins, Andreessen Horowitz, Coatue, Conviction, Elad Gil, Evantic, GIC, Goldman Sachs Alternatives, Verified Capital, WNDR, Sapphire Ventures, Whale Rock

Amount Raised: $550 million

Total Raised: More than $1.55 billion based on disclosed funding

Funding Stage: Growth financing; round label not disclosed

Funding Date: September 9, 2026

Headquarters: San Francisco, California

Sector: Legal AI / Enterprise Software Cylake raises $245 million to build a cybersecurity platform for operational sovereignty Cylake raised $245 million in convertible notes from Lightspeed Venture Partners, Picture Capital and Redpoint Ventures. Axios describes the Sunnyvale company as building a cybersecurity platform for “operational sovereignty,” while the funding announcement says Cylake is approaching the beta release of its next-generation security product. The most interesting part of the deal is not simply its size but its structure. A $245 million convertible-note financing ahead of broad product disclosure gives investors exposure while postponing the valuation mechanics that normally accompany a priced venture round. That is unusually substantial optionality capital for a cybersecurity company at this point in its public life. It suggests Lightspeed, Picture and Redpoint see a potential platform opportunity large enough to justify funding ahead of clearer commercial benchmarks. A broader security thesis is embedded here. As companies deploy autonomous software into production, cybersecurity increasingly has to protect not just networks and identities, but an organization’s ability to keep operating when software, agents, credentials, or infrastructure are compromised. Cylake has not yet disclosed enough publicly to judge how differentiated its architecture will be, so view the financing primarily as a strong investor signal rather than proof of product-market leadership. The large convertible structure also makes valuation conclusions premature. Funding Details

The Boston biotech is focused on a second-generation CTLA-4 immunotherapy program and is associated with Harbour BioMed, which announced the financing for its partner company. The company says more than 1,000 machine shops worldwide use its technology, including hundreds in the United States. This is one of the day’s smaller rounds but one of the clearest examples of AI entering the industrial base. Reducing programming time can directly affect quoting speed, machine utilization, and manufacturing throughput. Sector: Industrial AI / Precision Manufacturing / Developer Tools for CNC What Today’s Funding Activity Reveals The first pattern is extreme capital concentration. These ten rounds represent about $1.47 billion, but Harvey, Cylake, Solstice, Clay, Perry Weather, and Savvy Wealth alone account for roughly $1.35 billion, or about 91% of the sample. Venture capital may be active, but it is not behaving democratically. The largest pools of money are going to companies investors believe can become category-defining platforms, companies with unusually high technical or regulatory development costs, or companies already demonstrating strong enterprise distribution. Second, the application layer is becoming more important, not less. Early generative-AI investing centered heavily on models, chips, and compute. Today’s rounds show capital moving into the systems that decide where AI actually gets used: Harvey in legal work, Clay and Lightfield in revenue operations, Savvy in wealth management, Euno in enterprise data, and CloudNC in machining. Investors appear to be betting that the companies capturing proprietary workflow context can preserve pricing power even as access to capable models becomes cheaper and more interchangeable. Third, “AI defensibility” is shifting from the model to the data-and-workflow loop. Lightfield wants every customer interaction to improve its representation of a business. Euno wants organizational context to accumulate as agents use enterprise data. Harvey sits inside legal work where auditability, institutional knowledge, and domain-specific behavior matter. Clay sits in go-to-market operations where enrichment, integrations, and customer history can create a compounding dataset. That is a more credible source of differentiation than simply calling a third-party model through an API. Fourth, venture capital remains heavily U.S.-centered even in a global search. Eight of the ten selected companies are headquartered in the United States, based on the locations reported in today’s coverage; Euno has a dual U.S.-Israel presence, while CloudNC is based in London. The imbalance is especially visible in large rounds. Harvey, Cylake, Solstice, Clay, Perry Weather and Savvy account for nearly all of the capital in the sample and are all U.S.-headquartered. Finally, software and the physical economy are converging. Weather risk, water management, and machining are receiving institutional venture checks because software increasingly drives real-world operational decisions. The implication is that the next generation of valuable “AI companies” may not look like conventional AI startups. They may look like manufacturing software, compliance infrastructure, safety systems, or vertical operating platforms whose machine intelligence is largely invisible to the end user. Comparative Funding Table Startup Amount Raised Sector Funding Stage Lead Investors Country Harvey $550M Legal AI Growth financing Diffusion, Lightspeed Venture Partners United States Cylake $245M Cybersecurity Convertible notes Lightspeed, Picture Capital, Redpoint United States Solstice Oncology $225M Biotechnology / Oncology Series A RA Capital Management United States Clay $115M AI Sales Software Series D Wellington Management United States Perry Weather $110M Weather / Safety Software Series C Silversmith Capital Partners United States Savvy Wealth $100M Wealthtech Series C Halo Fund United States Lightfield $47M AI / CRM Series A Andreessen Horowitz United States WINT $36M Water Intelligence Series D LIP Ventures, Inven Capital United States Euno $23M Enterprise AI / Data Series A N47 United States / Israel CloudNC $20M Industrial AI / Manufacturing Not disclosed Nimble Ventures United Kingdom Strategic Takeaways for Founders and Investors For founders, today’s strongest message is that “AI-powered” is no longer an investment thesis on its own. Companies attracting premium capital can explain why their position strengthens as models improve. Harvey owns legal workflows and distribution. Lightfield wants to own customer context. Euno is building organizational context for agents. CloudNC embeds intelligence in specialized manufacturing processes. The common thread isn’t the model; it is the system around it. That puts pressure on founders to identify a source of defensibility that survives model commoditization. Proprietary data can help, but only when itis hard to recreate and tied to repeated customer activity. Workflow ownership is stronger when the product becomes part of how decisions are made. Distribution matters when customers trust the platform with high-stakes tasks. Regulatory knowledge matters when compliance limits the number of credible vendors. Hardware or industrial integrations matter when deployment requires real-world engineering rather than a browser interface. Today’s rounds reward several of those characteristics. The second lesson is about pricing and valuation discipline. Harvey at $15.5 billion and Clay at $7.1 billion show that late-stage investors are again willing to pay aggressively for perceived winners. But those valuations are not free capital. They set much higher exit thresholds and put pressure on sustained revenue growth. Harvey’s valuation has risen from $8 billion in December to $11 billion in March and $15.5 billion today; Clay has moved from $3.1 billion last August to $7.1 billion. For founders considering large step-ups, the relevant question is not whether investors will pay the number, but whether the company can grow into it without making the next financing strategically restrictive. The third lesson is that investors are increasingly willing to fund capital intensity when it’s inherent to the opportunity. Solstice needs a large Series A because drug development is expensive. CloudNC is attacking slow-moving industrial systems. Cylake has raised an unusually large convertible financing before broad product rollout. The market is not demanding capital efficiency in a simplistic “spend less” sense; it is demanding a credible relationship between capital consumed and strategic position created. For investors, the most interesting opportunities may increasingly sit below the foundation-model layer. As access to leading models broadens, economic value can migrate toward companies that own the customer relationship and can decide which model to use for a given job. Enterprise context, security, orchestration, vertical data and physical-world execution all provide ways to capture that value. The risk is that many such businesses will prove to be features rather than independent platforms. The investor’s job is therefore to distinguish companies that merely package AI from those accumulating durable control over data, distribution and execution. And the geography offers a useful warning. Today’s funding cohort is overwhelmingly U.S.-weighted even after a global search. Europe contributes CloudNC and part of Euno’s operating footprint, but the biggest application-software rounds remain clustered around San Francisco, New York, Boston, Dallas and Silicon Valley. For non-U.S. founders, that reinforces the importance of selling into American enterprise budgets early; for investors, it suggests that some of the more mispriced opportunities may lie in technically strong ecosystems where financing remains less abundant. Conclusion Today’s venture activity is a useful snapshot of where the startup market is heading after several years in which “AI” itself was enough to command attention. Capital is becoming more specific. Investors are asking which company owns the workflow, which one accumulates proprietary context, which one can prove customer value, and which one sits in a part of the economy where replacement is genuinely difficult. Harvey’s $550 million round is the headline, but the more revealing story is the breadth underneath it. Legal work, cybersecurity, oncology, sales, wealth management, weather operations, water systems, enterprise data and CNC machining all attracted fresh capital within the same twelve-hour window. The common denominator is not industry. It is investors’ willingness to finance software and science that sits close to high-value decisions and hard operational problems. That points toward a more mature phase of the current technology cycle. Foundation models remain economically important, but increasingly they are becoming inputs into larger businesses. The next enduring venture franchises may be built by companies that make those models useful inside legal departments, factories, advisory firms, security teams, and other environments where context, trust, and execution matter more than benchmark scores. For founders, that is a demanding message but a constructive one: access to advanced AI is becoming common. Owning a problem that customers cannot afford to leave unsolved is becoming scarce. 0 Shares

proofCandidates.title: Clay completes $115m Series D, valued at $7.1bn
proofCandidates.summary: Clay, a US-based AI business-growth company, raised $115m in a Series D round led by Wellington, valuing it at $7.1bn. The company serves over 17,000 customers, including 80% of the Forbes AI 50 list, and announced a $1m scholarship scheme.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Clay, a US-based company developing AI tools for business growth, has secured $115m in Series D funding round, bringing its valuation to $7.1bn.
The fundraising was led by Wellington, with additional participation from Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), Sequoia, Perennial, StepStone, Meritech, CapitalG, DST, Boldstart, BoxGroup, Bloomberg Beta, and Evolution.
Access deeper industry intelligence
Experience unmatched clarity with a single platform that combines unique data, AI, and human expertise.
Clay offers technology designed to help businesses identify potential customers, monitor market signals, and personalise outreach. It integrates data from sources including customer relationship management systems, product usage, campaign metrics, calls and emails.
Its platform also incorporates external data such as funding events and hiring activity, in order to map a company’s addressable market dynamically.
The company reports serving more than 17,000 customers, including what it describes as 80% of the Forbes AI 50 list, as well as organisations such as Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, ElevenLabs, Stripe, Workday, and Siemens.
Clay co-founder and CEO Kareem Amin said: “AI is unleashing the biggest wave of company creation in history, and Clay’s goal is to be the engine those companies use to grow to their full potential. We started by aggregating the best data for B2B companies.
“Then we built the infrastructure to run any personalised campaign on top of it. Now we’re building agents that can help grow your company for you. We’re building a self-learning revenue engine. The better a company gets at learning, the faster it grows.”
In addition to the funding, Clay has set up a $1m scholarship scheme aimed at training future “go-to-market” engineers and professionals who focus on building business revenue systems.
Amin said: “We believe the next wave of companies will be built by teams that think about growth in a systematic way. We want to make this career accessible to more people. If we do it right, we’ll be powering the next wave of the world’s economic growth.”
In August 2025, Clay raised $100m in a Series C funding round, bringing its post-money valuation to $3.1bn.

proofCandidates.fullText:
Clay, a fast-growing start-up that provides artificial intelligence tools for sales and marketing, has drawn investor interest in recent years.

Now, the company plans to announce on Wednesday that it has raised more money — $115 million — and pushed its valuation to $7.1 billion, more than double what it attained in its last primary fund-raising round in August 2025.

Perhaps more notable is the round’s leader: Wellington Management, a big asset manager investing in start-ups that are likely to go public within a few years. Other participants include Sequoia Capital; A16Z Perennial, an affiliate of Andreessen Horowitz; DST Global; and CapitalG, an investment arm of Alphabet.

The round underscores how many A.I. start-ups are coming of age. They are still posting the kind of vertiginous growth that attracts investors, but they are also keeping an eye on the next potential growth stage, including possible initial public offerings. (Databricks, an A.I. data analytics start-up now valued at $190 billion, has suggested that it is considering an I.P.O.)

proofCandidates.title: Clay hits $7.1B valuation with $115M raise as it sees AI agents running future of sales — TFN
proofCandidates.summary: Clay raised $115M in a Series D led by Wellington Management, hitting a $7.1B valuation. The go-to-market platform serves over 17,000 customers, including Anthropic and Google, and is launching a $1M fund to train GTM engineers. The company's AI agents aim to automate sales and marketing tasks.
proofCandidates.fullText:
- Clay raised $115M in a Series D led by Wellington Management, hitting a $7.1B valuation.
- The go-to-market platform now serves more than 17,000 customers, including Anthropic and Google.
- Clay is launching a $1M fund to train ‘GTM engineers’, a title it coined for the role.
Kareem Amin and Nicolae Rusan did not set out to build a sales tool. In 2017, the pair, who met at McGill University and worked together at Microsoft, wanted to make programming accessible to people who could not code. Eight years, several pivots and one much sharper use case later, that idea is worth $7.1 billion.
Clay, the New York-based go-to-market platform, has raised $115 million in Series D funding led by Wellington Management, with existing backers Sequoia Capital, StepStone, Andreessen Horowitz, Perennial, Meritech, DST, CapitalG, BoxGroup, Boldstart, Bloomberg Beta and Evolution Equity Partners all returning.
The valuation marks a rapid re-rating: Clay closed its $100 million Series C at $3.1 billion just over a year ago, then saw a $5 billion employee tender offer in January before this round more than doubled that mark again.
“AI is unleashing the biggest wave of company creation in history, and Clay’s goal is to be the engine those companies use to grow to their full potential. We started by aggregating the best data for B2B companies. Then we built the infrastructure to run any personalised campaign on top of it. Now we’re building agents that can help grow your company for you,” said Amin, co-founder and chief executive.
From spreadsheets to a “self-learning revenue engine”
Clay’s platform pulls together CRM records, product usage, campaign engagement, calls and emails, then layers in external signals such as funding announcements and hiring activity.
AI agents use that combined picture to decide what a sales team should do next. For example, a team could ask Clay to identify fintech marketing leaders, research their companies, draft personalised outreach and launch it, with the system adjusting future campaigns based on what worked.
Nicolae Rusan co-founded the company alongside Amin, and Varun Anand joined as a third co-founder in 2021 as Clay pivoted from a general-purpose data tool toward go-to-market teams specifically. Amin, who was born in Egypt and raised in a community of expat hospital workers in Saudi Arabia before studying electrical engineering in Canada, has described the shift as building “an integrated development environment” for revenue teams rather than another point solution.
A crowded and increasingly well-funded field
Regie.ai raised a $30 million Series B in February, taking its total past $50 million.11x, which builds fully autonomous “digital workers” rather than a workflow layer, has raised roughly $76 million since its Benchmark-led Series A. Established data providers Apollo.io and ZoomInfo remain in the mix too, though Clay argues its bet is broader than any single sales role: it wants to be the infrastructure underneath the whole go-to-market function, not a replacement for one job title.
The category itself is growing fast enough to support several large bets at once. The global AI-in-sales market was worth an estimated $50.8 billion in 2026 and is projected to reach $383 billion by 2034, according to Global Market Insights, a pace that helps explain why investors are willing to underwrite a valuation that has more than doubled twice in thirteen months without a matching public revenue disclosure.
Alongside the raise, Clay is putting $1 million into training people for the go-to-market engineer role it popularised. “We believe the next wave of companies will be built by teams that think about growth in a systematic way. We want to make this career accessible to more people,” Amin concluded.
If Clay’s agents really can decide what a company should do next and then do it, the harder question is what happens to the sales and marketing hires that job used to belong to, and whether Wellington’s late-stage, public-markets pedigree signals investors are now pricing AI-native GTM software for an IPO.

SUBSCRIBER EXCLUSIVE Inside Clay’s $5 Billion, AI-Powered Bid to Make Lead Gen Fun Sales administrators step aside. Clay’s “go to market engineers” are turning spreadsheets into an art. READ MORE

In recent years, the company, which was founded by Amin and Varun Anand in 2017, has continued in its mission to give access to the power of programming. The AI-powered data operations platform has helped automate sales prospecting, lead generation, and data enrichment for marketing and revenue teams. “We’re building a self-learning revenue engine,” Amin said in Wednesday’s announcement. “The better a company gets at learning, the faster it grows.”

proofCandidates.title: CORRECTING and REPLACING Tekion, Increase, and Core Bank Partner to Bring Industry-First Embedded Banking to Automotive Retail
proofCandidates.summary: Tekion, Increase, and Core Bank announced embedded banking inside Automotive Retail Cloud, with Tekion Spend offering a fully-featured bank account for dealerships. The solution, built on Increase's API and Core Bank's banking, is available to US ARC dealerships in Q4.
proofCandidates.fullText:
ⓘ This article is third-party content and does not represent the views of this site. We make no guarantees regarding its accuracy or completeness.

Tekion Spend offers the first fully-featured bank account native to an automotive dealer management system.

Please replace the release issued September 23, 2026, with the following corrected version due to multiple revisions.

This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260923757647/en/

The updated release reads:

TEKION, INCREASE, AND CORE BANK PARTNER TO BRING INDUSTRY-FIRST EMBEDDED BANKING TO AUTOMOTIVE RETAIL

Tekion Spend offers the first fully-featured bank account native to an automotive dealer management system.

Tekion, Increase, and Core Bank today announced embedded banking inside Automotive Retail Cloud (ARC). Built from the ground up as AI-native, ARC unifies all departments across more than 2,000 dealerships today. Tekion Spend, built on Increase in partnership with Core Bank, provides the first fully embedded banking solution designed for automotive dealerships.

Automotive dealerships are operationally complex businesses. Every year, a single dealership makes hundreds of thousands of payments to various suppliers, vendors, and customers. Until now, dealerships have had to make those payments outside of the software platform they use to run the rest of their business. Dealership staff have to manage an external bank account and print thousands of checks annually to make payments. Most still reconcile payments manually in their dealership management system at month end.

Tekion Spend solves this by embedding banking directly into ARC. Dealerships can now:

Open a fully-featured, FDIC-insured bank account in their name

Store and earn money on their deposits

Send money over any US payment rail and see exactly where it is at every moment

Reconcile payments in real-time

Manage every rooftop from one account

Increase makes this all possible via API, offering bare-metal infrastructure that gives Tekion full access to the Federal Reserve's data and capabilities, in partnership with Core Bank. Increase provides accounts and scaled accounts payable for Tekion Spend.

Accounts payable is the first step in Tekion’s larger plans for embedded banking. Dealerships move billions annually just to manage their floorplans. They also move money in service, sales, finance and insurance, and payroll. Today, each of those flows ends in a separate portal. Through Tekion Spend with banking powered by Increase, dealerships can soon manage the vast majority of their funds' flows from within ARC.

“Tekion Spend gives automotive dealerships a fully-featured bank account inside their existing system of record,” said Jamie Fox, GM of Fintech at Tekion. “It sees the invoice, the payment, and the ledger entry as one object rather than three systems reporting to each other after the fact. This is a natural step in Tekion’s mission to deliver end-to-end service for automotive retail.”

“Increase exists to help ambitious technology companies build great financial products,” said Jack Flintermann Reed, Head of Product at Increase. “We help our users get to market faster than they imagined possible. Prior to building the full product that’s launching today, Tekion built an initial working prototype on Increase APIs in less than three weeks.”

“Tekion has built an impressive platform and has a deep understanding of the operational needs of today’s dealerships,” said Lindsay Borgeson, President of Core X. “We are excited to partner with Tekion to bring even greater value to the automotive retail market and give their customers the confidence that comes from having their dealership funds held with a trusted, regulated financial institution. We believe this partnership will deliver meaningful value to dealerships and are thrilled about what we can accomplish together.”

Tekion Spend is available to US ARC dealerships beginning in Q4.

Tekion Spend banking products and services are provided by Core Bank, Member FDIC. Technology services are provided by Increase Technologies, Inc. Tekion is not a bank.

About Tekion

Tekion is redefining automotive retail with its end-to-end AI-native, platform purpose-built for the industry. By embedding AI into every workflow, Tekion delivers intelligent automation, real-time insights, and advanced decision support - driving efficiency, revenue, and modern consumer experiences. As the first and fastest cloud-native platform for automotive, Tekion brings OEMs, dealers, partners, and consumers together through its revolutionary suite: Automotive Retail Cloud (ARC) for retailers, Automotive Enterprise Cloud (AEC) for manufacturers and large automotive enterprises, and Automotive Partner Cloud (APC) for technology and industry partners. With AI-powered, cloud-native technology, Tekion enables the most seamless, transparent, and profitable retail experiences in the industry. For more information, visit www.tekion.com.

About Increase

Increase offers API-first banking for ambitious technology companies. Companies like Coast, Gusto, and Ramp rely on Increase technology to process more than $500B annualized in payments, card transactions, and loans. Increase built its own bank core technology from scratch: it’s transparent, reliable, and flexible so users can build great financial products on top. Increase has offered banking infrastructure since 2020 and introduced Increase Bank, Member FDIC in 2026. Learn more at increase.com.

About Core Bank

Core X, a division of Core Bank, is a technology-forward, solutions-driven financial institution built for fintech and Vertical SaaS companies that need more from their banking partner. Core X delivers a differentiated partnership built around speed to market, deep compliance expertise, strong risk management, and strategic support. Through our managed compliance model, partners can focus on growing their businesses while Core Bank provides the regulatory oversight and banking expertise to scale responsibly. Connect at www.corebank.com/core-x-partner-banking

proofCandidates.title: August 2026: Top five new launch stories of the month
proofCandidates.summary: August 2026 saw five fintech launches, including Revolut's EURR stablecoin, Decade's $85M seed round, Increase Bank, and the US Treasury's quantum-readiness task force. Revolut's EURR is being rolled out in Denmark, Poland, and Portugal, while Decade's AI wealth manager integrates custom models with human advisors.
proofCandidates.fullText:
August delivered a wave of new fintech innovations, including new stablecoins and wealth management platforms. Here, we run through five of the top new launch stories from the month, featuring Revolut, Decade, the US Department of the Treasury, and more.

Revolut launches euro-backed stablecoin EURR

UK challenger Revolut has launched EURR, an Ethereum-based, euro-denominated digital token, marking the first stage of its stablecoin strategy.

Revolut, which serves over 80 million customers globally and boasts a user base of more than 16 million crypto users, has begun a phased rollout of EURR to eligible customers in Denmark, Poland, and Portugal, with "wider availability in other EEA markets expected later this year", the company says.

Revolut does not issue the token itself. Instead, Stripe's stablecoin infrastructure firm Bridge mints it under its newly secured MiCA Crypto-Asset Service Provider licence and Luxembourg Electronic Money Institution authorisation. Revolut's crypto arm, Revolut Digital Assets Europe, then integrates the token into the bank's consumer retail app.

Related:Lunar founders launch new AI audit company Repodo

Read more here

Ex-Nubank execs launch AI wealth manager Decade following $85m seed round

Decade, a Brazilian AI wealth management start-up, has emerged from stealth with $85 million in seed funding. The round, which Decade claims as the largest seed investment ever raised by a start-up in Latin America, was backed by Greenoaks, Benchmark, and Diffusion.

Based in São Paulo, Decade offers a financial wealth management platform that integrates custom financial AI models with human advisors to consolidate asset tracking, diagnose portfolio inefficiencies, and provide investment guidance.

Decade is the brainchild of former Nubank CTO Vitor Olivier and Felipe Meneses, founder of data intelligence firm Hyperplane, which Nubank acquired in 2024. Meneses subsequently spent a year within Olivier's technology unit as a machine learning engineer.

Read more here

Exclusive: Clayton Hayward steps down as EFT Corporation group CEO to launch AI venture Tharvos

Clayton Hayward is stepping down as the group CEO of EFT Corporation to create a new AI venture builder called Tharvos, FinTech Futures can exclusively reveal. Hayward announced the career move on LinkedIn, stating: "After 8+ years, my time as group CEO of EFT Corporation has come to an end."

Hayward is not departing the business in full. His departure statement further explains: "I'm not going anywhere as a shareholder in EFT, and I'll continue to support my co-founders Mike Smits, Paul Carter-Brown, and Jason Penton in an advisory capacity."

Related:Maltese start-up Mrkts debuts prediction markets infrastructure offering

Hayward has now come together with software entrepreneur George Gericke to create Tharvos. On his new company, Hayward's departure statement continues: "We invest in, build and operate AI-native ventures and we stand them up next to the industry leaders they're built to compete with."

He further elaborates to FinTech Futures: "We have already launched our first project, NIJA, a prepaid AI token platform similar to OpenRouter," adding that "We will launch several others before end of the year in insurance, longevity and wellness, and financial services."

Read more here

Former Stripe exec launches Increase Bank in US

US fintech Increase is launching a new FDIC-insured financial institution called Increase Bank. The entity combines regulated banking services with the financial infrastructure platform Increase has been building under founder Darragh Buckley since 2020.

Increase Bank will provide businesses with deposit accounts, payment services, and card issuing through the same API-based platform the fintech already offers to clients like Gusto, Ramp, and Stripe.

This platform serves as the system of record for customer balances and transactions at Increase Bank, and connects directly to payment networks including the Federal Reserve, the Clearing House, and Visa.

Related:Former MoneyLion execs debut wealthtech infrastructure venture Astraeus with $10m in total funding

Read more here

US Treasury launches Quantum-Readiness Task Force

The US Department of the Treasury has established the Quantum-Readiness Task Force to support the financial sector's "transition to quantum-safe technology in an orderly and operationally resilient manner", according to a launch statement.

The public-private initiative brings together technology providers, government bodies, financial institutions, financial market infrastructures, and other private-sector representatives to facilitate "coordinated preparation for quantum-related cyber risks".

The unit will focus on "practical, risk-based approaches to quantum readiness, including identifying critical dependencies, improving cryptographic agility, promoting interoperability, strengthening operational resilience, and addressing implementation challenges related to third-party dependencies and digital assets", the statement continues.

Read more here

proofCandidates.title: Stripe’s First Employee Built a Bank to Fix Payments’ Last Mile
proofCandidates.summary: Darragh Buckley, Stripe’s first employee, launched Increase Bank to improve the last mile of payment infrastructure by integrating banking systems with software companies. The initiative aims to enhance operational visibility and compliance, leveraging direct bank ownership to streamline payments, payroll, and data transparency. Buckley’s strategy focuses on making banking infrastructure more accessible and understandable for modern financial technology applications.
proofCandidates.fullText:
This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Highlights Darragh Buckley went from Stripe’s first employee to bank owner with a contrarian bet: The biggest opportunity in payments sits inside regulated banking, not outside it. Increase Bank isn’t trying to rip out America’s payment rails. It’s built to fix the stubborn last mile between modern software companies and the bank infrastructure moving trillions of dollars. Buckley said richer data, continuous visibility and compliance designed into the software can reshape payroll, embedded finance and the meaning of community banking.

Watch more: Digital Shift With Increase’s Darragh Buckley

An engineer sits across the table from a bank examiner. How does that conversation go? Better than you might think, Darragh Buckley would argue. The engineer wants to know what the system is doing at every step. The examiner wants to know it’ll do the right thing every time. Those aren’t competing demands. They’re the blueprint for a better bank. That idea runs against one of FinTech’s founding stories: Banking’s future depends on replacing legacy infrastructure. But after helping build Stripe’s earliest banking integrations, Buckley reached a different conclusion. The rails weren’t broken. The trouble was the distance between those rails and the software companies trying to build on top of them. That conviction eventually carried Buckley beyond banking-as-a-service partnerships and all the way into bank ownership. Increase’s launch of Increase Bank is where that journey landed. Founder and CEO Buckley told PYMNTS CEO Karen Webster that his time as the first employee of Stripe revealed capabilities banks possessed but rarely exposed in ways modern software companies could actually use. “The systems are good and reliable,” Buckley said. “And they serve very much the use cases that they were built for.” But, he added, “many of our current use cases, especially around ambitious technology companies, run into edge cases that perhaps weren’t contemplated. If you’re rebuilding the technology stack anyway, contemplating those compliance regimes from the start makes it easier to build a safe and sound system.” Plenty of FinTech executives would happily send ACH and Fedwire to the museum. Buckley won’t. He credited the Federal Reserve with operating dependable systems. “The Federal Reserve is fantastically reliable,” Buckley said. “They changed the messaging format for Fedwire… across 3,500 institutions… and everything succeeded. Everyone got paid. Lights stayed on. Traffic still moved.” His analogy isn’t a blockchain or a rocket ship. It’s public transportation. The tunnels don’t change often. What riders feel are better schedules, easier payments and clearer explanations when something goes wrong. The infrastructure can stay put while the experience gets better. That mindset helps explain why Increase didn’t start by pursuing a banking charter. It first built its own technology stack, connected directly to payment networks, and developed the operations developers need to build financial products. Only after years of working with partner banks, serving on a community bank board, and learning how regulated banking really works did Buckley conclude that the final piece required owning a bank. The strategy grew out of the kind of operational frustration Buckley knew firsthand from Stripe. Take wire transfers. Sending the money usually wasn’t the hard part. Handling the exceptions was. A failed wire might arrive as an email demanding manual intervention, workable at dozens of transactions, painful at thousands. Buckley doesn’t blame partner banks. “They were built for a different kind of client,” he said. Software companies can’t treat payments as black boxes. They need to see when an instruction is received, transmitted and acknowledged. That status data can be as valuable as settlement itself because it’s what lets developers build dependable products around the payment. Buckley said. Webster put her finger on what buying a bank actually changed. “It seems like the bottlenecks come in many different ways, including the access part,” she said, referring to direct connectivity to Federal Reserve services and card networks. Buckley agreed, but direct access isn’t the whole story. Bank ownership also removes the final operational layer between payment networks and the businesses that depend on them. “Increase’s role is improving that last mile delivery as opposed to burning the house down and trying to build something new,” Buckley said. Data Turns Banking Into Software Fixing the last mile doesn’t stop at processing a payment. It means turning a bank’s operations into something software can see, test and trust. Consider Increase’s continuous test transactions that monitor connections to the Federal Reserve, Visa and other networks. Instead of waiting for customers to report a problem, the system keeps checking whether the infrastructure upstream is behaving as expected. Then there’s payroll, the invisible machinery of household finance. Buckley called payroll engineers “one of the great unsung heroes of the U.S. economy” because millions of consumers don’t think about payroll until it fails. Mortgages, rent payments and countless household obligations depend on those files arriving on schedule every pay period. “For most banks, that’s not the way it works,” Buckley said. “If you’re the payroll engineer, you send the instructions to your bank. Your bank may or may not turn around and say, ‘We got it,’ and that is the terminal point in that interaction. The next point you will know whether everything succeeded will be user support questions telling you, ‘I didn’t get my money.’” Increase answers the silence. As processing advances, it confirms receipt, submission to the Federal Reserve, and the Fed’s acceptance and action on the file. The goal isn’t simply faster payments. It’s knowing where the money is before support tickets start telling you where it isn’t. Buckley brings the same software lens to community banking. Community doesn’t have to mean geography, he said. Technology can group businesses by the financial problems they share. “The dentist in Bend [Oregon] looks more similar to the dentist in Boston than they do to the restaurant next door from a banking services perspective,” Buckley said. “We should end up with the bank for dentists, not the bank for Bend, Oregon.” That’s the engineer-and-examiner conversation in practice. Regulation supplies the guardrails; software makes the system visible. Buckley isn’t trying to tear banking down. He’s trying to make it legible to the companies building on top of it. Watch the full interview with Darragh Buckley to learn more about: Why Buckley said he believes owning a bank changes the economics and operational flexibility of API-first financial infrastructure.

How technologists and bank regulators approach the same operational problems from different perspectives, and why both disciplines benefit from closer collaboration.

Where stablecoins fit alongside the FedNow® Service, Fedwire and ACH, and why Buckley said domestic payment rails and blockchain networks solve different problems.

proofCandidates.title: UPDATE -- Vic.ai Partners with Increase to Power VicPay™
proofCandidates.summary: Vic.ai announced a partnership with Increase and Core Bank to power VicPay's accounts payable payment capabilities, integrating invoice automation with payment execution and reconciliation in a unified platform. The integration enables enterprise finance teams to process ACH, check, and virtual card payments through a single workflow, eliminating the fragmented handoffs that historically separated invoice automation from money movement. Vic.ai's autonomous finance platform has processed over one billion invoices with accuracy rates reaching 99%, and the partnership extends this operational depth through payment execution with human oversight controls.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Increase technology powers an API-first banking platform for ACH, check, and virtual card payments within VicPay, connecting the AP lifecycle from invoice ingestion through payment execution and reconciliation NEW YORK, Aug. 06, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Enterprise finance teams are moving from digitized workflows to autonomous finance operations, yet payments remain the most fragmented step in the AP lifecycle, often spread across separate providers, portals, and manual reconciliation processes. Vic.ai, the AI-native autonomous finance platform, today announced a partnership with Increase and Core Bank to power VicPay™'s account and payment capabilities. Increase’s technology is trusted by some of the largest fintechs and software platforms in the United States, providing flexible, transparent, and reliable tools for money movement, storage, and card issuance. Today, the Increase platform powers VicPay payments within the same environment where invoices are captured and approved. From approved invoice to settled payment For many AP teams, the handoff between invoice approval and payment execution is where visibility breaks down. By integrating with Increase technology, Vic.ai creates a seamless platform where approved invoices carry the customer's payment instructions, approval controls, and selected payment method through to execution, with funds moving through the customer's individual account at Core Bank before disbursement to vendors. Payment status and transaction information synchronize back into Vic.ai for tracking, exception handling, and reconciliation. The result is one unified operational loop rather than a patchwork of disconnected systems. Get the latest news

delivered to your inbox Sign up for The Manila Times newsletters By signing up with an email address, I acknowledge that I have read and agree to the Terms of Service and Privacy Policy Enterprise-grade controls, by design The integration includes safeguards designed to prevent duplicate payment attempts, provide real-time status synchronization with backup polling, and reconcile transactions against Vic.ai ledger activity. Customer funds are held in individual deposit accounts opened in each customer's own name at Core Bank, providing clear account titling and direct ownership of funds. The unified provider architecture strengthens the resilience of the VicPay platform and enhances its ability to support varied vendor requirements without manual workarounds. As across the Vic.ai platform, autonomy in payments operates under human oversight: approval hierarchies, user permissions, audit trails, and exception management remain in the customer's hands. Advertisement Flexibility across payment methods Finance teams can choose the payment method that best fits each vendor, whether ACH, check, or virtual card, without leaving VicPay. Increase provides the banking infrastructure behind each payment rail and serves as the check payment provider for VicPay checks. With Increase’s checking solution, checks process and ship the next business day, arrive with remittance details enclosed, and return a deposited check image once the check clears. That eliminates a long-standing visibility blind spot in check reconciliation. The unified infrastructure also provides Vic.ai with a common foundation to continue expanding payment capabilities, status visibility, and operational controls. Vic.ai's autonomous finance platform has been trained on more than one billion invoices, delivering invoice-processing accuracy of up to 99% and no-touch rates above 80% at its highest-performing enterprise deployments. Extending that operational depth through payment execution reduces the handoffs, bottlenecks, and siloed systems that have historically separated invoice automation from money movement. "Payments have historically been where AP automation stops short,” said Alexander Hagerup, CEO & Co-Founder of Vic.ai. "The invoice work gets automated, and then the money movement happens somewhere else. Partnering with Increase gives our customers one connected loop from invoice to payment, with the controls, visibility, and choice of payment method that enterprise finance operations require." proofCandidates.title: Former Stripe exec launches Increase Bank
proofCandidates.summary: US fintech Increase is launching Increase Bank, a new FDIC-insured financial institution that combines regulated banking services with its existing API-based financial infrastructure platform. The launch marks a shift in Increase's business model from relying on sponsor banks to operating as both a technology provider and a direct bank. Founder Darragh Buckley, a former Stripe executive, enabled this transition by acquiring Twin City Bank, a $114 million-asset community bank based in Longview, Washington.
proofCandidates.fullText:
US fintech Increase is launching a new FDIC-insured financial institution called Increase Bank. The entity combines regulated banking services with the financial infrastructure platform Increase has been building under founder Darragh Buckley since 2020.

Increase Bank will provide businesses with deposit accounts, payment services, and card issuing through the same API-based platform the fintech already offers to clients like Gusto, Ramp, and Stripe.

This platform serves as the system of record for customer balances and transactions at Increase Bank, and connects directly to payment networks including the Federal Reserve, the Clearing House, and Visa.

Now instead of relying on sponsor banks to provide regulated banking services, Increase is switching its business model to operate as both a technology provider and as a bank itself.

CEO Buckley created Increase after spending six years working for Stripe, where he developed banking and payments infrastructure as part of the payment giant's early founding team.

Related:Revolut secures two new licences in the UAE as it gears up for full-scale launch

Buckley's efforts to build a bank were made possible by the stake he acquired last year in Twin City Bank, a $114 million-asset community bank based in Longview, Washington.

Although the size of this initial stake was not disclosed, the sale was large enough to require disclosure by the Federal Reserve in June 2025. It's now understood that Buckley acquired Twin City Bank in full, including the banking licence it has used since 2000.

proofCandidates.title: Ex-Stripe employee debuts converted community bank
proofCandidates.summary: Darragh Buckley, former Stripe employee and founder of payment fintech Increase, has officially launched Increase Bank after acquiring and converting Twin City Bank, a Washington-based community bank, through its parent holding company last June. The underlying bank's assets grew 48% year-over-year to $114.5 million following the acquisition, with Buckley leveraging the bank's regulatory infrastructure—including its charter, FDIC insurance, and Federal Reserve master account—to build a proprietary banking platform. This deal represents a shift in the fintech-banking model, moving from API-layer partnerships with third-party banks to owning direct banking infrastructure and control.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Key insight: Fintech entrepreneur Darragh Buckley has re-launched the community bank he bought last year under the name Increase Bank.

Supporting data: The underlying bank's asset size grew by 48% in the fiscal year after Buckley acquired it for his enterprise payments fintech.

Expert quote: "The value [for Buckley] comes from obtaining the institutional status and control that Increase could not fully achieve by relying solely on third-party banks." —Bank Slate Consulting's Paul Davis Darragh Buckley, founder and CEO of payment fintech Increase and one of Stripe's first employees, has officially launched his own bank. Buckley announced this week that Increase now has its own banking division called Increase Bank. The bank is a rebuilt conversion of Twin City Bank, a Washington-based community bank that Buckley acquired through buying its parent holding company last June. "Buckley bought a small bank to serve as the regulated chassis of a much larger tech business," Bank Slate Consulting founder Paul Davis told American Banker. "The value comes from obtaining the institutional status and control that Increase could not fully achieve by relying solely on third-party banks." Fintechs buying banks has been a part of the bank M&A scene for a while, but this deal involved a fintech entrepreneur buying a community bank's regulatory infrastructure for a custom rebuild rather than layering APIs on top of a conventional bank operating model. "By acquiring Twin City Bank, Buckley obtained an existing charter, FDIC insurance, a regulated legal entity, payment-system access and an institution with an exam history," Davis said. "The acquisition still required extensive scrutiny, but it provided a functioning banking chassis." Davis also noted that Twin City Bank was "big enough to have institutional infrastructure but small enough that Buckley didn't inherit a big branch network or legacy balance sheet to unload or unwind." Buckley initially filed a request to purchase 100% of Twin City Bancorp's voting shares in April of last year, according to Federal Register archives . The deal was subsequently permitted by the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco two months later. Twin City Bank had $70 million in assets under management when Buckley initially filed to acquire it via the holding company share purchase, according to its FDIC call reports . By the time it rebranded to Increase Bank a year later, its asset size had grown 48% to $114.5 million, with the largest single-quarter increase (40%) occurring between Q4 2025 and Q1 2026. The community bank has one physical branch in Longview, Washington, which continues to do business under the Twin City Bank name according to the branch's website . Banking services at that brick-and-mortar location are now offered by Increase Bank doing business as Twin City Bank. Read more:

Inside Upstart's journey to get a bank charter approval After the initial acquisition last summer, according to a company spokesperson, Twin City Bank received subsequent regulatory approvals for a name change and business plan change. Increase Bank "is a bank built by a team of product-obsessed operators for ambitious companies that are just as obsessed with building the best possible products for their customers," Buckley said in a statement. Fintech and banking consultant Annie DeStefano told American Banker that as the financial services ecosystem is growing, fintechs are exploring different ways to work with community banks. "New strategic options and paths will emerge," she said. "There is space for all the model types to work together, but the map will be redrawn [with] new specificity about which models make sense where." Increase, founded in 2020 by Buckley after his departure from Stripe, offers money movement APIs to fintechs such as Ramp and Stripe. The company's new banking core now offers direct connections to the Federal Reserve, The Clearing House and Visa, according to a company statement. "Increase Bank is the bank I needed at Stripe," Buckley said in a LinkedIn post . A company spokesperson confirmed with American Banker that Increase gained its own Federal Reserve master account through acquiring Twin City Bank, which has a master account according to Federal Reserve records. Increase's technology maintains the system of record for account balances and transactions and reconciles to the Federal Reserve through the FedNow rail system. "Increase Bank and our other bank partners each use the Increase banking core to connect directly to the Federal Reserve's payment systems," the spokesperson said. Increase's current sponsor bank partners include Grasshopper Bank, First Internet Bank of Indiana and Core Bank. Over time, according to Davis, Increase will no longer need to rely exclusively on its sponsor banks as it did before the acquisition. "It can potentially move faster, retain more of the economics tied to deposits and payments and give customers more confidence that the banking layer is strategically committed to the platform," he said. Davis also said that even with the new bank launch, Increase doesn't need to fully abandon its partner-bank model. "It can keep working with outside banks while using Increase Bank as a proprietary channel, giving it diversification and flexibility as the platform grows," he said.

proofCandidates.title: Fintech Increase Acquires Bank Charter, Eliminating BaaS Middleware That Broke Synapse
proofCandidates.summary: Increase acquired Twin City Bank of Longview, Washington, rebuilt it as Increase Bank, and became a federally regulated FDIC-member institution, collapsing the traditional three-layer BaaS structure into a single entity that simultaneously serves as technology provider and chartered bank. The charter eliminates the middleware ledger divergence risk responsible for the Synapse collapse that stranded approximately 100,000 consumers in 2024, replacing three separate ledgers with one authoritative system of record reconciling directly to the Federal Reserve in real time. Whether the charter's regulatory credibility and structural advantages outweigh the capital adequacy requirements, CRA obligations, and direct FDIC examination it imposes will determine if this model proves more durable than traditional BaaS under sustained regulatory pressure.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Fintech builders who route payments through Stripe, Ramp, or Gusto have been moving money through Increase's rails for years without knowing it. On Wednesday, the company behind that infrastructure did something the BaaS sector has talked about but rarely executed: it became the bank.

Increase launched Increase Bank — a federally regulated, FDIC-member institution — by acquiring and rebuilding Twin City Bank of Longview, Washington, into a purpose-built fintech infrastructure bank. The result collapses the three-layer structure that has defined banking-as-a-service for a decade, and that regulators have spent the past two years trying to police. There is no longer a sponsor bank on one side and a technology provider on the other. Increase is now both.

For fintech builders, that architectural change has a concrete implication: they can access payment rails, FDIC deposit accounts, and a real-time reconciling ledger through a single regulated entity — without stitching together a relationship with a sponsor bank and a separate API provider, and without the compliance handoffs between them that produced the Synapse disaster.

How BaaS Builds the Middle Layer That Keeps Breaking

The standard banking-as-a-service arrangement has always had a structural seam. A fintech facing the end customer, a middleware provider handling ledger management and API connectivity, and a chartered sponsor bank holding the regulated relationship — three entities, three ledgers, three sets of compliance obligations, and a cascade of third-party dependency that regulators have characterized as fundamentally difficult to supervise.

In July 2024, the Federal Reserve, FDIC, and OCC issued a joint statement flagging heightened risks in bank-fintech arrangements — risks that arise specifically when banks rely on partners to manage customer-facing activities. That statement came after a torrent of BaaS-related enforcement actions in early 2024, following which analysts at Klaros Group predicted that virtually every bank with a BaaS or embedded finance line of business would face some level of regulatory action. The core regulatory complaint was consistent: a fintech cannot outsource regulatory credibility to its sponsor bank, and the bank remains responsible for the customer-facing activity delivered through third parties — even when it cannot see or control what that third party's ledger says.

The specific mechanical failure that produced the Synapse bankruptcy illustrates why. When Synapse — the middleware provider at the center of dozens of fintech-bank arrangements — collapsed in 2024, neither the partner banks nor the fintech apps could resolve a ledger discrepancy that stranded an estimated 100,000 consumers and locked them out of their accounts. The discrepancy existed because Synapse maintained its own ledger, the partner banks maintained theirs, and the two did not agree. There was no authoritative single record.

What Increase Bank Does Differently at the Architecture Level

Increase has connected directly to the Federal Reserve since its founding in 2020 — not through an intermediary bank — which means its core has always been the system of record for account balances and transactions. That direct connection is what makes the bank charter a structural completion rather than a strategic pivot.

Increase Bank's technology maintains the system of record for account balances and transactions and reconciles to the Federal Reserve in real time. There is no middleware ledger that can diverge from the bank's records, because the bank and the technology are the same entity. A fintech client's account events are recorded once, in one ledger, held by one FDIC-member institution that also maintains direct connections to FedACH, Fedwire, Check 21, The Clearing House's Real-Time Payments network, FedNow, and Visa.

That architecture answers the specific failure mode the Synapse collapse made visible. The reconciliation gap that stranded 100,000 consumers was a ledger divergence problem — three entities maintaining separate records that could disagree. With Increase Bank, there is one entity and one record.

The combination also changes what a fintech client can do from day one. Karim Atiyeh, co-CEO of Ramp, described the operational difference in the bank's launch materials: "From the ability to open accounts synchronously, fully featured for every payment rail, from day one to the pace they ship new features, Increase just gets it." Synchronous account opening — an account that exists the moment an API call returns, rather than after a back-office process runs — is an architectural capability, not a product decision. It requires that the ledger and the charter be under the same roof.

Darragh Buckley's Methodical Path From Stripe to Bank Founder

The path from infrastructure provider to chartered bank ran through Twin City Bancorp, Inc., a small community bank holding company in Longview, Washington, about an hour north of Portland, Oregon. In April 2025, Buckley filed a change in bank control notice with the Federal Reserve Board, disclosing the acquisition of voting shares in Twin City Bancorp — a transaction that required FDIC approval before closing. The deal received FDIC non-objection for control and closed, and the renamed institution is now Increase Bank.

The acquisition was Buckley's third investment in a Washington community bank. That detail matters: Twin City Bank, with assets of approximately $75 million and a single branch, was a deliberately modest acquisition target — not a platform with an existing BaaS book of business to integrate, but a charter, an FDIC certificate, and a clean regulatory record with a Satisfactory Community Reinvestment Act rating.

Buckley's motivation traces directly to his time as Stripe's first employee, where he spent six years building and scaling Stripe's bank partner relationship with Wells Fargo and designing the programmatic controls for deposit account structures, money movement, regulation, cybersecurity, and privacy. The lesson he took from that work: when you are simultaneously solving business, technical, and risk problems, you need to drop down a layer. At Increase, dropping down a layer meant connecting directly to the Federal Reserve instead of relying on an intermediary bank to hold those connections. At Increase Bank, it means owning the intermediary entirely.

Increase became profitable in 2025, remains self-funded, and processed hundreds of billions of dollars annually across ACH, wires, RTP, FedNow, checks, and cards before the bank charter was added. Monthly payment volume tripled year over year. The company referred overflow business to competitors — including Grasshopper Bank and First Internet Bank of Indiana — rather than take on clients it could not serve well. That restraint is what makes the charter announcement legible as a natural evolution rather than an opportunistic pivot.

What the Charter Costs, and Why That Matters

Owning a bank charter is not a cost-free architectural upgrade. The same regulatory framework that gives Increase Bank its compliance credibility now imposes obligations that a pure-software BaaS provider does not face.

As an FDIC-member institution, Increase Bank is subject to regular safety-and-soundness examination, capital adequacy requirements, and full Community Reinvestment Act obligations — not just the contractual compliance commitments a fintech makes to a sponsor bank. Capital requirements constrain how quickly the bank can grow its balance sheet. CRA obligations require documented investment in the communities it serves. And regulatory examination means a federal agency now has direct access to the bank's records and operations, not just to its sponsor bank partner's records.

That tradeoff is the specific cost of eliminating the compliance handoff problem. A sponsored fintech can structure its relationship to minimize regulatory surface area. Increase Bank cannot. Whether that constraint produces a competitive disadvantage or a durable credibility advantage will depend on how the regulatory environment for BaaS alternatives evolves over the next several years. The sector that will watch that answer most closely is the one that just watched Synapse demonstrate what happens when the unregulated middle layer fails.

Diede van Lamoen, former Head of International at Stripe and an Increase advisor, framed the competitive stakes plainly: "A fintech company's ability to scale often comes down to whether they have a banking partner that can move at their pace, build solutions to the edge cases they are solving, and give them direct access to payment rails." The question the market will answer over the next two to three years is whether "banking partner" and "banking infrastructure" are more valuable when they are one entity subject to a single regulator — or whether the operational discipline the charter imposes makes Increase Bank slower to move than a lighter-weight BaaS competitor.

What Comes Next for a Sector Sorting Out Its Architecture

The fintech sector generated more than $650 billion in revenue in 2025 and grew at approximately 21% annually, according to McKinsey data cited in Increase's launch materials. That growth has happened almost entirely on top of the three-layer BaaS architecture the sector is now reassessing.

Increase is not the only fintech to pursue vertical integration through a bank acquisition. Column Financial Technologies, founded by William Hockey of Plaid, took the same approach with Northern California National Bank in 2021 and has built a national-charter-backed API banking infrastructure serving clients including Mercury and Brex. Lead Bank in Kansas City followed a similar trajectory under former Block executives. The common thread in each case is the same architectural insight Increase articulates: the compliance problem in BaaS is not a process problem that better contracts can fix — it is a structural problem that requires owning the regulated layer, not partnering with it.

What Increase Bank represents, in the context of an industry sorting out which BaaS models survive sustained regulatory pressure, is a data point: the charter-acquisition path is executable, and it is executable by a company that built its reputation specifically on engineering discipline and financial soundness rather than growth at speed.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between Increase Bank's model and standard banking-as-a-service?

Standard BaaS involves three separate entities: the fintech serving end customers, a middleware provider managing ledger and API connectivity, and a chartered sponsor bank holding the regulated relationship and deposit insurance. Each layer maintains its own records. When those records diverge — as they did in the Synapse bankruptcy — neither the bank nor the fintech has a clean path to resolution. Increase Bank collapses those three layers into one: Increase is the technology provider and the chartered FDIC-member bank simultaneously. Its core maintains a single system of record that reconciles directly to the Federal Reserve in real time, with no intermediate ledger that can diverge.

What happened with Synapse, and why does it matter here?

Synapse Financial Technologies was a BaaS middleware provider whose 2024 bankruptcy exposed a structural failure in the layered model: when Synapse's ledger diverged from its partner banks' records, approximately 100,000 end users were locked out of their accounts, with an estimated shortfall of $65 to $96 million. No single entity had an authoritative record of who was owed what. The Synapse failure demonstrated that the middleware layer in a BaaS arrangement carries a specific systemic risk — ledger divergence — that no amount of contractual language between the parties can fully resolve. Increase Bank's architecture eliminates the middleware layer, removing the divergence risk at its source.

Is owning a bank charter purely an advantage for a fintech company, or does it come with constraints?

Both. The charter gives Increase Bank regulatory credibility, direct payment rail access, and a single reconciling ledger — advantages that pure-software BaaS providers cannot match. But it also subjects Increase to capital adequacy requirements that constrain balance sheet growth, Community Reinvestment Act obligations that require investment in served communities, and direct regulatory examination by the FDIC. A partner-model BaaS provider can structure its operations to minimize regulatory surface area in ways a chartered bank cannot. Whether the credibility advantage outweighs the flexibility constraint is the competitive question the next several years of operating data will answer.

Who does Increase Bank currently serve, and what payments can it handle?

Increase's existing clients include Gusto, Ramp, and Stripe — companies that move money at scale across a range of payment types. Through Increase Bank's direct connections, it can process ACH transfers, wire transfers, Real-Time Payments via The Clearing House, FedNow transactions, check transfers under Check 21, and card issuance through Visa — all via a single API and a single chartered institution. The bank's FDIC membership and Federal Reserve connections were in place operationally before the charter conversion, meaning clients did not need to rebuild integrations when Increase Bank launched.
