proofCandidates.title: Founder of fintech Increase buys a bank in Washington state
proofCandidates.summary: Increase, a fintech founded by former Stripe employee Darragh Buckley, has acquired Twin City Bancorp (holding company for Twin City Bank in Longview, Washington) and rebranded it as Increase Bank after receiving Federal Reserve regulatory approval in June 2025, adding bank charter capabilities to serve as a \"regulated banking partner\" for fintech clients. Twin City Bank had approximately $114.6 million in assets as of March 31, and Buckley declined to disclose the purchase price. Increase processes an estimated $500 billion annually for clients including Stripe, Ramp, and Gusto, positioning the newly chartered bank to compete for new fintech business seeking culturally aligned banking partners.
proofCandidates.fullText: After acquiring a small Longview, Washington lender, a former Stripe employee has added bank charter capabilities to his fintech Increase, aiming to be a “regulated banking partner” for fellow fintech clients. Increase founder Darragh Buckley acquired Twin City Bancorp, the holding company for Twin City Bank, about one year ago and rebranded it as Increase Bank after receiving regulatory approval for the name and business plan changes. Buckley declined to share a purchase price. Increase, which handles money movement and storage and card issuing for firms such as payroll service providers, neobanks, loan servicing and payment companies, launched its bank identity Wednesday. The move was a long time coming and not necessarily influenced by the bank regulatory environment, Buckley said, noting he started the company six years ago with the goal of marrying a bank and technology company. Buckley called Increase a lender “for ambitious technology companies,” and the bank launch is geared more toward winning new business over expanding existing business. “For years, I needed a bank with good product sense,” he wrote in a Wednesday LinkedIn post. “One that grasped the possibilities of software and couldn’t stand to see them stifled. Increase Bank is the bank I needed at Stripe.” Buckley spent six years at Stripe before founding Increase in 2020, according to his LinkedIn profile. Increase works with Stripe and fintechs Ramp and Gusto, which use Increase’s technology to process some $500 billion annually, Buckley wrote. Increase offers a modern banking core with direct connections to the Federal Reserve, The Clearing House, and Visa. The fintech’s technology holds the system of record for account balances and transactions and reconciles to the Fed in real time, allowing fintechs to control accounts and interact with their bank more quickly, according to a news release. “Being able to work more closely with a bank, especially with a bank that’s culturally similar to us, and therefore has a lot of product-centricity, to enable our users to have reliable, transparent, flexible services is great,” Buckley said Thursday. The Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco approved Buckley’s acquisition of 100% of the voting shares of Twin City Bancorp in June 2025. Single-branch Twin City had about $114.6 million in assets as of March 31. “I’ve been making bank investments for a few years now. Twin City Bank is a tidy, profitable bank that happens to be relatively close to me,” Buckley said. Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Banking Dive free daily newsletter Jon Jones is president and CEO of Increase Bank. Jones was CEO of Washington Business Bank, which was bought by Sound Credit Union in January 2025. Jones has also been a board member of the Federal Home Loan Bank of Des Moines for about six years, according to his LinkedIn profile. Increase also works with Grasshopper Bank, Indiana-based First Internet Bank and Core Bank, and those partnerships remain important, Buckley said. “We have many users who fundamentally need to be multi-bank, either for operational reasons or even their own corporate governance reasons,” he said. “A lot of times, the financial services that get provided through us are crucial to the business.” Clarification: This story’s headline has been updated to more clearly reflect that Buckley bought the bank.

proofCandidates.title: The Banking Infrastructure Founder Is Buying Community Banks - and That's the Point
proofCandidates.summary: Darragh Buckley, founder of Increase (a fintech processing over $100 billion annually by connecting directly to the Federal Reserve), has made a personal investment in Twin City Bank in Longview, Washington, acquiring a stake exceeding the 10% FDIC disclosure threshold—this being his third investment in a Washington community bank. Unlike typical fintech-bank partnerships where founders seek charters or regulatory control, Buckley frames this as an effort to understand banking infrastructure from the inside rather than building around it through APIs. The move positions Buckley's approach as distinct from the 2026 trend of fintechs and banks acquiring each other to own the opposite side of the relationship, with the article suggesting this strategy reflects a deeper bet on community banking's role in modernizing financial services.
proofCandidates.fullText: News/ Articles/ Articles Details The Banking Infrastructure Founder Is Buying Community Banks - and That's the Point Generated by AI Agent Arjun Varma Reviewed by The Newsroom Wednesday, Jul 29, 2026 9:19 am ET 3min read Aime Summary Overview The 5 Ws Opposite Sides Infobox - Darragh Buckley, founder of $100B/year fintech865201-- Increase, invested in Washington community bank Twin City, exceeding 10% FDIC threshold as personal stake. - Unlike typical fintech-bank partnerships, Buckley emphasizes understanding banking infrastructure from within, not through API layers or charter acquisitions. - His third Washington bank investment signals strategic focus on community banking's role in modernizing relationships while avoiding corporate control. - The move contrasts with 2026 fintech trends of charter chasing and bank acquisitions, highlighting infrastructure founders who prioritize operational depth over regulatory expansion. Darragh Buckley was employee number one at Stripe. He helped build the system that lets millions of companies accept payments online. Then he left and started Increase, a company that sits a layer below most fintech infrastructure: it connects directly to the Federal Reserve and exposes core banking functions through APIs. With fewer than 20 people, Increase now processes over $100 billion annually. And he just bought a significant stake in a small community bank in Longview, Washington. The headline version of this story would be about a fintech founder trying to own his rails. Buckley says that's not what's happening. The Twin City Bank stake - which exceeds the 10% threshold that requires FDIC disclosure - is a personal investment, not a corporate one. It's also his third investment in a Washington community bank. The FDIC approved it in 2026. The obvious question is why someone building next-generation banking infrastructure would invest in legacy institutions that exist in a town an hour north of Portland. The less obvious question, which is the more interesting one, is whether Buckley is doing something most fintech founders don't bother with: learning what the actual plumbing of banking looks like from the inside, rather than from the outside looking in. Most fintechs treat banks as black boxes. You build an API, you find a partner bank that will lend you its charter, you share revenue, and you hope the compliance layer doesn't blow up. That's the banking-as-a-service model. It works until it doesn't - and over the past two years, it hasn't. Regulatory scrutiny of BaaS partnerships has intensified. Compliance burdens have grown. Several high-profile BaaS relationships have collapsed, leaving fintechs scrambling. Increase was founded to avoid that problem at the architectural level. Instead of connecting to banks one by one - which is how most BaaS platforms work - Increase connects directly to the Federal Reserve and operates its own banking core. Its customers, including Ramp and Pipe, are other fintechs that need reliable money movement. But even if you've built a better layer, you still need to understand what happens at the bottom. The way to build software that improves an industry is not to read about it from the top. It's to look at the smallest instance of the problem and see what's actually broken. Buckley has said publicly that he envisions a future where community banks serve specific communities - dentists, families managing elderly parents' finances, local businesses that still need a relationship with someone who understands their cash flow. That's not a sexy vision. It doesn't read well in a pitch deck. But it's also not wrong. Community banks hold roughly a quarter of U.S. banking deposits, and they're the ones that will need to modernize or lose their customers to whoever figures out how to serve them digitally without killing the relationship model. The Twin City investment sends a signal, but not the one the competitor-funded PR campaign apparently tried to paint. This isn't about Increase trying to own a bank. Buckley's been clear about that. It's about a founder who understands that the people building the rails need to understand what's running on them. I suspect the real bet here is simpler than any of the narratives. Buckley probably thinks that if fintech infrastructure companies stay disconnected from the institutions they're trying to serve, they'll keep building the wrong things. The way to avoid that is not to buy the bank. It's to understand it well enough that you don't need to. This is part of a broader pattern in fintech right now. The first half of 2026 has seen two dozen fintech-related companies apply for or conditionally receive bank charters from the OCC. Circle Internet Group received its national trust bank charter in July. Morgan Stanley and Nomura's Laser Digital both got conditional approvals. On the flip side, banks are buying fintechs - Capital One announced plans to acquire Brex, Coastal Community Bank announced plans to acquire its BaaS partner GreenFi. Everyone is trying to own the other side of the relationship. Buckley is doing something different. He's not chasing a charter for Increase, and he's not trying to make Twin City Bank into an Increase project. He's putting his own money where the action is - in the small institutions that the fintech industry talks about serving but rarely visits. The limitation, of course, is that I don't know exactly how large his Twin City stake is - the disclosure only says it exceeds 10%. It could be 11%, it could be a controlling interest. The exact number changes the read. At the low end, it's a genuine community investment. At the high end, it's a quiet power play that Buckley isn't yet ready to describe publicly. Either way, the pattern of three Washington bank investments is a signal about where he thinks the future of banking infrastructure needs to connect. The test to watch is whether Increase's product decisions start reflecting a deeper understanding of community banking. If they do, Buckley bought insight. If they don't, he just bought a nice diversification. The product will tell. What this suggests for anyone evaluating fintech infrastructure companies: the founders who understand the institutions they're serving - not just the APIs they're building - tend to build things that last. The ones who don't, tend to get acquired by the banks they were supposed to replace. The question for Buckley's investors isn't whether Increase needs a bank charter. It's whether Increase can stay small, stay focused on the plumbing nobody else wants to touch, and process $100 billion with fewer than 20 people while the bigger companies spend hundreds of millions chasing charters they can't figure out how to use. That's a different kind of leverage, and it's harder to see coming. Announcing the launch of Increase Bank, bringing a modern bank core together with regulated banking services to help teams build the best financial products with greater speed, precision, and control. Founded in 2020, Increase’s banking infrastructure and APIs enable companies like Gusto, Ramp, and Stripe to move, store, and lend hundreds of billions of dollars. With the addition of Increase Bank, an FDIC-member institution, fintech companies now have access to a bank engineered for their needs. proofCandidates.fullText:
core offering: Increase operates an enterprise-grade, API-first banking platform that gives technology companies direct programmatic access to U.S. payment and banking rails (FedACH, Fedwire, FedNow, Visa, Mastercard, and The Clearing House RTP). The platform exposes bare-metal primitives for storing, moving, and reconciling money, plus a unified API and dashboard to monitor balances and transactions in real time. Increase partners with Federal Reserve member banks to sponsor the programs it powers.
differentiator: Increase differentiates by offering bare-metal, direct-to-network API access rather than abstracted banking layers. It provides transparent data, fewer dependencies, stability and redundancy, and faster build times. The company operates as a standalone parallel core, eliminating dependencies on legacy bank core systems for both fintech companies and banks.
functional benefit: Direct access to FedACH, Fedwire, Check 21, RTP, FedNow, and Visa networks. Same-day ACH by default hitting every Fed window. Real-time settlement tracking from the Federal Reserve. Automatic correlation of ACH and Check returns. Instant virtual and physical card issuance with real-time authorization control. Push-to-card transfers to billions of eligible Visa and Mastercard cards. FDIC insurance access via IntraFi network for deposits. Flexible account structures with unlimited account numbers for reconciliation. Custom compliance programs tailored to specific businesses.
problem solved: Technology companies building financial products face limitations with traditional banking infrastructure that abstracts away network complexity. Increase enables them to programmatically store, move, and reconcile money by connecting directly to Federal Reserve networks (FedACH, Fedwire, FedNow), The Clearing House RTP network, and Visa, providing bare-metal API access with full visibility into payment lifecycles, real-time authorization control, and flexible account structures.
quantifiable outcome: Increase customers store and send billions of dollars per month through the platform.
product overview: Increase is an enterprise-grade banking API platform providing a unified suite of payment and banking primitives for technology companies. The core platform consists of 8 payment products: ACH (FedACH), Bank Accounts, Cards (Visa), Checks (Check 21), FedNow, Real-Time Payments (RTP), Push-to-Card (Visa Direct/Mastercard Send), and Wires (Fedwire). These are complemented by 7 solution modules—Bill Pay, Payroll, Wallets, Embedded Lending, Fund Administration, Vertical SaaS, and Sponsor Banking—that address specific use cases built on top of the core APIs. The platform connects directly to Federal Reserve networks and major financial networks (Visa, The Clearing House), offering bare-metal API access rather than abstracted complexity, with a focus on transparent data, stability, and faster build times.

proofCandidates.title: Why AI Compute Comes in Rectangles — Erik Bernhardsson, Modal CEO — Latent Space
proofCandidates.summary: Modal CEO Erik Bernhardsson discussed the company's growth, including a $750 million Series D at a $16B valuation and nearly three billion sandboxes. He explained that GPU demand is irregular, not rectangular, and that sandboxes now account for about a third of revenue. He also noted the risk of GPU prices falling if capacity is locked in.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Warm welcome to Basil Chatha, our newest cohost from the Forward Deployed side of the AI Engineering world! We’ll be ramping up a new show with him and couldn’t pass up an interview with Modal’s CEO Eric on the occasion of their monster Series D! Two years ago, we spoke with Erik Bernhardsson about his vision for truly serverless AI infrastructure: developers should be able to run code without provisioning clusters, predicting load, or paying for idle resources. CTO Akshat then joined us to talk about Modal’s infra primitives and stack to offer those primitives and agent experience. A lot has changed in the past 5 months. Since their $5B series C, Modal now reports it crossed $1 billion in annualized run rate, raised a $750 million Series D at a $16B valuation, and has spun up nearly three billion sandboxes. In this conversation, Erik joins Vibhu to explain the infrastructure and economics behind that growth—and why demand for compute rarely looks like the contracts used to buy it. Watch the full conversation on YouTube → GPU demand isn’t rectangular A typical capacity contract gives a customer a fixed number of GPUs for a fixed period. Plot capacity against time and you get a rectangle. Real workloads behave differently: they grow, spike, and fall throughout the day. Buy enough for the peak and you pay for idle hardware; buy less and you risk missing demand. Erik describes Modal’s bet as a kind of duration transformation: pool demand across thousands of customers, secure capacity underneath, and let each customer use what they need when they need it. The smoother the aggregate demand, the more useful that pool can be. It’s a useful companion to our conversation with SF Compute’s Evan Conrad: Evan focuses on making capacity tradeable; Erik focuses on making it usable in smaller, elastic slices. There is a financial risk on the other side. If a provider locks in capacity at today’s prices and GPU prices later fall, it can be left holding expensive supply. Erik says he doesn’t expect an imminent collapse, but thinks the possibility matters when building the business. Jump to the GPU price discussion → The sandbox that almost didn’t make it Modal launched sandboxes after Erik and cofounder Akshat Bubna noticed that language models could generate code—and that someone would need a place to run it. Early adoption was modest enough that the team discussed shutting the product down. Then coding agents, background agents, and reinforcement learning created new demand. Erik says sandboxes have grown to roughly a third of Modal’s revenue, a result he didn’t predict at launch. That growth also changes what infrastructure has to do. An agent may create an environment, run code, inspect the result, and try again many times. The latency of starting and restoring those environments becomes part of the experience. In our recent interview with Akshat, we explored this shift from developer experience to agent experience; here Erik adds the product and business story. Jump to the sandbox discussion → Fast startup is an infrastructure feature Elasticity only works if capacity can arrive quickly enough to matter. Modal’s serverless GPU write-up describes the machinery: a buffer of available GPUs, a custom filesystem, process checkpointing, and GPU memory snapshots. Those pieces reduce the work needed to bring another model replica online. It is a concrete example of how infrastructure decisions show up in an application’s responsiveness and cost. We also discuss Erik’s path from Spotify’s recommendation system to Modal, how the company buys compute, alternatives to NVIDIA, forward-deployed engineers, and why code review is optional at Modal. proofCandidates.title: Nvidia wins fast-growing AI startup Modal for new central processors
proofCandidates.summary: Modal, an AI cloud-computing startup, will adopt Nvidia's Vera central processor for hosting AI agents, after raising $750 million at a $15.75 billion valuation. The company expects $1 billion in sales next year and will run Nvidia chips alongside Intel and AMD in a mixed fleet.
proofCandidates.fullText:
- Artificial Intelligence
- 2 min read
Nvidia wins fast-growing AI startup Modal for new central processors
Modal, a cloud-computing startup dedicated to AI development, has partnered with Nvidia to adopt their new Vera chip, transitioning away from Intel and AMD processors. This strategic shift comes after raising $750 million in funding, boosting Modal's valuation to $15.75 billion. The company has also reported substantial revenue growth over the past year and will continue to explore additional hardware options as they arise.
Nvidia has won central processor chip business with another fast-growing AI startup that until now relied entirely on chips from Intel and AMD, an early sign that its push into a market long controlled by those two rivals has traction.
Modal, a cloud-computing startup that rents out computing power to AI developers, said it plans to start using Nvidia's new Vera central processor for the first time for hosting agents, the AI systems that can carry out long-running tasks for human users. Modal until now has run such work only on Intel and AMD chips.
Modal last week raised $750 million in a funding round led by Accel at a $15.75 billion valuation, saying it is on track to record $1 billion in sales over the next year. Modal said usage of its services has tripled and revenue has grown more than 15 times year-over-year.
Modal said Monday that early tests showed the new Nvidia chip doubled the amount of work that AI agents can get done, prompting the company to support Nvidia's chip design for the first time, which will require some deep software changes on Modal's side.
But Chief Executive Erik Bernhardsson was careful to stress it is not abandoning its existing suppliers. The company said it will run the Nvidia chips alongside its current Intel and AMD offerings in a mixed fleet, putting each job on whatever hardware runs it best.
Bernhardsson said the tests were run against the Intel and AMD chips already on the market. Both Nvidia rivals are developing newer models that could narrow the gap with Nvidia.
"We'll test them when they're available," he said, adding that running a mixed setup means the company "can always deploy whatever hardware performs best."
Nvidia has told investors it expects to generate at least $20 billion from Vera chip sales this fiscal year, its opening bid for a market it values at roughly $200 billion. Nvidia has previously said OpenAI, Anthropic and Oracle also plan to use the chips, along with AI startups such as Perplexity.

proofCandidates.title: Modal taps Nvidia Vera CPUs after firm's internal tests show 2x throughput over Intel and AMD chips — AI agentic workflows said to favor Arm chips, but firm will keep x86 chips deployed in heterogeneo
proofCandidates.summary: Nvidia's Vera CPUs delivered twice the throughput of AMD and Intel processors in Modal's tests, but Modal will keep x86 chips in a heterogeneous fleet. Modal expects $1 billion in annual revenue within a year, and Nvidia expects Vera sales to generate at least $20 billion this fiscal year.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Nvidia has earned billions selling AI accelerators, but with the emergence of agentic AI, CPUs are going to play a considerably more significant role than before, which creates new opportunities for the company. Reuters reports that Nvidia has secured a major design win with its Vera CPUs with AI cloud provider Modal. According to Modal, preliminary evaluations showed that Vera could deliver twice the throughput of its existing AMD and Intel processors, although the company does not intend to cease using CPUs from its current suppliers.

Modal provides cloud infrastructure that enables AI developers to deploy AI agents that can perform complex operations autonomously over extended periods. Such workloads require substantial CPU resources for software execution, data processing, and other tasks that cannot be efficiently handled by GPUs. Modal currently relies exclusively on AMD and Intel processors for these operations, but its tests indicate that Nvidia's new Vera CPUs could significantly improve performance in its specific workloads. Of course, since Vera is based on an Arm instruction set architecture, Modal's decision to adopt Vera will require substantial modifications to its software. Nevertheless, Modal believes that the potential performance improvements justify the additional engineering effort.

The reported 2x throughput advantage is particularly interesting because agentic AI workloads can involve numerous independent tasks that compete for CPU cores, cache capacity, and memory bandwidth. However, Modal has not disclosed detailed benchmark configurations it used, specific AMD and Intel processor models, or performance-per-watt figures. Consequently, it remains unclear whether Vera's advantage is enabled by advantages of its Arm v9.2-based Olympus CPU cores that can decode and execute up to 10 instructions per cycle, its memory subsystem with 1.2 TB/s of bandwidth, or other architectural characteristics. Also note that tests compared Vera against currently available AMD and Intel processors rather than their upcoming generations that will compete against Vera in the coming years.

Latest Videos From Tom's Hardware Watch full video here:

Since Modal cannot port all of its software to Arm ISA overnight, the company will continue using x86 CPUs from AMD and Intel, according to Modal chief executive Erik Bernhardsson. Rather than sticking to one ISA for everything, Modal intends to operate a heterogeneous server fleet and select the most suitable processors for each workload. Naturally, the company intends to evaluate upcoming AMD and Intel processors once they become available to make its choices in the future.

For Nvidia, the agreement represents a major step toward making Vera a standalone server processor that commands a major share of the server market. The company expects Vera sales to generate at least $20 billion during its current fiscal year and estimates the potential total available market for these CPUs is approximately $200 billion. The company is on track to sell at least four million Vera CPUs in fiscal 2026.

The announcement comes shortly after Modal secured $750 million in financing led by Accel, which valued the company at $15.75 billion. Modal expects its annual revenue to reach $1 billion within the next year. The company's service consumption has increased 3X in the last 12 months, while revenue has surged more than 15 times compared with the previous year, Reuters reports.

Modal Had To Make Massive Changes To Move To NVIDIA's Vera CPUs As They Previously Relied on x86 Chips, But The Shift Granted Them A 2x Boost The NVIDIA Vera CPU continues to be changing the market perception of Arm-based CPUs for Agentic AI use cases. Arm itself has highlighted the advantages of its AGI CPUs over x86 options, but NVIDIA's option seems to be quickly becoming the choice for many firms that were previously running an x86 chip. Related Story Intel’s Jeff McVeigh Says Developers Shouldn’t Need Separate Software Paths For x86 CPUs, As AMD Folds Its ZenDNN Optimizations Into oneDNN Modal is one such firm that recently received its first Vera CPU servers at their San Francisco offices. The company has so far relied solely on x86 systems featuring AMD & Intel chips, so the move to an Arm-based ecosystem required changes to the infrastructure & image-built systems. Despite the painstaking changes, Modal terms the move to NVIDIA Vera as very impressive, delivering a 2x increase in AI throughput across Agentic AI sandboxes, and calling it an "incredibly compelling option". In most systems, throughput and latency are a tradeoff. Latency can be defined as the time that elapses from the start to the end of a task.

Throughput is the quantity of completed tasks per unit time. This tests the host system’s ability to concurrently interleave processes and make progress on them all simultaneously. The more densely you pack tasks, the higher the throughput. But once the CPU becomes fully utilized, individual task latency suffers due to contention. In terms of the Modal scheduler, it’s always tempting for us to run at a higher packing density, to squeeze more juice out of the host machines we have, and to offer a higher absolute scale that users can reach. But just as workloads are spiky within their containers, the absolute scale of the containers in our cluster is also spiky, which leaves us at the risk of overpacking host machines. To test NVIDIA Vera, Modal built a set of representative workloads and benchmarks for agentic sandboxes. This involves the development of "Agentless Agent Bench," which hosts a collection of 50 Terminal-Bench oracle solutions and verifiers. The benchmark shows both linear completion and concurrent throughput figures. The first tests showcased a nice improvement over x86 chips, but these were run without any load, essentially making them a pure straight-line latency test. Under load, NVIDIA's Vera CPU becomes a completely different beast. In throughput, Vera offered a 2x increase over an equivalent Intel Xeon "Granite Rapids" chip. This lead comes from the fact that unlike x86 CPUs, Vera doesn't slow down as jobs accumulate but rather rips through each one of them at its original pace. The results speak for themselves: Versus Intel Xeon: Up to 2x the task throughput per core.

Versus AMD EPYC: Over 6x the task throughput at 150 concurrent containers, with 124 logical CPUs enabled on each system. Vera’s killer feature is the ability to hold up under contention. Its high memory bandwidth allows for significantly more container workloads to pack per core, without CPU throttling - which explains why Vera pulls so far ahead of the alternatives in our benchmarks. At added CPU counts, the alternatives hit early throughput plateaus, while Vera continues to improve, suggesting we could push it even further than the node we had access to for benchmarking. Modal’s shift to NVIDIA’s Vera CPUs, despite the significant infrastructure and image-building changes needed to move from x86, delivered a clear 2× throughput boost in Agentic AI sandboxes. Under load, Vera maintains strong performance without the throttling typical of Intel and AMD CPUs, thanks to its high memory bandwidth and ability to pack more concurrent workloads per core. The result is a compelling Arm-based option that scales more effectively for dense, contention-heavy agentic workloads. proofCandidates.title: Modal Plans NVIDIA Vera Rollout for Sandboxes in First Arm Move
proofCandidates.summary: Modal announced plans to roll out NVIDIA's Vera Arm-based CPUs for its Sandboxes, its first departure from an all-x86 fleet. Benchmarks showed up to double the task throughput of an equivalent x86 machine under load. The company will work with NVIDIA and cloud providers to scale the Vera fleet.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Modal said in a company blog post on October 19, 2026 that it plans to roll out support for NVIDIA’s Arm-based Vera CPU to power Modal Sandboxes, the company’s first departure from an all-x86 fleet, after benchmark results it published showed up to double the task throughput of an equivalent x86 machine under load. NVIDIA hand-delivered Modal’s first Vera CPU server to the company’s San Francisco office in the week before the announcement, Modal said. Vera is NVIDIA’s Arm-compatible processor, built for the Vera Rubin GPU platform but also available as a standalone CPU server. Bringing Arm into the fleet would require changes across Modal’s infrastructure and image build system, which the company described as a huge change after a long history of running exclusively x86 machines. Multi-Tenant Noise and Burst Capacity Orchestrating a Sandbox product means running hundreds of concurrent containers and virtual machines on each cloud host, and Modal said the resulting multi-tenant clusters are noisy. Resource usage can be extremely spiky: a sandbox may sit mostly idle while waiting on a language model and then see CPU usage surge 10x above baseline because of an npm install or an expensive grep command. The shape of each workload is only known at runtime, so resource sizing is often a guess, and heterogeneous tenants packed into a single pool of compute create noisy-neighbor problems, where one customer’s behavior degrades another’s performance. Rather than require fixed reservations sized to maximum usage, Modal Sandboxes support bursting, which lets users reserve guaranteed capacity for their P50 usage and trust that padding inside the host node will absorb transient spikes. Modal said the approach has saved users millions of dollars, but acknowledged that it raises exposure to the noisy-neighbor effects that strict limits would otherwise avoid. Modal identified two prevalent Sandbox use cases: background agents, citing Ramp Inspect and agents running on Niteshift, and reinforcement-learning rollouts. Most training setups are still synchronous, the company said, so an entire fanout of CPU-bound rollouts must complete before idle GPUs can move to the next step, which means time saved on CPU is time saved on GPU. For background agents, the company said, faster execution means faster answers and lower CPU time, driving down the cost of goods sold. The Agentless Agent Bench To measure Vera, Modal built and released Agentless Agent Bench, a collection of 50 Terminal-Bench oracle solutions and verifiers with all network calls stripped out, prewarmed in concurrent Docker containers. Modal said building an agentic benchmark is difficult because most of the work done on its sandbox servers is not CPU-bound, so it assembled a concurrent and heterogeneous mix of the tasks agents and reinforcement-learning processes actually perform on the CPU, including compilation, file grepping, git operations and device emulation. According to the public repository, the benchmark is built on the terminal-bench-2.1 task dataset with Dockerfiles ported for Arm compatibility, and a run counts as completed only if the task verifier passes. In serial testing on an unloaded machine, which measures straight-line per-task latency, Modal found Vera was often faster than the other processors tested — Intel GNR, AMD Zen 5, and AWS Graviton 4 and 5 — but not always, and not by a particularly large margin, and the post’s author described being initially skeptical of the results. Under load, Modal reported, the results diverged. The throughput test increases the number of concurrent containers on the machine and loops as many verified task completions as possible in a fixed time. Modal said its early benchmarking runs showed up to double the task throughput on Vera compared with an equivalent x86 GNR machine, while individual task latency measured equal to or lower than on x86. In most systems, throughput and latency trade off as packing density rises until the CPU saturates, but Modal said Vera did not slow down as jobs accumulated and kept completing tasks at its original pace. Modal reported that Vera kept improving as logical CPU counts rose, while the other tested processors hit early throughput plateaus. The physical core boundaries of the tested machines were 128 for Intel GNR, 96 for Graviton and the GNR virtual machine, and 88 for Vera. Because the alternatives plateaued early, Modal said its results suggest it could push Vera even further than the single benchmark node it had access to. The company attributes Vera’s advantage under contention to its high memory bandwidth, which it said allows significantly more container workloads to pack onto each core without CPU throttling. For Modal’s scheduler, that means greater packing density and more forgiving burst protection; for Sandbox users, the company said, it means higher absolute scale and throughput without sacrificing latency. Vera’s Design and Production Status NVIDIA launched Vera on March 16, 2026 at its GTC conference, describing it as a processor purpose-built for agentic AI and reinforcement learning. The chip has 88 custom NVIDIA-designed Olympus cores, each able to run two tasks through a feature NVIDIA calls Spatial Multithreading, and a second-generation low-power memory subsystem built on LPDDR5X that delivers up to 1.2 TB/s of bandwidth. NVIDIA claims Vera delivers results with twice the efficiency and 50% faster than traditional CPUs. At the launch, NVIDIA also introduced a Vera CPU rack integrating 256 liquid-cooled CPUs, which it said can sustain more than 22,500 concurrent CPU environments, each running independently at full performance. NVIDIA said Vera is in full production, with partner availability in the second half of 2026, and named Alibaba Cloud, ByteDance, CoreWeave, Lambda, Nebius, Nscale and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure among the cloud providers planning to deploy the CPU. Modal said it intends to work closely with NVIDIA and cloud providers to scale up its Vera fleet as the rollout proceeds.

proofCandidates.title: Modal Labs Sandboxes Hits $300M Run Rate: Isolated Code Execution Becomes Its Own Market
proofCandidates.summary: Modal Labs crossed $1 billion in annualized run rate and closed a $750 million Series D at a $15.75 billion valuation. Its Sandboxes product, an isolated code execution environment, now generates $300 million in annualized revenue, accounting for 30% of total ARR. proofCandidates.fullText: AI infrastructure startup Modal has crossed $1 billion in annualized run rate and closed Modal's $750M Series D announcement at a $15.75 billion post-money valuation, cementing its status as New York City's highest-valued private AI infrastructure company — more than tripling a number it had set just five months earlier. The round's headline figure is striking, but the detail that signals a structural shift in the AI stack is buried a few paragraphs into CEO Erik Bernhardsson's October 14 announcement blog post: a product Modal launched in 2023 that almost nobody predicted would become a standalone business — Sandboxes, the company's isolated virtual machine execution environment — has grown into a $300 million annualized revenue line on its own, accounting for roughly 30 percent of Modal's total ARR and powering close to 3 billion sandboxes spun up since launch. That number is not a rounding error or a promotional figure. It is the first public evidence that isolated code execution — the infrastructure layer that lets AI agents run untrusted, dynamically generated code safely — has crossed the threshold from niche feature to billion-dollar market category. Bernhardsson wrote in the announcement: "Just five months ago, when we announced our Series C, I wrote that demand was accelerating. Since then, usage has tripled and we've grown more than 15x year-over-year. We recently crossed $1B in annualized run rate with no sign of slowing down." From $300M to $1B in Five Months When Modal announced its Series C at $4.65 billion in May 2026, it had just crossed $300 million in annualized revenue. In the five months since, usage tripled and revenue grew more than 15 times year over year. The leap from $4.65 billion to $15.75 billion — a 3.4x step-up in under half a year — reflects a market now pricing AI infrastructure companies at premiums that would have looked implausible in any prior software cycle. The $750 million raise brings Modal's cumulative funding past $1.2 billion. Kleiner Perkins joined as a new investor alongside Accel's lead, with returning backers Menlo Ventures, General Catalyst, Redpoint, Lux Capital, Amplify Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures all participating. The near-consensus participation from that group of investors is itself a data point: each of those firms had already evaluated Modal's growth trajectory and chose to increase its exposure. What Modal Actually Does Founded in 2021 and headquartered in New York, Modal lets developers run compute-intensive workloads — AI model training, large language model inference, batch processing, agent pipelines — without managing their own servers. To do it, the company discarded most of the standard cloud software stack and built a custom Rust container runtime from scratch alongside its own file system, image builder, scheduler, and networking layer. That infrastructure draws on spare capacity from a pool now spanning more than 20 clouds, including AWS, Google Cloud, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The result is a platform that can spin up a container in milliseconds and scale GPU workloads elastically from zero to thousands of GPUs in seconds — without the provisioning overhead of traditional cloud infrastructure or the Kubernetes complexity of managing it manually. Modal's core primitive, called Functions, lets a developer write ordinary Python code with a decorator — @app.function() — and have it execute on GPUs anywhere in the capacity pool with a .remote() call. Real-world deployments include image generation with diffusion models, music generation (Suno's AI music platform runs on Modal), LLM inference via open-source serving frameworks including vLLM and SGLang, and large-scale model training runs. Sandboxes: Isolated Code Execution Becomes Its Own Market Perhaps the most editorially significant detail in Bernhardsson's announcement is what the Sandboxes numbers reveal about the AI stack's evolving structure. The product launched in 2023 after Modal's team noticed a pattern: developers were using large language models to generate code that also needed to run, and they needed a safe place to execute it. Sandboxes provide ephemeral, isolated virtual machine environments for running untrusted or dynamically generated code. Infrastructure now supports up to 1 million running concurrently, and the virtual machine layer became generally available with the Series D announcement. Customers including Ramp and Cognition have deployed Sandboxes in production for background agent pipelines; additional customers span AI coding platforms, reinforcement learning researchers, and teams building autonomous agent systems. Sandboxes have grown this fast because AI systems are changing. As agentic AI — models that autonomously plan and execute multi-step tasks using tools, loops, and code — moves from prototype to production deployment, the need for isolated execution environments scales proportionally. Every agentic system that generates and runs code needs a clean, parallel container that cannot interfere with its host or adjacent runs. Reinforcement learning post-training pipelines, which require thousands of simultaneous rollout executions, are the same story at training scale. Modal's ability to spin up and tear down a million concurrent containers positions it as potential default infrastructure for both workload classes. The Founders Behind the Platform Modal was co-founded by CEO Erik Bernhardsson and CTO Akshat Bubna. Bernhardsson, a Swedish engineer who trained in physics at KTH in Stockholm, joined Spotify in 2008 and spent roughly six years there building Spotify's music recommendation engine — including the groundwork for Discover Weekly, Related Artists, and Radio. Along the way he open-sourced two widely adopted infrastructure tools: Luigi and Annoy open-source tools — Luigi being a workflow engine with more than 10,000 GitHub stars, and Annoy an approximate nearest-neighbor library. He later served as CTO of online mortgage lender Better.com, where he ran an engineering organization of roughly 300 people, before founding Modal in 2021. Bubna, Modal's CTO, previously worked as an early engineer at Scale AI, the data infrastructure company. The team has grown past 200 people and operates from offices in New York, San Francisco, and Stockholm. Modal opened a London office in Marble Arch earlier this year with capacity for up to 40 staff. What's Next: Reinforcement Learning and Post-Training Infrastructure Modal has been explicit about where the fresh capital is headed. The company is building dedicated reinforcement learning and post-training products — the techniques used to refine and align AI models after initial pre-training — and plans to expand its multi-node training clusters for customers running large-scale GPU jobs. On the inference side, Modal is expanding Modal Servers, its product for persistent HTTP model serving, and shipping new features for LLM serving efficiency, including Endpoint Candidates. The push into RL and post-training reflects a structural shift in competitive AI development. As frontier model weights from Meta, Mistral, and others become widely available, differentiation for AI product companies is shifting to the post-training layer—custom fine-tuning, reward modeling, and continual learning loops. All of those workflows require elastic, parallel GPU infrastructure at scale, and Modal's architecture is built for exactly that kind of bursty, massively parallel compute demand. A Market Pricing Infrastructure Aggressively Modal's decacorn milestone arrives as its immediate competitive tier is moving equally fast. Inference-serving platform Baseten closed a $1.5 billion Series F at a $13 billion valuation in June 2026. Fireworks AI Series D round — $1.5 billion at a $17.5 billion valuation — closed in July 2026. Modal, however, is positioning itself as a broader platform than pure inference-serving competitors: a single roof covering serverless compute, code execution environments, and training infrastructure — with a developer experience centered on Python rather than infrastructure configuration. Demand for cloud GPU capacity tied to AI workloads continues to outpace what hyperscalers alone can deliver, and infrastructure startups like Modal are filling that gap by aggregating capacity across dozens of providers and removing the operational overhead from engineering teams building on top of them. At $15.75 billion, Modal is currently the highest-valued private company in the AI infrastructure serving space — a distinction that would have been implausible when a 200-person New York startup with a Python-native serverless platform was competing against cloud-native hyperscalers for the same workloads. By the Numbers Metric Figure Series D round size $750M Post-money valuation $15.75B Total funding raised ~$1.2B Annualized run rate (ARR) >$1B ARR growth (YoY) >15x Sandboxes ARR ~$300M Sandboxes spun up (total) ~3 billion Max concurrent sandboxes 1 million Cloud providers in capacity pool 20+ Employees 200+ Series C valuation (May 2026) $4.65B Valuation step-up in 5 months ~3.4x Frequently Asked Questions What is Modal Labs, and how is it different from AWS or Google Cloud? Modal is a serverless compute platform purpose-built for AI workloads. Unlike AWS or Google Cloud, which require teams to provision and manage GPU instances, containers, and schedulers, Modal abstracts all of that behind a Python interface. A developer adds a single decorator to a Python function, and Modal handles everything — spinning up GPUs from a pool of 20+ cloud providers, scaling from zero to thousands of instances in seconds, and tearing down when the job is done. The key architectural difference is that Modal built its own Rust container runtime, file system, image builder, and networking from scratch, enabling sub-second cold starts that traditional cloud orchestration cannot match. What does it mean that Sandboxes is a $300M business, and why does it matter beyond Modal? Sandboxes is Modal's product for running untrusted or dynamically generated code in isolated virtual machine environments. Its growth to $300 million in annualized revenue — accounting for 30 percent of Modal's total ARR — is the first public evidence that isolated code execution has moved from a niche feature to a standalone infrastructure category. The demand driver is agentic AI: systems that autonomously write and execute code at runtime need clean, parallel containers to run that code safely. The same need exists in reinforcement learning post-training, where thousands of simultaneous execution environments are required. Sandboxes' scale suggests this demand is not experimental — it is already a multi-hundred-million-dollar production workload, and growing. Who are Modal's investors and how did the Series D valuation compare to the Series C? Accel led the Accel-led $750M Series D, with Kleiner Perkins joining as a new investor and returning backers Menlo Ventures, General Catalyst, Redpoint, Lux Capital, Amplify Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures all participating. The post-money valuation of $15.75 billion represents a 3.4x step-up from the $4.65 billion valuation set at Modal's Series C in May 2026 — a five-month gap. That pace of valuation appreciation reflects the AI infrastructure market's current pricing dynamics, in which GPU compute platforms with documented revenue trajectories are being valued at multiples that would have been unusual in any prior software cycle. Is Modal planning to go public, and what does the RL and post-training roadmap mean for enterprise customers? Modal has not publicly commented on IPO plans. On the product roadmap, the company's stated priorities — dedicated reinforcement learning infrastructure, expanded multi-node GPU clusters, and new Modal Servers capabilities for persistent LLM serving — indicate that it is targeting the post-training layer of the AI development stack, not just inference. For enterprise customers currently running RL fine-tuning or reward modeling jobs on traditional cloud infrastructure, that roadmap is relevant: it signals that Modal is building for the compute-intensive, massively parallel workloads that define the next wave of AI model development, not just the deployment and serving workflows that define the current one.

proofCandidates.summary: Ten U.S. startups raised over $1.5 billion in funding this week, with Modal Labs leading at $750 million and Icon at $200 million. Other rounds included biotech, insurance, and AI sectors, with most deals in the $60-135 million range.

Want to keep track of the largest startup funding deals in 2026 with our curated list of $100 million-plus venture deals to U.S.-based companies? Check out The Crunchbase Megadeals Board.

This is a weekly feature that runs down the week’s Top 10 announced funding rounds in the U.S. Check out last week’s biggest funding deal roundup here.

Startup investors aren’t exactly hitting pause, but they did scale back on giant rounds this past week, with just two startup financings in the multiple hundreds of millions. The biggest round went to AI infrastructure provider Modal Labs, which picked up $750 million, followed by construction automation unicorn Icon, which secured $200 million. Other sectors that attracted larger rounds this past week included biotech, insurance and AI.

1. Modal Labs, $750M, AI infrastructure: Modal Labs, a provider of cloud infrastructure for AI inference and other applications, secured $750 million in a Series D funding round led by Accel at a $15.75 billion valuation. The New York-headquartered company said it recently exceeded an annual revenue run rate of $1 billion.

2. Icon, $200M, construction tech: Austin-based Icon, a developer of robotic construction systems known for its 3D-printed homes, closed on $200 million in Series D funding led by Baillie Gifford and BlackRock. The company says it is on pace for 4x revenue growth in 2026.

3. Soufflé Therapeutics, $135M, RNA therapies: Boston-based Soufflé Therapeutics, a developer of RNA therapies, raised $135 million in Series B funding led by Juvia Group as part of a large syndicate of investors.

4. Estuary Biotherapeutics, $103M, gene therapies: Menlo Park, California-based Estuary Biotherapeutics, a developer of genetic medicines for patients with serious kidney diseases, launched with $103 million in financing. The funding includes $93 million in a Series A round led by RA Capital Management as well as $10 million in previously undisclosed seed capital.

5. Labelbox, $100M, AI tools: Labelbox, a developer of technology to train and evaluate AI models and to help deploy agents that improve with experience, picked up $100 million in Series E funding. Infinitum Partners led the financing for the 8-year-old, San Francisco-based company.

6. Suki, $90M, health AI: Redwood City, California-based Suki, a provider of AI tools that turn clinical conversations into intelligence for documentation, coding and other healthcare workflows, announced a $90 million Series E financing from backers including Healthier Capital and Crosslink Capital.

7. Abby Care, $82M, caregiver platform: Abby Care, a platform for family members to become certified, paid caregivers and deliver care at home, closed on $82 million in Series C funding, per a Fortune report. Transformation Capital led the financing for the 5-year-old, San Francisco-based startup.

8. Stand, $70M, insurance: Stand, a provider of insurance for homes in areas at higher risk of natural disasters, secured $70 million in Series C funding at a $1 billion valuation. Saga Ventures led the financing for the 3-year-old, San Francisco-based company.

9. Mueon, $65M, semiconductor systems: Mueon Corp., a semiconductor systems company building a modular platform for AI and hyperscale computing, completed a $65 million Series A funding round. Maverick Silicon led the financing for the Portland, Oregon-based company.

10. North.cloud, $60M, AI spend management: New York-based North.cloud, provider of an infrastructure spend intelligence and automation platform, raised $60 million in a Series B round led by PeakSpan Capital.

Methodology

We tracked the largest announced rounds in the Crunchbase database that were raised by U.S.-based companies for the period of Oct. 10-16, 2026. Although most announced rounds are in the database, there may be a small time lag, as some rounds are reported late in the week.

proofCandidates.fullText:
Artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure startup Modal was valued at $15.75 billion in a Series D funding round in which it raised $750 million, CEO Erik Bernhardsson said in a Wednesday (Oct. 14) blog post.

Modal’s new valuation is more than triple the $4.65 billion valuation the company achieved in a May Series C round in which is raised $355 million. “Just five months ago, when we announced our Series C, I wrote that demand was accelerating,” Bernhardsson said in the Wednesday post. “Since then, usage has tripled and we’ve grown more than 15x year-over-year. We recently crossed $1B in annualized run rate with no sign of slowing down.” Modal provides a platform for production AI, with cloud infrastructure for teams that develop, train and serve AI applications at scale. The company’s offerings span inference, training, sandboxes and functions, according to its website. Companies use the Modal platform to get apps from experimentation to production, to build agents, to generate lifelike video, to train robots and to run drug discovery, according to the post. proofCandidates.fullText:
Listen to article

A cloud infrastructure platform for AI has been valued at $15.75 billion after launching in London.

Modal Labs was founded by Swede Erik Bernhardsson, who began his career at Spotify, to allow developers to run AI and machine learning workloads without managing physical servers.

Headquartered in New York, it maintains a base in Stockholm but recently announced a big push into Europe with the opening of an office in London.

Hiring across sales, solutions engineering, partnerships and marketing, Hugh Killingbeck-Jones has joined Modal as VP EMEA to build out the teams in London.

“We think London is the AI capital of Europe, and over time this office will grow to include engineering and other functions too,” wrote Bernhardsson.

With a focus on both startups and enterprise, he added of the opening: “European companies will sometimes have a different set of requirements than US ones, especially when it comes to local regulation.”

Modal has now raised a $750 million Series D round at a $15.75bn post-money valuation, led by Accel.

“Just five months ago, when we announced our Series C, I wrote that demand was accelerating. Since then, usage has tripled and we’ve grown more than 15x year-over-year,” said Bernhardsson.

“We recently crossed $1bn in annualised run rate with no sign of slowing down.

“It’s clear that AI has unlocked a whole new set of software capabilities. So many incredible applications exist now that couldn’t have been built before. The old stack doesn’t quite fit them. They need different building blocks and a new way to think about infrastructure.

“We’re powering a ton of these applications.”

Kleiner Perkins joined the round while all of the firm’s existing investors participated, including Menlo Ventures, General Catalyst, Redpoint, Lux Capital and Bain Capital Ventures.

proofCandidates.title: Modal becomes latest decacorn after $750M raise to build cloud infrastructure for AI agents — TFN
proofCandidates.summary: Modal raised $750M at a $15.75B valuation, led by Accel, with Kleiner Perkins joining. The company's annualized run rate crossed $1B, and its Sandboxes product reached a $300M run rate. The valuation is more than three times its May 21 Series C.
proofCandidates.fullText:
- Modal raised $750M at a $15.75B valuation, led by Accel, with Kleiner Perkins joining.
- The valuation is more than three times the $4.65B set in its May 21 Series C.
- Its run rate passed $1B, and its Sandboxes product alone reached $300M.
Erik Bernhardsson helped build Spotify’s music recommendations, then spent six years as CTO of Better.com, and came away convinced the cloud held developers back. On October 14, the company he founded in 2021, Modal, said it had raised $750M at a $15.75B valuation, led by Accel, less than five months after it was valued at $4.65B.
Kleiner Perkins joined the round, and all of Modal’s existing investors took part, including Menlo Ventures, General Catalyst, Redpoint, Lux Capital, and Bain Capital Ventures.
Modal said usage has tripled since its Series C, has grown more than 15x year on year, and its annualised run rate has crossed $1B.
Bernhardsson’s pitch starts with scarce graphics processing units (GPUs) and large AI models that are slow to load. Developers can work around both on older tools, he wrote, “but you end up in YAML hell and GPU procurement purgatory.”
The sandbox business behind the run rate
Modal, founded in 2021, pools computing capacity from more than 20 cloud providers into one network and lets developers run code on it without managing servers. It built its own file system, container runtime, scheduler, and networking to do that, and it does not run its own data centres.
The sharpest growth is in Sandboxes. Modal launched the product in 2023, when developers began using large language models to write code that needed somewhere isolated to run.
For example, a coding assistant can test a script it just wrote inside a sandbox, away from the customer’s own systems. Sandboxes have since reached a $300M run rate, just under a third of the total, with close to 3 billion sandboxes launched and capacity for 1 million running at once.
Customers include DoorDash, whose AI platform team uses Modal to move apps from experiment to production, Cognition, Ramp, Linear, and Hebbia, which build background agents on it. Runway generates video there, while Physical Intelligence, Generalist AI, and 1X train robots.
Modal says TypeSafe AI’s Jev, which it calls one of the fastest-growing products ever, served 1 trillion tokens, the chunks of text a model reads and writes, on the platform in its first three days.
Bernhardsson, who created the open-source Annoy library for search and recommendations, is chief executive. Co-founder Akshat Bubna, an early engineer at Scale AI, is chief technology officer. Modal has more than 200 staff across New York, San Francisco, and Stockholm, up from more than 120 at the time of the Series C.
How fast the price moved
Modal was valued at $1.1B in September 2025, when it raised an $87M Series B led by Lux Capital. Its $355M Series C followed on May 21 at $4.65B, led by General Catalyst and Redpoint. The Series D at $15.75B is more than 14 times the Series B figure in just over a year.
The Series C came in two tranches, Reuters reported: the first at a $2.5B valuation, the second at $4.65B once more investors came calling. Accel and Menlo Ventures were in the second tranche, so Accel went from first-time investor at $4.65B to leading this round at $15.75B. Modal has raised roughly $1.2B across its disclosed rounds, including a seed round led by Amplify Partners and a $16M Series A in October 2023.
Two investors weighed in on X. Mamoon Hamid, a partner at Kleiner Perkins, wrote that every serious AI team his firm talks to eventually says the same thing: “We run it on Modal.” Lux Capital partner Grace Isford, whose firm led the Series B, wrote that Modal “radically reimagined a seamless developer experience” from the start.
A crowded race for inference
The money is chasing a market that has changed shape. Gartner forecasts worldwide spending on AI-optimised infrastructure-as-a-service of $42B in 2026, up 96%, and expects inference, the running of trained models, to account for $23.3B of it, ahead of $19B for training.
Rivals are raising just as fast. Baseten took $300M at a $5B valuation in January, then a $1.5B Series F at $13B on June 22. Bloomberg reported on September 23 that Baseten and Modal were both in talks to at least double their valuations, with Baseten’s talks at $26B. Together AI raised $800M at $8.3B on July 1, led by Aramco Ventures, and said its annual bookings passed $1.15B in the prior quarter. Fireworks AI raised $1.505B at $17.5B on July 16 and reports a run rate above $1B.
Modal’s valuation is no more than about 16 times its run rate. Fireworks sits at no more than about 17.5 times, and Together AI at roughly seven times its bookings, though the two measures are not the same. While Together AI and Fireworks centre on running and customising open models, Modal describes itself as a set of building blocks, from functions to Sandboxes to training, that developers combine themselves.
The number to watch is Sandboxes. If AI agents keep writing code that needs a safe place to run, a product launched in 2023 could carry more of Modal’s valuation than GPU rental ever did. If the biggest clouds or the model makers build their own sandboxes, a multiple near 16 will be hard to defend.

proofCandidates.fullText:

More than $1.51 billion in newly announced funding transactions flowed into 10 major startups over the past 24 hours, alongside a separate €50 million investment in France. The biggest deals reveal a venture market financing two very different priorities: the infrastructure needed to run artificial intelligence at scale and specialized technologies that can solve expensive problems in healthcare, manufacturing, energy, and enterprise operations. San Francisco-based Modal led the day’s funding activity with a $750 million Series D at a $15.75 billion valuation, after reporting that its annualized revenue run rate surpassed $1 billion. Oxford biotech startup OMass Therapeutics secured $310 million to advance experimental treatments for hormonal and autoimmune diseases. Meanwhile, European energy-storage company Skeleton Technologies raised more than $100 million in Siemens-led financing, becoming a unicorn as it expands into the U.S. AI data center market. The activity extends across several layers of the AI economy. Salience Labs raised $125 million to commercialize optical networking chips that connect increasingly large GPU clusters. Labelbox announced more than $100 million in financing for reinforcement learning and enterprise AI agents. Harmonic Security secured $50 million to address the security risks created by employee AI use, while Duvo raised $32 million to automate operational processes across retailers and consumer-goods companies. Beyond AI software, India’s Scimplify raised $25 million to expand specialty-chemical and critical-materials production, with Hitachi Ventures leading the investment. France’s Dougs secured €50 million to accelerate AI-based accounting services. Boston-based Tamr raised $21 million to improve the fragmented enterprise data that increasingly autonomous AI systems depend on. The broader signal is that investors are financing the systems that make AI commercially useful, not just the models themselves. That includes computing capacity, optical networking, energy management, reliable data, security controls, and industry-specific execution. The 10 selected transactions represent more than $1.513 billion in disclosed dollar-denominated financing, plus €50 million. The Macro Environment: AI Infrastructure Spending Meets a Growing Demand for Financial Discipline The latest funding activity arrives as venture investors confront an increasingly complicated AI economy. Demand for AI computing continues to grow, but the financial requirements of building and operating that infrastructure are becoming harder to ignore. GPU clusters require enormous capital commitments, substantial electricity supplies, specialized networking, and increasingly sophisticated workload-management systems. That creates opportunities for companies such as Modal, Salience Labs, and Skeleton Technologies. Each addresses a different constraint in the same market: Modal provides computing infrastructure developers can access without managing their own GPU clusters; Salience is developing optical switches to improve communication between processors; and Skeleton is building energy-storage systems designed to manage sudden fluctuations in data-center electricity demand. The distinction matters because AI infrastructure economics extend far beyond GPU prices. A data center can own expensive accelerators and still operate inefficiently because of networking bottlenecks, power fluctuations, poor utilization, or software overhead. Growing evidence also suggests public-market investors are becoming more sensitive to those costs. Shares of AI cloud provider CoreWeave fell sharply on October 14 amid concerns about borrowing costs and the sustainability of debt-financed infrastructure expansion. Financial Times reporting has also highlighted a slowdown in AI-related debt issuance as lenders become more selective. That does not mean private investors are abandoning AI infrastructure. Modal’s $750 million financing shows strong, ongoing demand for businesses that can turn compute into commercial revenue. But it suggests investors may increasingly distinguish between companies with demonstrated customer demand and infrastructure projects whose financial returns depend on uncertain future utilization. Outside computing infrastructure, OMass Therapeutics and Scimplify show that substantial capital remains available for difficult scientific and industrial problems. OMass is financing clinical development, where success ultimately depends on generating convincing evidence that experimental medicines work safely in patients. Scimplify is building a distributed manufacturing network for chemicals and critical materials, where customer qualification and production consistency determine commercial value. Those risks differ significantly from software economics. Yet both investments reflect a willingness to fund businesses whose capabilities require years of research, specialized facilities, regulatory expertise, and operating experience. The day’s enterprise software rounds introduce another important theme: AI is moving from experimentation into operational responsibility. Labelbox, Harmonic Security, Duvo, Tamr, and Dougs address different consequences of that transition, from reinforcement learning and agent execution to data accuracy, security, and regulated professional services. Together, the announcements suggest investors are looking beyond whether AI can perform a task. They increasingly want to know whether companies can deploy it reliably, measure its performance, control its risks, and generate durable revenue. That creates opportunities for energy technology companies whose products improve computing performance without requiring additional generation capacity. 10. Large announced financing totals require financial interpretation Today’s rounds demonstrate why investors and journalists should separate equity, credit facilities, secondary transactions, valuation figures, and operating metrics. Those distinctions determine how much capital a company actually receives and what obligations may accompany it. They also help distinguish genuine business progress from impressive but incomplete headline figures. Conclusion October 15’s startup funding activity reveals a venture market still willing to make substantial commitments, but increasingly focused on the infrastructure and operating capabilities required to turn technology into economic value. Modal’s $750 million financing demonstrates investor confidence in AI computing infrastructure backed by significant reported usage. Salience and Skeleton are developing the networking and energy systems needed to support increasingly demanding GPU clusters. OMass shows that investors continue to finance difficult biotechnology research as programs advance toward clinical validation. Scimplify is building manufacturing capabilities in strategically important materials, while Dougs is combining AI automation with regulated professional services. Labelbox, Harmonic Security, Duvo, and Tamr are addressing another stage of AI adoption: the transition from applications that produce information to systems that perform work inside organizations. The deals differ in scale, maturity, and risk. Yet they share a common economic argument. As AI capabilities become more widely available, investors are placing substantial capital behind companies that control the infrastructure, data, industrial processes, and customer relationships required to make those capabilities useful. The next competitive advantage may come less from access to the most advanced technology and more from owning the systems that let it operate reliably, economically, and at scale. 0 Shares

proofCandidates.title: Modal raises $750M at $15.75bn valuation as run rate tops $1bn
proofCandidates.summary: Modal raised $750 million in a Series D round at a $15.75 billion valuation, led by Accel with Kleiner Perkins joining. The company now earns over $1 billion annually, with usage tripling since its Series C. It plans to launch more AI training and fine-tuning products.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Modal, a cloud company that runs AI models and code for developers, announced on Wednesday that it has raised $750 million in a Series D round at a $15.75 billion valuation.
Accel led the round, and Kleiner Perkins joined. All of Modal’s existing investors also took part, including Menlo Ventures, General Catalyst, Redpoint, Lux Capital, Amplify Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures.
The New York-based company said it now earns more than $1 billion in revenue a year. Usage has tripled in the five months since its Series C, co-founder and chief executive Erik Bernhardsson wrote in a blog post. The business has grown more than 15 times in a year, he said.
Modal rents out computing power on graphics chips, which AI companies use to run and train their models. It says it built its own file system, container software, and scheduler, and draws on spare capacity from more than 20 cloud providers.
One of its fastest-growing products is Sandboxes, which lets AI agents run the code they write in isolated environments. Sandboxes alone now bring in $300 million a year, the company said. It has started close to 3 billion of them since 2023.
Customers include DoorDash, Ramp, Linear, Cognition, and video AI firm Runway, according to Modal. Robotics firms such as Physical Intelligence and 1X use it to train robots.
“GPUs are scarce, and models are quite large and slow to load,” Bernhardsson wrote.
Modal plans to launch more products for training and fine-tuning AI models. It has more than 200 staff across New York, San Francisco, and Stockholm.
In July, Modal’s chief technology officer confirmed that an OpenAI agent that broke out of its test environment had also compromised a Modal account, after breaching Hugging Face.

Update: This story has been updated to reflect that ServiceNow says it is no longer in talks with Decagon.
Buzzy AI agent startup Decagon could be the latest company swept up in a growing wave of AI dealmaking.
The company, which was last valued at $4.5 billion earlier this year, has hired a bank to evaluate acquisition interest, according to people familiar with the matter.
Decagon held early discussions with cloud software giant ServiceNow, but a spokesperson for ServiceNow says they're not ongoing. People familiar with the matter told Business Insider there have also been early talks with other companies; if a deal does not materialize, Decagon could instead raise a new funding round.
"Our approach to M&A has not changed: we remain an organic growth company first. M&A is a tool to accelerate our roadmap or open meaningful new innovation," said Amit Zavery, president, chief product officer, and chief operating officer of ServiceNow.

ServiceNow shares fell 1.22% to close at $138.61 on Tuesday. They gained 1% in the overnight session ahead of Wednesday's session.

proofCandidates.fullText:
Decagon announced on October 2, 2026 that it is a launch partner for OpenAI Marketplace, OpenAI’s new B2B marketplace, under which eligible OpenAI enterprise customers can apply part of their existing OpenAI commitment toward Decagon’s customer-facing AI agents. The announcement was authored by Roger Liang, Decagon’s strategic alliances and partnerships lead, and Ariana Xiang, a senior product marketing manager at the company. Decagon said the partnership makes it easier for businesses building on OpenAI to deploy its customer-facing AI agents, and said that letting eligible customers apply an existing OpenAI commitment toward Decagon simplifies procurement and helps teams move from AI investment to production faster. Procurement, Deployment, and Compliance Decagon said it has been a preferred partner in OpenAI’s enterprise ecosystem since earlier this year, with the two companies working together to bring frontier AI to enterprise customer experiences, and described its launch on the marketplace as building on that foundation. On procurement, Decagon said eligible enterprise customers can apply part of their existing OpenAI commitment toward Decagon, characterizing the mechanism as reducing the procurement friction that can slow AI deployments. On deployment speed, the company said it goes live in weeks with Agent Operating Procedures (AOPs), and said purchasing through the marketplace further simplifies the path from decision to deployment. Decagon also described a technical relationship extending beyond the marketplace, calling OpenAI models an important part of its constellation of models alongside the specialized models Decagon Labs post-trains for customer experience. On compliance, the company listed SOC 2 Type 2, HIPAA, GDPR, and CCPA compliance, configurable PII redaction, and layered guardrails that run before, during, and after every conversation. How OpenAI Marketplace Works OpenAI introduced the marketplace in its DevDay 2026 recap, stating that eligible enterprise customers can apply part of their existing OpenAI commitment toward approved partner software. OpenAI said its first 32 partners include Figma for creative work; Adobe, Sierra, Decagon, HubSpot, Salesforce, and ServiceNow for customer experience; Harvey and Legora for legal; Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike for cybersecurity; and Baseten for open-source models. The OpenAI Marketplace page describes the program as a way for enterprise customers to discover partner products and use part of an existing OpenAI commitment toward eligible products. Its partner directory lists Decagon with the description “Decagon builds AI agents that resolve customer issues end to end, not deflect.” According to the FAQ on the marketplace page, whether a customer can apply an existing commitment depends on the customer’s OpenAI agreement, the partner product, and the program’s terms, and eligibility applies to specific products rather than every product from a listed partner. Customers contract with and pay the partner directly, while OpenAI reconciles use of the commitment under the program’s terms. Enterprise customers can submit a request to buy, prospective partners can join a waitlist, and participation is subject to eligibility and approval. OpenAI’s Help Center documentation states that the initial rollout is managed directly with OpenAI and participating partners. It lays out a four-step purchasing flow: OpenAI and the partner confirm whether the customer and the proposed purchase qualify; the customer contracts directly with the partner; the partner invoices the customer; and OpenAI records the eligible amount against the customer’s OpenAI commitment. The documentation states that the initial marketplace experience supports product discovery and expressions of interest and does not include self-service checkout, with purchases arranged directly with OpenAI and participating partners. Eligible customers can apply part — not all — of a commitment, with the qualifying amount depending on the applicable program terms and the purchase, and eligibility is specific to the customer, product, and purchase. OpenAI also distinguishes marketplace purchases from using an organization’s OpenAI-funded inference inside a participating partner application, stating that participation in one program does not automatically establish eligibility for the other. Partner Ecosystem and Next Steps Decagon described the OpenAI work as one example of a broader ecosystem it is building. It said Decagon Partnerships brings together technology, alliance, and sales and services partners, and it offers a Partner Essentials course through Decagon University, which it described as a training program to help partners build, deploy, and scale Decagon’s AI concierge solutions. Decagon said its listing goes live on the OpenAI B2B marketplace soon, with deployment options, pricing, and details on applying an OpenAI commitment toward Decagon.
