The three services rarely get compared fairly because they were built for different jobs. Resend launched as a Y Combinator startup aimed squarely at developers who wanted email to feel like any other npm package. SendGrid grew up as an independent email service provider before Twilio acquired it, and its feature set still reflects a decade of enterprise procurement cycles and marketing-team requirements. Amazon SES was never a standalone product at all. It is a primitive inside AWS, priced and operated the same way S3 or DynamoDB is, which explains both its rock-bottom cost and its lack of any consumer-friendly dashboard. Understanding that history helps explain why a direct price-per-email comparison, while useful, only tells part of the story.

Resend vs SendGrid vs Amazon SES at a Glance

Before digging into pricing tiers and deliverability numbers, here is how the three platforms stack up on the specs that matter most for a typical engineering team choosing an email API in 2026.

Spec Resend SendGrid (Twilio) Amazon SES Free tier 3,000 emails/mo, 100/day cap 100 emails/day for a 60-day trial No dedicated free tier for new accounts since July 2026 Cheapest paid entry $20/mo (Pro, 50,000 emails) $19.95/mo (Essentials, 50,000 emails) $0.10/1,000 emails, a la carte, no minimum Cost per 1,000 at 100K/mo $0.35 (Pro $35 tier) $0.3495 (Essentials 100K) $0.16 (Essentials plan) or $0.10 (a la carte) Overage rate $0.90 per 1,000 About $1.10 per 1,000 (Pro tier) Flat rate per plan tier, no separate overage Dedicated IP $30/mo add-on Bundled at Pro ($89.95/mo) or $30/mo extra $24.95/mo standard, or $15/mo plus $0.08/1,000 managed SSO $150/mo add-on Included on Pro and Premier Handled through AWS IAM, no separate charge React Email support Native, first-class SDK Not supported natively Not supported natively Primary integration path HTTPS API, Vercel/Next.js marketplace app REST API and SMTP relay API, SMTP, deep AWS service integration (Lambda, SNS, CloudWatch) Attachment cost Included in plan Included in plan $0.12 per GB Rate limit note No daily cap above the free tier Email Activity API capped at 6 requests/minute since Dec 9, 2025 Sending rate tied to account reputation and region quota Recorded major incidents No widely reported outage in 2026 32 major/critical incidents since 2015 (status page history) Standard AWS regional SLA, tracked via AWS Health Dashboard Best fit Startups, Next.js/Vercel apps, small teams Enterprise SaaS mixing marketing and transactional AWS-native backends, cost-sensitive high volume

Three things jump out immediately. Amazon SES is still the cheapest raw sending option if you stay on the legacy a la carte rate. Resend is the only one of the three built specifically around modern frontend frameworks. And SendGrid is priced like an enterprise tool because it is one, complete with subuser management, dedicated account teams at the Premier tier, and a feature set built up over more than a decade as a Twilio product.

What Is Resend?

Resend is a Y Combinator-backed email API built for developers who write React and TypeScript, not marketers who click through drag-and-drop template builders. Its entire pitch rests on one idea: emails are just React components, and the Resend SDK ships them through a plain HTTPS call instead of forcing teams to manage SMTP connections or wrestle with a legacy templating language.

The integration that put Resend on the map for most developers is its official Vercel Marketplace listing, which lets a team generate an API key and start sending from a serverless or edge function within minutes. Resend also ships a dedicated Vercel template pairing Next.js, React Email, and its own SDK, and the company confirmed in September 2026 that this template is now the recommended starting point for new projects on the platform. That tight loop between framework, template library, and API is the biggest reason teams pick Resend over incumbents that predate the React ecosystem entirely.

On the business side, Resend keeps pricing simple by design: a free tier, a Pro tier at $20 a month, and a Scale tier that climbs from $90 a month for 100,000 emails up toward roughly $1,150 a month at 2.5 million emails, according to pricing breakdowns published by FlexPrice’s 2026 Resend cost guide. There is no quote-only enterprise tier hiding behind a sales call for teams under a few million emails a month, a sharp contrast to how SendGrid and SES structure their top plans.

What Is SendGrid?

Twilio SendGrid has been the default choice for transactional and marketing email at mid-size and enterprise companies for more than a decade, and its 2026 pricing structure reflects that maturity. The platform runs on four tiers: a 60-day free trial capped at 100 emails a day, an Essentials plan starting at $19.95 a month for 50,000 emails, a Pro plan at $89.95 a month for 100,000 emails that scales to 2.5 million, and a custom-quoted Premier plan for senders above roughly 5 million emails a month.

What separates SendGrid from the other two is depth of feature set rather than raw price. Every paid tier includes REST and SMTP relay support, event webhooks, and a dynamic template editor, while the Pro tier adds a bundled dedicated IP, subuser accounts for managing multiple sending identities under one roof, and deliverability insight tooling that smaller teams rarely need. That subuser system is why large SaaS platforms running white-label or reseller programs still default to SendGrid. One account can host dozens of isolated sending identities with separate reputation tracking, something neither Resend nor a raw SES setup handles out of the box.

SendGrid’s maturity carries a maintenance cost, too. Twilio changed the rate limit on the Email Activity API on December 9, 2025, dropping it from 30 requests per five-minute window down to 6 requests per minute, a change that broke dashboard integrations for teams polling the API aggressively. Twilio’s own status page shows a steady cadence of maintenance windows through 2026, alongside a historical record of 32 major or critical incidents since 2015 tracked by third-party uptime monitors. None of that makes SendGrid unreliable by industry standards, but a platform this old carries more operational scar tissue than a five-year-old challenger.

SendGrid also remains the only one of the three built around a genuine marketing-and-transactional hybrid model. Its dynamic template editor supports drag-and-drop design for non-engineers, contact list segmentation, and A/B testing tools that neither Resend nor raw SES attempt to replicate. That breadth is why marketing teams at mid-size companies frequently push engineering toward SendGrid even when a leaner transactional API would technically suffice for password resets and receipts. The tradeoff is that a platform built to serve both audiences at once inevitably carries more surface area, more settings screens, and a steeper onboarding curve for a developer who just wants to send one templated email from a webhook handler.

What Is Amazon SES?

Amazon Simple Email Service has spent over a decade as the default answer for any team already running infrastructure on AWS. Its pitch is not developer experience or feature richness. It is price, control, and native integration with Lambda, EventBridge, SNS, IAM, and every other AWS service that already sits in a typical backend stack.

On July 21, 2026, AWS restructured SES pricing in a way that changes the math for new accounts. According to the official AWS announcement, every new SES account created after that date starts on the Essentials plan rather than the old free tier, and the historical allowance of 62,000 free emails a month for EC2-hosted senders is closed to new customers entirely. The legacy a la carte rate of $0.10 per 1,000 outbound emails still exists and remains technically the cheapest option on this list, but Essentials now charges $0.16 per 1,000 for the first 10 million emails a month, $0.14 per 1,000 from 10 to 100 million, and $0.11 per 1,000 above that. Pro and Enterprise plans add fixed monthly fees of $105 and $500 respectively on top of slightly higher per-email rates, in exchange for bundled dedicated IPs and Virtual Deliverability Manager access.

The official SES pricing page confirms the tiered rate bands and makes clear that engineering teams provisioning new accounts today need to model both the a la carte and Essentials paths before committing, since the two can produce very different bills at the same volume. A workload sending 100,000 emails a month costs $10 flat on the legacy rate but $16 on Essentials, a 60% jump for functionally the same service.

SES also differs from Resend and SendGrid in how it treats new customers before they can send at all. Every new account lands in the SES sandbox by default, which restricts outbound mail to a small set of verified test addresses until AWS reviews and approves a production access request. That review typically clears within a few hours to two business days, but it means SES is the only one of the three platforms where a team cannot simply generate an API key and start sending to real customers the same afternoon. Teams that plan a product launch around SES need to file that request well ahead of any hard deadline.

SDKs, Frameworks, and Ecosystem Fit

The gap between these three platforms shows up most clearly in how they fit around the rest of a team’s stack. Resend leans entirely into the JavaScript and TypeScript ecosystem. Its Vercel integration announcement describes a setup flow where a project owner links a Vercel project, generates a scoped API key, and stores it as an environment variable without ever leaving the Vercel dashboard. That same pattern extends to Resend’s official SDKs for Node, Python, Ruby, PHP, Go, and Rust, though the React Email integration remains the feature that draws most new signups, since it lets a team version-control email templates the same way it version-controls UI components.

SendGrid’s SDK coverage is broader in raw language count, reflecting its longer history, with official libraries for C#, Go, Java, Node.js, PHP, Python, and Ruby, plus a mature set of community-maintained integrations for frameworks like Laravel and Django. Amazon SES, by contrast, does not ship a dedicated SDK at all. It rides on the general-purpose AWS SDK, meaning a Node.js team calls SES through the same @aws-sdk/client-sesv2 package it would use for S3 or DynamoDB, which keeps credential and IAM handling consistent across an entire AWS-based backend but adds a layer of AWS-specific boilerplate that Resend and SendGrid avoid by design.

Pricing Breakdown: What You Actually Pay at Scale

Sticker prices rarely tell the full story once volume climbs. The table below models effective cost per 1,000 emails at four common sending volumes, using each provider’s standard published plan (Resend Pro/Scale, SendGrid Essentials/Pro, and SES Essentials, with the SES a la carte rate noted separately since it requires manual account configuration rather than a default plan).

Monthly volume Resend SendGrid Amazon SES (Essentials) Amazon SES (a la carte) 10,000 emails Free ($0) Free trial only (60 days) $1.60 $1.00 50,000 emails $20.00 $19.95 $8.00 $5.00 100,000 emails $35.00 $34.95 (Essentials) or $89.95 (Pro, with dedicated IP) $16.00 $10.00 500,000 emails $350.00 Roughly $220-260 on Pro tiering $80.00 $50.00

The pattern holds across every volume tested: Amazon SES’s a la carte rate is the cheapest raw sending cost by a wide margin, roughly a third of what Resend or SendGrid charge at 100,000 emails a month. But that price comparison ignores everything SES does not include out of the box. There is no template editor, no built-in analytics dashboard, and no managed deliverability tooling unless a team pays extra for the Virtual Deliverability Manager or builds its own reporting layer on top of CloudWatch and SNS. Resend and SendGrid both fold dashboard, template, and webhook tooling into the base price, which is part of why they cost more per email.

SendGrid’s Pro tier is worth flagging separately because its sticker price of $89.95 for 100,000 emails looks worse than Essentials at $34.95 for the same volume, until you account for the bundled dedicated IP, which would otherwise cost $30-plus a month on Resend or $24.95 on SES. Teams evaluating SendGrid Pro against a competitor’s base plus add-ons should always compare the fully loaded price, not the headline number.

Add-on costs compound faster than most teams expect once a product scales past its initial launch. A startup that begins on Resend Pro at $20 a month, adds a dedicated IP at $30, and later adds SSO for a security-conscious enterprise customer at $150 a month is suddenly paying $200 a month before counting a single email beyond the base 50,000 allowance. Run the same math on SendGrid Pro, where the dedicated IP is already bundled but SSO and subuser tiers push the effective price toward $150-250 a month depending on configuration, and the two platforms land closer together than their headline prices suggest. SES avoids most of these line items entirely since dedicated IPs are billed a la carte and SSO rides on existing AWS IAM at no extra charge, which is part of why cost-sensitive teams gravitate toward it once volume and add-on requirements both climb.

Deliverability and Inbox Placement

Pricing only matters if the email actually lands in the inbox. All three providers support the same core authentication stack, SPF, DKIM, and DMARC, and all three let a sender configure custom domain authentication rather than relying on a shared subdomain. Where they diverge is in the tooling built around that foundation.

SendGrid ships deliverability insights and subuser-level reputation tracking as part of its Pro tier, aimed at teams that need to isolate a bad sender from a good one inside the same account. Amazon SES offers the Virtual Deliverability Manager, a bolt-on analytics layer that surfaces bounce, complaint, and reputation data across sending identities, billed separately from base sending costs on some plan tiers. Resend keeps its deliverability tooling simpler, leaning on domain-level dashboards and recommending dedicated IPs once a sender crosses roughly 3,000 emails a day, the same threshold where its free tier’s daily cap becomes a practical ceiling anyway.

None of the three publish a head-to-head inbox placement study against each other, which is common in this market since deliverability depends heavily on sender reputation, list hygiene, and content, not just the platform. The practical takeaway for engineering teams is that authentication setup and warm-up discipline matter more than the provider chosen, though dedicated IPs on any of the three meaningfully reduce the risk of shared-IP reputation problems once volume grows past a few hundred thousand emails a month.

Developer Experience and API Design

This is where the three platforms feel most different in daily use. Resend’s SDK is built around a single HTTPS call, no SMTP connection pooling, no queue management on the client side, and first-class TypeScript types. A minimal send from a Node or edge function looks like this:

import { Resend } from 'resend'; const resend = new Resend(process.env.RESEND_API_KEY); await resend.emails.send({ from: 'onboarding@yourdomain.com', to: 'user@example.com', subject: 'Welcome aboard', react: WelcomeEmail({ name: 'Alex' }), });

That single call replaces what would otherwise be a React Email render step, an SMTP transport configuration, and a manual HTML string assembly on SendGrid or raw SES. SendGrid’s REST API and SMTP relay both work well and are documented thoroughly after more than a decade in production, but the platform was not designed around component-based templating, so teams that want React Email support on SendGrid have to build their own render-and-send wrapper.

Amazon SES sits at the opposite end of the developer experience spectrum from Resend. It is a low-level primitive, not a polished product. Sending an email means either calling the SES API directly, routing through the SMTP interface, or wiring up Lambda functions triggered by EventBridge or SNS. That flexibility is exactly why AWS-native teams like it: SES becomes just another IAM-scoped resource inside an existing Terraform or CloudFormation stack, with the same access control and observability patterns the rest of the infrastructure already uses. Teams already comfortable with managing AWS Secrets Manager or configuring Cognito user pools tend to find SES a natural extension of the same toolkit, while teams without that AWS context often find the setup slower than either Resend or SendGrid.

Rate Limits, Sending Caps, and Scaling

Resend’s free tier enforces a hard 100 emails a day cap alongside the 3,000 emails a month allowance, which pushes any real production workload onto the Pro tier almost immediately. Once on a paid plan, there is no daily send limit beyond the monthly quota, and Resend recommends a dedicated IP, available from $30 a month, once daily volume crosses roughly 3,000 emails to protect deliverability.

SendGrid’s sending limits scale with plan tier and account reputation, but the more immediately relevant limit for engineering teams in 2026 is the Email Activity API change that took effect December 9, 2025. Any dashboard or monitoring tool that polls SendGrid’s activity data now has to work within 6 requests per minute, down from the previous 30 requests per five minutes, a change that broke some existing observability integrations and forced teams to batch their polling logic.

Amazon SES ties sending rate directly to account reputation and region-specific quotas rather than a flat plan limit. New accounts start in the SES sandbox, which restricts sending to verified addresses only until AWS approves a production access request, a step that has no equivalent friction on Resend or SendGrid. Once approved, sending rate and daily quota scale automatically based on sending history, which rewards consistent, low-complaint senders but adds an unpredictable ramp period that teams need to plan around before a launch date.

Real-World Use Cases

The theoretical comparison only goes so far. Here is how the pricing and API differences actually play out across five common scenarios engineering teams face in 2026.

Next.js SaaS startup sending onboarding and password-reset emails. A two-person team building on Vercel with a Supabase backend typically wires Resend directly into a serverless function, using React Email components for every template. At under 10,000 emails a month, this costs nothing and takes under an hour to wire up end to end.

Solo developer or indie hacker shipping a side project fast. A single founder wiring up a waitlist or launch email typically reaches for Resend first, since the free tier covers early traffic and the SDK integrates with a serverless deploy on Render, Railway, or Fly.io without any SMTP configuration at all.

Reliability and Uptime History

Uptime rarely makes headlines until it fails at the wrong moment. SendGrid’s status page history shows 32 major or critical incidents recorded since 2015, a number that reflects both the platform’s age and its scale rather than a specific reliability problem. Twilio’s status page through August and September 2026 mostly logs routine maintenance, including a planned deprecation of legacy IP ranges previously used to reach the SendGrid API and SMTP endpoints, with no widely reported catastrophic outage in that window.

Amazon SES inherits the reliability profile of the broader AWS region it runs in, tracked through the standard AWS Health Dashboard rather than a dedicated SES status page. Teams already monitoring AWS service health for other workloads get SES visibility for free as part of that existing process. Resend, as the youngest of the three platforms, has no widely reported major outage on record through September 2026, though it also has the shortest operating history and the smallest published incident data set of the three, so that track record carries less statistical weight than SendGrid’s decade-plus history.

Migration Guide: Moving Between Providers

Switching email providers is lower risk than most infrastructure migrations since email sending is usually isolated behind a single service or utility function, but domain reputation and DNS records need careful handling. Here is a practical path for moving from SendGrid or SES to Resend, which is the most common direction teams move in 2026 as they consolidate onto simpler tooling.

Create a Resend account and add your sending domain before touching any DNS records tied to your current provider. Add the Resend-provided SPF and DKIM records to your DNS zone alongside your existing provider’s records. Both can coexist during the transition window. Wait for domain verification to complete in the Resend dashboard, typically within minutes but occasionally up to an hour depending on DNS propagation. Convert your highest-volume email templates to React Email components first, since these deliver the biggest maintenance win once migrated. Replace your SMTP or REST API calls with the Resend SDK in a single service or utility module, not scattered across the codebase, to keep the rollback path simple. Route a small percentage of production traffic, such as password resets for internal test accounts, through Resend first and monitor bounce and complaint rates for 48 to 72 hours. Migrate webhook handlers for delivery, bounce, and complaint events to Resend’s webhook format, checking that any downstream analytics or suppression-list logic still fires correctly. Gradually shift the remaining email categories over 1-2 weeks, watching deliverability metrics at each step rather than cutting over all traffic at once. Once fully migrated, remove the old provider’s DNS records and cancel the subscription only after confirming at least one full billing cycle of stable sending on the new platform.

The same sequence works in reverse for teams moving from Resend to SendGrid or SES, though moving toward SES adds an extra step: requesting production access to exit the SES sandbox, which should be submitted as early as possible in the migration timeline since AWS approval can take anywhere from a few hours to a couple of business days.

Pros and Cons of Each Platform

Weighing tradeoffs side by side makes the right choice clearer for most teams than pricing tables alone.

Resend pros: Native React Email support, simple flat pricing, fast Vercel/Next.js integration, generous free tier for early-stage products.

Native React Email support, simple flat pricing, fast Vercel/Next.js integration, generous free tier for early-stage products. Resend cons: Smallest feature set of the three, no subuser system for multi-tenant sending, shortest operating track record, overage pricing gets expensive fast at high volume.

Smallest feature set of the three, no subuser system for multi-tenant sending, shortest operating track record, overage pricing gets expensive fast at high volume. SendGrid pros: Deepest feature set, subuser accounts for multi-tenant or white-label sending, over a decade of production hardening, strong marketing-plus-transactional combo tooling.

SendGrid cons: Highest cost per email among the three at comparable feature levels, recent API rate-limit cuts hit some integrations, dated template authoring compared to component-based tools.

Amazon SES pros: Cheapest raw sending cost by a wide margin on the a la carte rate, deep native AWS integration, scales to any volume without a sales call.

Amazon SES cons: No built-in template editor or polished dashboard, sandbox approval friction for new accounts, July 2026 pricing changes closed the old free tier for new customers, steepest learning curve for teams outside the AWS ecosystem.

Which Email API Should You Choose?

The right answer depends almost entirely on team size, existing infrastructure, and sending volume rather than any single platform being universally better.

Choose Resend if you are building on Next.js or Vercel, want to write emails as React components, and are sending under 500,000 emails a month. The developer experience advantage outweighs the higher per-email cost at that scale, and the free tier removes any barrier to getting started.

Choose SendGrid if you need to manage multiple sending identities under one account, run both marketing and transactional email through the same platform, or need enterprise support and SLAs that come with the Premier tier. The cost premium buys operational maturity that smaller platforms have not built yet.

Choose Amazon SES if your backend already lives on AWS, you are comfortable configuring IAM policies and DNS records by hand, and you are sending high enough volume that the price gap between $0.10 and $0.35-plus per 1,000 emails actually shows up on a monthly invoice. Budget extra setup time for sandbox approval and expect to build your own dashboard and template tooling on top of the raw API.

The Verdict

None of the three platforms wins outright, and the data backs that up. At 100,000 emails a month, Amazon SES’s a la carte rate of $10 beats Resend’s $35 and SendGrid’s $34.95 by more than 3x, but that number ignores the engineering time SES requires to build the template, dashboard, and sandbox-approval tooling the other two ship out of the box. Resend wins on integration speed for anything built on React or Next.js, cutting a send-email workflow down to a single SDK call with no SMTP configuration. SendGrid wins on feature depth for any team managing multiple sending identities or blending marketing and transactional email in one platform.

For most new projects starting in late 2026, the practical default is to start on Resend’s free tier for speed, move to Amazon SES once volume and AWS infrastructure maturity justify the setup cost, and reach for SendGrid specifically when subuser management or enterprise support becomes a hard requirement rather than a nice-to-have.

Run the numbers on a mid-size SaaS product sending 200,000 emails a month, a common threshold where teams start reevaluating their original choice. On Resend Scale, that volume lands around $160 a month at the $0.80-per-1,000 overage band. On SendGrid, it falls between the Essentials and Pro tiers, likely pushing a team onto Pro at roughly $90-130 a month once the dedicated IP is factored in. On Amazon SES Essentials, the same 200,000 emails cost $32, and on the legacy a la carte rate, just $20. That gap, $140 a month between Resend and SES a la carte at identical volume, is exactly the threshold where engineering time spent building SES’s missing dashboard and template layer starts to pay for itself, particularly for a team that already has AWS expertise in house and does not need to hire for it.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which is cheaper, Resend or Amazon SES?

Amazon SES is cheaper on raw per-email cost, charging $0.10 per 1,000 emails on the legacy a la carte rate compared to Resend’s effective $0.35-0.40 per 1,000 on the Pro tier. SES requires more setup work and does not include a template editor or dashboard, which Resend bundles into its price.

Does Amazon SES still have a free tier in 2026?

Not for new accounts. As of July 21, 2026, AWS closed the historical 62,000 free emails a month allowance to new customers, and all new SES accounts start on the paid Essentials plan. Existing accounts that were active before that date may retain legacy access depending on their account history.

Can I use React Email templates with SendGrid or Amazon SES?

Not natively. Neither SendGrid nor SES ships built-in support for React Email the way Resend does. Teams can still render React Email components to HTML manually and pass the output through SendGrid’s or SES’s send API, but that requires building a custom render step that Resend provides out of the box.

What is the SendGrid Email Activity API rate limit in 2026?

Since December 9, 2025, the Email Activity API is limited to 6 requests per minute, down from the previous limit of 30 requests per five-minute window. This applies to querying activity and analytics data, not to sending emails, but it affects any dashboard or monitoring tool that polls SendGrid frequently.

Is Resend suitable for high-volume marketing email?

Resend can handle marketing sends and offers plans up to roughly 2.5 million emails a month, but it was designed primarily as a transactional and developer-focused email API. Teams running large marketing campaigns alongside transactional traffic often find SendGrid’s subuser system and dedicated marketing tooling a better fit at scale.

How do I migrate from SendGrid to Resend without breaking deliverability?

Add Resend’s SPF and DKIM records alongside your existing SendGrid records, verify the domain, then shift a small percentage of low-risk traffic first while monitoring bounce and complaint rates for 48 to 72 hours before migrating remaining email categories over one to two weeks.

Does Amazon SES support dedicated IPs?

Yes. SES offers standard dedicated IPs at $24.95 a month each, or a managed dedicated IP option at $15 a month plus $0.08 per 1,000 emails sent, which includes automated IP warm-up handled by AWS.

What happens if I exceed Resend’s free-tier limits?

Resend’s free tier caps out at 3,000 emails a month with a 100-emails-per-day limit. Sends beyond that cap fail until you upgrade to the Pro plan at $20 a month, which raises the allowance to 50,000 emails and removes the daily cap entirely.

proofCandidates.title: Giving Your AI Agent an Email Address Is Now a Real Product Category
proofCandidates.summary: AgentMail raised $6 million in seed funding in March 2026, led by General Catalyst, to provide AI agents with durable inboxes. The company has delivered over 100 million emails and serves more than 500 B2B customers. The article contrasts this with existing email APIs like Postmark, Resend, and AWS SES for agent email needs.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Sending email from an AI agent is easy now. Giving that agent a durable inbox, a thread history, and a way to act on replies is where the real product fight has started.

Ask an AI agent to send a confirmation email and almost any provider can handle it in a few lines of code. Ask it to wait for the reply, pull a verification code from that message, and keep the same thread straight three hours later. The list gets shorter. That gap between sending and receiving is the whole story.

The clearest signal is AgentMail. The San Francisco startup raised $6 million in seed funding in March 2026, led by General Catalyst, according to TechCrunch. Y Combinator, Phosphor Capital, Paul Graham, HubSpot CTO Dharmesh Shah, Supabase CEO Paul Copplestone, and Ramp CTO Karim Atiyeh all put money in. The company came out of YC's Summer 2025 batch. It was founded by Haakam Aujla, Michael Kim, and Adi Singh. That is a real cap table for a product category most teams barely had a name for a year ago.

AgentMail gives each agent a real inbox through one API call. Not just a send-only endpoint, an inbox. The company says it has delivered more than 100 million emails, and TechCrunch reported that it had more than 500 B2B customers by the time of the seed round. Its newer Pods feature groups multi-tenant inboxes behind scoped API keys and custom domains, so a product with thousands of customer agents doesn't have to build tenant isolation by hand.

The older email APIs still matter

Most agents don't need their own mailbox. Plenty just need to send a receipt, a login link, or a password reset, and the established transactional players still do that better than anyone new. That's their whole job.

Postmark starts at $15 a month for 10,000 emails, while its free developer tier is capped at 100 emails a month. The important catch is inbound email. Postmark's current pricing page puts inbound processing on the Pro plan, which starts at $16.50 a month for the same 10,000-message volume. That small price difference matters if your agent has to receive a reply instead of only sending a note.

Resend is the fast-integration option. Its free tier covers 3,000 emails a month, and $20 a month buys 50,000 transactional emails. Resend's own docs say inbound messages arrive through the email.received webhook event, with the full body and attachments fetched through its Receiving API. Light plumbing, but still plumbing.

Mailgun and Twilio's SendGrid sit a level up in scale and complexity. Mailgun's validation API checks syntax, DNS, mailbox signals, disposable addresses, and role-based addresses before a sender burns reputation on bad mail. Its MCP server exposes more than 50 operations across sending, stored messages, domains, analytics, templates, suppressions, webhooks, routes, mailing lists, IPs, and tracking. That's real depth. SendGrid replaced its old free plan with a 60-day trial in 2025, and Twilio's current pricing page says Essentials starts at $19.95 a month. It remains a familiar choice when the job is mostly outbound volume rather than agent-owned inboxes.

Cheap infrastructure has its own price

There's always a catch. Amazon SES is still the low-cost anchor under this market, but you have to read the small print. AWS lists outbound email at $0.10 per 1,000 messages, and managed dedicated IPs start with a $15 monthly account fee plus usage charges. The old 62,000-message free tier tied to AWS compute was replaced in 2023, and AWS said in July 2026 that new SES accounts now begin on an Essentials plan, with new AWS customers using free-tier credits rather than the old SES-specific 3,000-message allowance.

Then there is the sandbox. AWS documentation says new SES accounts can send only to verified addresses and domains while in the sandbox, with a cap of 200 messages per 24 hours and one message per second. Getting production access means asking AWS to lift those limits. That's fine for a mature product with a queue to spare. It's a bad fit for an agent that needs to send its first real email today.

Mailtrap belongs in this conversation for a different reason: testing. Its MCP server lets tools such as Cursor, VS Code, and Claude Desktop work with email workflows, including sandbox testing and transactional sends. Its Email API plan starts at $15 a month for 10,000 emails, but the more useful point is the sandbox. A developer can inspect what an agent actually sent before it ever reaches a real inbox. Frankly, that is where many agent email systems should start.

The actual decision

Here's the decision most teams are actually facing. If your agent only sends, Resend or Postmark will get you moving quickly. SES can cut the unit cost once volume is real, if you can live with AWS setup and account limits. That's the tradeoff. If your agent needs to have a conversation, wait on a reply, or manage a mailbox on behalf of a customer, that's a different product entirely. Send and receive are not the same problem. It is why a company built around the inbox rather than the send button could raise $6 million, and why the rest of the email API market is suddenly talking to agents instead of only developers.

proofCandidates.title: Top Transactional Email Tools to Improve Deliverability
proofCandidates.summary: The article reviews various transactional email tools, detailing their features, strengths, and ideal use cases. It compares SendGrid, Mailgun, Postmark, Amazon SES, SparkPost, Brevo, Resend, SMTP2GO, and other platforms based on deliverability, control, ease of use, and technical requirements.
proofCandidates.fullText:
We independently review every app we recommend We independently review every app we recommend

SendGrid Visit Website From my testing and market experience, SendGrid remains one of the safest starting points for teams that want a broadly adopted transactional email platform with mature infrastructure. It’s especially appealing if you need a mix of SMTP relay, email APIs, templates, event webhooks, and scalable sending controls without stitching together multiple tools. What stood out to me is how well SendGrid handles the core operational layer: reputation management, deliverability tooling, IP options, suppression lists, and event visibility. For teams sending receipts, login links, alerts, or lifecycle product emails, it gives you enough depth to scale without immediately outgrowing it. It also has a large ecosystem, which makes integration with apps, backend systems, and third-party workflows fairly straightforward. Where you’ll want to evaluate fit carefully is usability versus complexity. SendGrid can do a lot, but once your setup gets more advanced — dedicated IP warmup, deliverability tuning, segmentation between traffic types — it starts to feel like a tool built for teams that are willing to manage email operations actively. If your team wants a more opinionated, transactional-first experience, some alternatives feel cleaner. Best for: teams that want a proven platform with broad integration support and room to scale. Mailgun Visit Website Mailgun has long been a favorite for developer-led teams, and that still makes sense. If your engineers want flexible email infrastructure with strong APIs, routing options, validation tools, and solid logs, Mailgun is easy to take seriously. I like it most for teams that think of email as part of product infrastructure rather than just another communication channel. One thing Mailgun does well is giving technical teams granular control. You can work through SMTP or API, set up inbound routing in some workflows, manage sending domains cleanly, and connect delivery events back into your app stack. For SaaS platforms that send account notifications, verification emails, and workflow-triggered product messages, that flexibility is genuinely useful. The tradeoff is that Mailgun feels best when there’s some technical ownership on your side. Non-technical teams can use it, but the product shines more in environments where developers are configuring and monitoring the system. If your priority is a polished business-user experience over technical control, you may prefer a simpler UI-first option. Postmark Visit Website If your top priority is transactional deliverability and speed, Postmark is one of the strongest tools in this category. What I like most is its clear product philosophy: it’s built for critical product emails, not as a general-purpose bulk marketing platform trying to do everything at once. That focus shows up in the experience. Postmark is especially compelling for password resets, OTPs, account alerts, onboarding messages, and receipts — the kinds of emails where delays or spam-folder placement create immediate support issues. The platform is known for fast delivery and strong inbox placement practices, and I find its interface refreshingly straightforward compared with more sprawling competitors. The main fit consideration is breadth. Postmark is excellent at transactional email, but if your team wants one vendor for extensive marketing automation, broad CRM-style campaign tooling, and transactional traffic under the same roof, you may end up pairing it with something else. For product-led teams, though, that focus is often a strength rather than a weakness. Best for: product teams that care most about reliable transactional inbox placement. Amazon SES Visit Website Amazon SES is the option I’d put in front of teams where cost efficiency at scale matters a lot and there’s enough technical capability to manage the setup properly. On raw sending economics, SES is hard to ignore. If you send high volumes of transactional email and already work inside AWS, it can be an especially logical choice. What you get is powerful infrastructure, flexible API/SMTP access, and the ability to build exactly the email pipeline you want. That’s a big advantage for engineering teams comfortable with AWS services, custom monitoring, and sender reputation management. In the right hands, SES can be extremely effective. But I wouldn’t call it the easiest tool on this list. Compared with more opinionated transactional email platforms, SES asks more from you around setup, monitoring, and operational ownership. If your team wants white-glove deliverability guidance or a more polished out-of-the-box workflow, other tools will feel faster to adopt. proofCandidates.title: Lenders Cooperative Integrates Moov to Embed Modern Payments Across Its Unified Lending Platform
proofCandidates.summary: Lenders Cooperative integrated Moov's modern payments ledger into its unified lending platform, embedding money movement into origination and servicing workflows. The integration lets banks and credit unions offer borrower repayment via ACH, card, or instant payment without touching their core. It is part of LC's strategy to embed third-party services inside one platform.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Lenders Cooperative Integrates Moov to Embed Modern Payments Across Its Unified Lending Platform DVLT +5.19% QBTS -0.21% HIMS +5.01% MA +1.21% IBRX +5.36% By GlobeNewswire an hour ago Updated ARLINGTON, Va., Oct. 20, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Lenders Cooperative (LC), a leading provider of commercial lending technology and services, today announced the integration of Moov, the modern payments ledger infrastructure, into its unified lending platform. The integration embeds money movement directly into the origination and servicing workflows, giving banks and credit unions faster, more flexible options for borrower repayment, and real-time visibility into every dollar that moves. Most lenders still originate in one system, service in another, and move money through the core or a separate payments vendor, with reconciliation happening in spreadsheets between them. Embedding a ledger and money movement into a unified origination and servicing workflow means funding, repayment, fee collection and remittance all post to the same record the loan lives in. “The banks and credit unions we predominantly serve in the $10B to $200B range often run batch-oriented cores that weren’t built for real-time rails, programmable disbursements, complex reconciliations, or for borrower self-service payments on commercial loans,” said Christopher McClinton, President & Chief Revenue Officer of Lenders Cooperative. “By embedding Moov, LC can give our lenders modern money movement options without touching their core.” The Moov integration marks the latest step in a deliberate strategy for LC: embed best-in-class third-party services inside one platform, so lenders and their borrowers get a better experience at every step of the loan life cycle, without adding another system, another login, or another vendor to manage. Where the platform's open finance integrations bring verified borrower financial data into the credit decision, Moov moves the money that follows it. “People should be able to pay and get paid however they want, and borrowers are no exception. A business owner should be able to receive loan funds the moment they're approved and repay by ACH, card, or instant payment on their own schedule. Lenders Cooperative is putting that choice directly inside the lending workflow, so institutions can compete on choice," said Wade Arnold, Co-Founder and CEO of Moov. The integration further strengthens Lenders Cooperative's position as a single platform that automates and manages the complete loan life cycle. Combined with the company's in-house Lender Service Provider (LSP) team, lenders gain both the technology and the talent to scale lending with greater speed, efficiency, and confidence. Financial institutions can learn more or request a demonstration at https://lenderscooperative.com/request-a-demo/. About Lenders Cooperative Lenders Cooperative is the provider of the leading platform in the market that automates and manages the complete loan life cycle from application intake to origination to servicing. Its customers have ready access to outsourced Lender Service Provider (LSP) support for credit underwriting, closing, loan operations, and more—empowering financial institutions to scale lending operations with greater speed, efficiency, and confidence. About Moov Moov is a cloud-native payment platform that enables businesses to accept, store, send, and spend money through a single API. Built on a high-precision ledger with real-time data streaming, Moov offers full payment orchestration with complete traceability and observability. As a licensed processor with direct connections to Visa®, Mastercard®, American Express®, Discover®, The Clearing House RTP®, and Fedline Direct®, Moov removes intermediaries while delivering enterprise-grade accuracy and real-time business intelligence. Media Contact If you have any questions about Lenders Cooperative or would like to schedule an interview, please contact media@lenderscooperative.com. proofCandidates.title: Moov adds P2P competition
proofCandidates.summary: Moov Financial partnered with Mastercard and Visa to launch a peer-to-peer payment service, Moov Money, that lets users send money via debit card and mobile phone without both parties needing the same app. The service integrates with Jack Henry's platform, available at about 1,000 banks and credit unions, and Moov has raised about $125 million in funding.
proofCandidates.fullText:
An article from Dive Brief Moov adds P2P competition Using Mastercard and Visa’s digital infrastructure, the tool facilitates peer-to-peer payments without requiring both parties to have the same app. Creative Getty Images

First published on Dive Brief: Moov Financial, the payment processor, has partnered with Mastercard and Visa to launch a peer-to-peer payment system, the company said in a Tuesday press release

The tool lets users send and receive money using an eligible debit card and a mobile phone. With the service, users can send money to others without both parties needing to use the same app, the release said, pointing to that as a differentiator vis-a-vis Block’s Cash App wallet, PayPal’s Venmo tool and the Zelle service from Early Warning Services.

“Cash App and Venmo built great experiences, and Zelle built reach inside banks,” Moov’s CEO, Wade Arnold, said in an email by way of a spokesperson for the company . “All three ask people to join their network while putting their own brand at the center of someone’s financial life.” By contrast, Moov’s new service is in an app users already have through their bank or credit union, he said. Dive Insight: Moov’s new payment service, called Moov Money, integrates its technology with that of Mastercard and Visa to send payments using the recipient’s phone number, other contact information or another payment credential. From there, the tool automatically populates the recipient’s card information, putting an end the need to manually enter card numbers, the release said. Denver-based Moov has built the tool on top of Jack Henry’s digital platform, enabling the P2P service to be available at some 1,000 banks and credit unions, the company’s spokesperson confirmed in an email. “Consumers get the experience they expect from Cash App, with more reach than any closed network,” Arnold contended. “For a decade, P2P has pulled customers out of their bank’s app. Moov Money brings them back.” Moov’s P2P service rollout follows years of fundraising efforts. In 2020, the company raised $5.5 million in seed funding from Bain Capital Ventures and other investors. A few years later, the company brought in another $27 million in venture capital funding from Bain, Andreessen Horowitz and Visa, among other investors. The company has raised about $125 million to date, the spokesperson said. Add us on Google

proofCandidates.title: Moov launches P2P Payments for financial institutions
proofCandidates.summary: Moov Financial launched Moov Money, a real-time P2P payments solution built on Visa Direct and Mastercard Move, enabling consumers to send and receive funds through existing digital banking apps. The platform targets the fragmented US P2P market, where no single provider reaches over 34.6% of consumers, and is available to banks, credit unions, neobanks, and brokerages.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Moov launches P2P Payments for financial institutions

By Divya Shah

Today Digital Banking

Digital Payments

Financial Institutions Share LinkedIn Email WhatsApp

US-based payments platform Moov Financial has launched Moov Money, a real-time person-to-person (P2P) payments solution built on Visa Direct and Mastercard Move, enabling consumers to send and receive funds through their existing digital banking applications.

The platform allows users to transfer money using an eligible Visa or Mastercard debit card and a verified mobile phone connection, eliminating the need for manual card number entry in many cases.

The solution is designed to address the fragmentation of the US P2P payments market by enabling payments to be delivered directly to accounts linked to eligible debit cards across card networks. The company said no single P2P provider currently reaches more than 34.6% of US consumers.

Moov Money combines Mastercard Move and Visa Direct infrastructure with Moov’s payments technology layer, which connects recipients’ mobile numbers, contacts, or payment credentials to payment destinations.

The platform also supports tokenised card credentials through Mastercard Credential Services and leading mobile wallets.

Wade Arnold, CEO of Moov, said the solution broadens access to digital money movement by enabling anyone with a debit card to send and receive payments securely.

He added that the combination of Visa and Mastercard’s reach with Moov’s payments infrastructure aims to simplify and enhance the user experience.

The platform incorporates identity verification, fraud controls, dispute management, passkey authentication, device intelligence, network-level card validation, real-time monitoring, and AI-powered fraud detection tools designed to reduce scams and fraud losses.

Moov said it will also manage disputes, fraud monitoring, and first-line customer support for participating institutions, helping reduce operational costs and resource requirements.

The solution is available to banks, credit unions, neobanks, and brokerages for domestic P2P payments and can be integrated directly into existing digital banking platforms.

Additionally, Jack Henry has integrated Moov Money into its Banno Digital Platform, enabling financial institutions to offer branded real-time P2P payment capabilities to their customers.

proofCandidates.fullText:
Moov has announced Moov Money, a real-time, person-to-person (P2P) payment solution.

Created in collaboration with Visa and Mastercard, Moov Money lets consumers send and receive funds through their digital banking provider with just an eligible debit card and a trusted mobile phone connection, the company announced Tuesday (Sept. 22). “Unlike other P2P services that depend on both parties participating in the same app or solution, Moov Money uses the debit card as the payment destination,” Moov said in a news release. The company cites data from the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta showing that 90.5% of American consumers carry a debit card, which gives participating financial institutions broad reach without requiring recipients to download apps or set up new accounts. The same Fed research also found that no one P2P provider reaches more than 34.6% of U.S. consumers today. Moov says its tool is designed to bridge various apps and solutions by delivering payments to the account associated with eligible Mastercard or Visa debit cards. Add as Preferred Source “Moving money shouldn’t depend on whether two people use the same app,” said Wade Arnold, CEO of Moov. “Moov Money breaks these restraints, enabling anyone with a debit card to securely pay and get paid. Combining the wide reach of Visa and Mastercard with Moov’s modern payments infrastructure, sophisticated fraud controls and intuitive user experience, we’re making it possible for financial institutions of any size to facilitate a better, easier money movement experience.” In related news, recent PYMNTS Intelligence research shows that debit cards have become a “daily financial control panel for many Generation Z consumers,” which in turn offers banks a new way to compete for loyalty. The PYMNTS Intelligence tracker “The Incremental Imperative: Why Debit Innovation Is the New Standard for Cardholder Loyalty,” a collaboration with FIS Global Payments, found that debit is important among young consumers who use it to keep on top of essential and discretionary spending. And 42% of these consumers used debit at the grocery store, versus 19% who used credit and 6% who used Apple Pay. “However, these consumers are also bringing different expectations to the relationship,” PYMNTS wrote in August. “Gen Z wants direct access to its money along with speed, visibility and control throughout the payment experience. For issuers, that creates an opportunity to make debit more useful through a series of practical improvements rather than a wholesale redesign.”

proofCandidates.title: Moov launches small- bank P2P alternative to Zelle
proofCandidates.summary: Moov Financial launched Moov Money, a peer-to-peer payment service using existing debit card accounts, with Jack Henry as an early adopter. The service aims to compete with Zelle, Cash App, and Venmo, citing that 90.5% of U.S. consumers carry a debit card while no P2P app reaches 34.6%.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Key insight : Moov launched a P2P service, using existing debit card accounts in an effort to make it easier to use than an app.

: Moov launched a P2P service, using existing debit card accounts in an effort to make it easier to use than an app. What's at stake : The P2P market is dominated by Zelle, Cash App and Venmo, though Moov contends there is space for adoption among small banks and credit unions.

: The P2P market is dominated by Zelle, Cash App and Venmo, though Moov contends there is space for adoption among small banks and credit unions. Forward look: Moov's early adopters include Jack Henry, and it will work to attract other partners in the coming weeks. While P2P payment apps like Venmo, Cash App and Zelle have existed for years, the fintech Moov Financial argues there's still room for another service, especially if it involves a payment device that most people already use.

Called Moov Money, it uses Jack Henry's Banno digital platform, Visa and Mastercard to enable banks and credit unions to support transfers via existing debit card accounts and a mobile phone connection. To argue there is a market for an additional P2P app, Moov Financial cited research from the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta that reports 90.5% of U.S. consumers carry a debit card, while no P2P app reaches more than 34.6% of U.S. consumers. Processing Content "A sender doesn't have to ask about an app download. If you have a debit card, we can send you money," Wade Arnold, CEO of Moov, told American Banker, adding that moving money "shouldn't depend on whether two people use the same app."

Moov's pieces Moov Money uses two card network real-time rails, Mastercard Move and Visa Direct, with Moov's technology connecting the card networks to Moov's P2P feature. This includes connectivity for a recipient's phone number, contact or payment credential. This information populates the payment destination and removes a need to enter card information. Moov also supports identity verification, fraud controls and dispute management — combining phone-based identity verification, network-level card verification, passkey authentication, monitoring and AI-supported fraud detection. For Mastercard and Visa, Moov Money contributes to a need to expand sources of payment volume — in this case using existing debit cards as another means for parties to send money to one another. "This is about enabling P2P without leaving the primary bank experience," Mike Kresse, executive vice president of commercial and new payments flows for Mastercard, North America, told American Banker. "Why should consumers have to understand the underlying nuances behind P2P? Moov Money is a simple, clear service." In a release, Justin Zhao, head of Visa Direct for North America, said, "Through our work with Moov, financial institutions can now use trusted Visa credentials and infrastructure to help consumers send and receive money with greater confidence and ease." Moov Money's initial users include Jack Henry's Banno Digital Platform, which gives the bank technology vendor an added feature to expand its client relationships. "[We have] a continued appreciation for Jack Henry's differentiated level of service, innovation, and execution within bank tech. Over the years, this strategy has driven success with clients and accordingly, strong financial results," William Blair said in a research note on Jack Henry.

The alternatives Jack Henry's clients include a large number of community banks and credit unions, making Moov Money a potential selling point for Jack Henry as it seeks to add smaller institutions, given large banks' role in managing Zelle. Jack Henry is also linked to Chuck , an early attempt at a community bank-focused P2P app that launched in 2021. Payrailz was among the initial developers of Chuck in 2022. Jack Henry later acquired Payrailz and folded Chuck into the acquired company. There is no connection between Moov Money and Chuck, according to Jack Henry. Given the headstart and brand recognition of the existing apps, payment experts say Moov Money will be challenged to build adoption. Most consumers already have Zelle, Cash app and/or Venmo; the need for an additional P2P solution doesn't seem to be that compelling, especially given the lack of economics associated with the transactions, according to Tony DeSanctis, a vice president at Cornerstone Advisors. "Similar to other P2P solutions, the challenge continues to be consumer adoption. While debit cards are broadly accepted, getting consumers to load their debit card into yet another solution could prove to be challenging," DeSanctis told American Banker. Zelle has made moves in the past year to expand its support among smaller financial institutions, and more than 95% of Zelle's members are community banks. "Not everyone has Zelle, and yes, our customers are concerned that Zelle is a large bank product," Jack Henry Chief Technology Officer Ben Metz told American Banker. "We support Zelle and always will but our customers have wanted an alternative for a very long time." Zelle has direct integration across more than 2,300 banks and credit unions, which cover over 80% of U.S. deposit accounts. In 2025, Zelle processed more than $1.2 trillion across 4.2 billion transactions, averaging $3.4 billion per day, with small-business volume accounting for roughly $400 billion. The PayPal-operated Venmo reported approximately $330 billion in total payment volume for 2025. Block has used its Cash App transfer service as a connective tissue for retail payments, small-business tools via Square, and buy now/pay later through Afterpay. Cash App offers debit cards, short-term credit, direct deposits, stock trading and support for cryptocurrency. Moov is offering Move Money to banks, credit unions, neobanks and brokerages for domestic person-to-person payments. Financial institutions enable Moov Money through existing digital banking experience or integrate directly with Moov. "I can see why Moov would be attractive to community banks and credit unions who are reluctant to sign up for Zelle," Aaron McPherson, principal at AFM Consulting, told American Banker, adding the real hurdle is getting financial institutions to turn it on. "While 90.5% is obviously more than 34.6%, that gap is where financial institutions are not promoting this type of service, or consumers are not adopting it, or preferring other solutions like Venmo, more than some sort of inherent limitation."

Stablecoins, AI & Payment APIs: The Crypto Integration Trend to Watch in 2026 Share:

Cryptocurrency is moving beyond simple buying, selling, and holding of digital assets. In 2026, the bigger shift is happening through integrations. Stablecoins, artificial intelligence, blockchain networks, and payment APIs are increasingly being connected to create faster and more automated ways to move value. Stablecoins Are Becoming Payment Infrastructure Stablecoins are gaining attention because they combine blockchain-based transfers with a value designed to remain relatively stable against a reference asset such as the U.S. dollar. Their role is expanding from crypto trading into payments, settlements, payouts, and digital commerce. A recent example is the Coinbase and Moov integration, which brings stablecoin payment acceptance, settlement, and real-time funding into payment infrastructure serving more than 1,000 community banks and credit unions in the U.S. The integration uses Coinbase's Payments API and custodial wallet infrastructure within Moov's existing platform. This type of integration shows how stablecoins can become part of existing financial infrastructure rather than operating as a separate crypto-only system. AI Agents Are Entering the Payment Loop AI is creating another major change. Traditionally, software could request information from an API, but payment usually required a person, account, subscription, or separate checkout process. New payment standards are exploring a different model. The x402 protocol, for example, allows an API to respond with an HTTP 402 payment requirement. An AI agent can interpret the payment instructions, make an on-chain payment, and continue the API request after settlement. Cardano's implementation supports this model and connects it with its blockchain and digital assets. This opens the door to machine-to-machine transactions where an AI agent could potentially pay for data, computing resources, digital services, or other API-based resources automatically. Payment APIs Are Connecting Crypto With Existing Systems Payment APIs are becoming an important bridge between blockchain infrastructure and conventional digital payment experiences. Instead of requiring businesses to create an entire crypto payment stack from scratch, APIs can provide access to wallets, settlement, payment processing, and blockchain transactions. This is also influencing Stablecoin Development , where the focus is expanding beyond simply creating a digital currency. Modern solutions can involve wallet infrastructure, payment APIs, merchant settlement, compliance considerations, transaction automation, and integration with existing financial platforms. The Bigger Shift: From Crypto Assets to Crypto Infrastructure The interesting part of this trend is not any single technology. It is the way different technologies are beginning to work together. AI + APIs + Stablecoins + Blockchain = programmable digital payments. As these integrations mature, cryptocurrency can become less dependent on standalone crypto applications and more connected to AI services, financial platforms, digital commerce, and automated software ecosystems. Conclusion The crypto landscape in 2026 is increasingly being shaped by integration rather than isolation. Stablecoins are moving toward payment and settlement infrastructure, AI agents are exploring autonomous transactions, and payment APIs are connecting blockchain capabilities with existing financial systems. For businesses exploring this changing landscape, Osiz, a Cryptocurrency Development Company , works across blockchain and digital-asset solutions, including areas such as Stablecoin Development, crypto payment solutions, wallets, and blockchain-based platforms. The broader trend points toward a future where cryptocurrency becomes an integrated layer within increasingly automated digital ecosystems.

Coinbase and Moov have entered a partnership that integrates stablecoin infrastructure into Moov's existing payments platform, giving community banks and credit unions access to digital asset capabilities without requiring them to build separate crypto technology stacks. Moov currently provides payments infrastructure, including card acquiring, issuing, and real-time payment rail connectivity, to more than 1.000 community banks and credit unions across the US.
Integration built on existing infrastructure
Under the partnership, Moov is embedding Coinbase's stablecoin payments infrastructure directly into its platform. The integration uses Coinbase Developer Platform's (CDP) Custodial Wallet accounts for fund custody and its Payments API to orchestrate stablecoin movement. For business and merchant-related payments, Moov will use Coinbase's fully disclosed custodial accounts.

Addressing a gap in merchant access
Wade Arnold, Co-Founder and CEO, Moov, said that business customers of community institutions are already being asked to accept stablecoins, and currently source that capability outside their primary financial institution. The partnership is intended to let community banks offer that service directly. The companies also pointed to further potential in real-time funding capabilities that would not be constrained by weekend or holiday settlement cycles.
Citizens Bank of Edmond, a US-based institution founded 125 years ago, was cited as an example of a community bank exploring the partnership. Jill Castilla, Chairman, President, & CEO, Citizens Bank, noted that its small business customers are seeking ways to lower interchange costs and receive payments faster.
Positioning community banks within digital asset infrastructure
Coinbase and Moov framed the partnership within a broader industry discussion about the role of community financial institutions as digital assets become integrated into mainstream payment systems. Community banks and credit unions collectively serve millions of consumers and businesses and play a role in local lending. As stablecoin regulation develops, the companies suggested these institutions should be positioned to participate in the resulting market rather than remaining reliant on external providers.
Acceptance, settlement, and real-time funding represent the initial phase of the partnership. Community banks urged to embrace stablecoins and digital payments for survival

Smaller lenders face a choice: adapt to digital money or watch customers walk toward bigger banks that already have.

by Editorial Team 2 hours ago

America’s community banks are not losing sleep over whether to mint their own stablecoin. They are losing sleep over something more mundane: keeping customers who increasingly expect their bank to work as smoothly as their phone. A Better Markets report from April 2025 found that banks with less than $10 billion in assets collectively held roughly $2.5 trillion, a number that had barely budged over thirty years. Meanwhile, the biggest banks compounded their advantages through better technology, faster payments, and treasury services that smaller rivals simply could not match. The stablecoin question community banks are actually asking Issuing a stablecoin requires regulatory scaffolding, capital allocation, and technical infrastructure that most community banks cannot justify building from scratch. Supporting digital payments, on the other hand, is increasingly something they can buy off the shelf. That is exactly what Coinbase and payment infrastructure firm Moov are betting on. The two companies announced a partnership to embed stablecoin payment solutions through Coinbase’s Payments API, targeting more than 1,000 community banks and credit unions. The arrangement covers real-time payments, merchant acceptance, and settlement, letting banks plug into the infrastructure without owning it. At the American Bankers Association’s community bankers conference in February 2026, the recurring advice from industry participants was disciplined: figure out your internal payment needs first, then think about customer-facing products. Stablecoins for domestic and cross-border payments kept appearing as the practical entry point, not the exotic endpoint. An industry-owned alternative is taking shape In August 2026, a coalition of 39 state banking associations launched the BankChain Alliance, a push to build an industry-owned blockchain framework focused on tokenized deposits and programmable payments. The target launch for a working network is 2027. Research cited from Charles River Associates during 2025 and 2026 found no significant correlation between stablecoin adoption and deposit outflows from community banks under realistic scenarios. The more persistent drain is simpler: customers moving to larger banks with better apps. What the competitive math actually looks like The passage of stablecoin legislation in 2025 gave institutions clearer guidance on what digital dollar instruments they could interact with and under what conditions, removing some of the compliance ambiguity that had made even exploratory conversations difficult.
